un-ga-res-a-69-20:
The question of Palestine returns, as it does each year, in Resolution A/69/20, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the long chain: partition in 1947, the refugee vote of 1948, and the rights votes of 1974 and 1975. It had read the yearly report of the Palestinian rights committee. The joint recognition of 1993, between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, is recalled as well.

Full heed of the deals struck by the two sides is demanded. The Assembly backs a full, just, and lasting peace for the conflict. Its terms rest on past UN votes and on the frame of the Madrid talks of 1991, with the rule of land for peace at their heart.
un-ga-res-50-220:
Guatemala's human rights mission had its mandate stretched in Resolution 50/220, passed in April 1996. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994 to check that both sides kept their pledges. A September 1995 vote had stretched its term by six months, to 18 March 1996. The Assembly now had the mission chief's third and fourth reports before it.

Those reports weigh how the state of Guatemala and the rebel URNG kept their word under the rights deal. Their findings and counsel are taken note of in full. The vote keeps the mission in place as talks moved toward the firm peace signed at the end of 1996.

un-sc-res-1820:
Resolution 1820, adopted in June 2008, named sexual violence in war as a threat to world peace itself. Reports from Congo and other conflicts described rape used as a weapon against whole communities. The Council moved the issue from the margins to its main agenda.

The text demands that armies and armed groups stop all such attacks, orders peace missions to protect women and girls, and presses for soldiers who commit these crimes to face punishment. It built on Resolution 1325's earlier promises with harder language. Advocates still cite it as the turning point in how the UN treats wartime rape.

plos-pone-0000020:
John Drake, Suok Kai Chew, and Stefan Ma looked back at the 2003 SARS outbreak in Singapore for a 2006 study of how societies learn during an epidemic. SARS, a new and deadly lung disease, hit the city hard. Officials responded with quarantines, screening, and strict hospital controls, adjusting as they went.

The authors call that adjustment societal learning: a population and its institutions changing behavior fast enough to bend the outbreak's curve. They weighed how effective the interventions were as learning took hold. The lesson outlived SARS. Later epidemics, including COVID-19, replayed the same pattern of early confusion, rapid learning, and hard choices about control measures.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d20: T. V. Soong, China's Minister of Foreign Affairs, wrote to Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, on June 21, 1943. The message is Document 20 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hopkins was Roosevelt's closest aide, and foreign envoys often worked through him. The catalog's title carries no date; its older note supplies June 21. No topic is recorded, so the note's errand must be read in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d120: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 12, 1943, and a second Stalin letter of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 120 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters in a day from Moscow, as the president sailed, suggests urgent or divided business, though the record names no topic for either. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d220:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington from Ankara on 14 November 1943, in telegram 1871, sent an hour after his previous report that day. It carries one hopeful signal from the Soviet ambassador in Ankara, Sergey Vinogradov, about Turkey's fears of Russia.

Vinogradov had told Foreign Minister Numan that if Turkey's worry was only about excessive Soviet demands in the Balkans, and not a general mistrust, a fair settlement should be easy to find. Numan answered that if Ankara could be sure Russia held no ambitions in the Balkans, the two countries could resume the cordial, close friendship they had shared for many years. The cable was repeated to Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d320:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408/1 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, answering the American proposal for a supreme commander over all operations against Germany. After careful study, they state at once that on military grounds they profoundly disagree.

Total war, they argue, is not a military affair alone. Nearly every big problem carries political, economic, and domestic weight. The commander would have to consult both governments on almost everything. He would become an extra link deciding only minor matters. The Foch parallel from the last war fails, since Foch never held so many fronts. They also attack the clause letting the Combined Chiefs reverse his orders, warning of troops marching on orders later countermanded in confusion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d420:
John Jernegan, third secretary of the American embassy in Iran, wrote to Major John Henry at Tehran on 3 December 1943. Henry was General Hurley's aide. The letter sets down the main facts behind the Declaration on Iran, signed two days before, as far as Jernegan's knowledge ran. It is the fullest inside account of how that document came to be.

Prime Minister Soheily asked Eden and Dreyfus on 29 November for a joint statement covering Iran's help in the war, the treaty pledges of independence, and her economic needs. Hurley won British agreement, and Dreyfus supplied the draft, shortened from Jernegan's own. The Soviets hung back until Roosevelt made a strong personal request of Stalin on 1 December and Stalin consented. That night the draft was accepted with small changes, signed at the final session's end, and shown to Foreign Minister Saed, who initialed a copy and agreed to hold its release.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d520:
President Roosevelt wrote to Brendan Bracken, Britain's Minister of Information, on December 18, 1943. Bracken was one of Churchill's closest friends and ran Britain's wartime information and propaganda effort. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A letter from an American president to a British cabinet minister outside the usual chain shows the personal web that bound the two governments. arxiv-2606-05920: Real users give vague instructions and change their minds — the opposite of benchmark prompts. Asuka-Bench tests code agents on underspecified user intent with multi-round refinement: clarifying, trying, and iterating like real development. The benchmark measures the conversational competence benchmarks usually ignore.
arxiv-2606-06320: Making a language model unlearn something — a copyrighted book, private data — is harder than it sounds. This paper improves unlearning by learning what to forget: token-level importance scores guiding the erasure. Targeted forgetting removes the knowledge without lobotomizing the model.
arxiv-2606-06920: Fine-tuning small models on math can backfire — negative transfer where training hurts. This paper evaluates that fine-tuning trap in sub-1B models and the role of PEFT methods. The findings warn that more training is not always better. Small models need gentle handling.
arxiv-2606-07320: The Klein-Gordon equation with an alpha-attractor potential — from inflationary cosmology — resists closed-form solution. This paper proves it has no Liouvillian solution, not even as a composition. The proof sets a hard limit on analytic cosmology. Analytic cosmology hits a hard wall here. Numerical methods must take over where symbols fail.
tob-10020:
William Walker Atkinson, a New Thought writer, published under the pen name Yogi Ramacharaka for books on Eastern-style spiritual teaching. In Mystic Christianity he turns that lens on Jesus, reading the Master's life and sayings as an inner teaching rather than mainly a matter of church doctrine. The work first appeared in the early 1900s.

Miracles and parables become lessons about the growth of the soul. Atkinson blends ideas from Eastern and Western religion into one system, arguing that hidden meaning lies beneath familiar Gospel stories. Readers get an early American attempt to join Christian devotion to a wider, comparative spirituality popular in his period.
tob-10220:
Bertrand Russell published The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers. He begins with a familiar object: the table in front of us. How do we know it is real, and what exactly do we know when we look at it or touch it?

From appearance and reality, Russell moves through matter, knowledge by acquaintance and description, universals, and truth and falsehood. He is candid that philosophy often raises questions it cannot finally settle. Readers get a clear demonstration of why the big questions matter anyway, and a model of thinking slowly and precisely about things common sense takes for granted.
tob-10920:
Albert Pike published Morals and Dogma in 1871 as lectures on the thirty-two degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. Each degree receives a chapter drawing morals from ancient symbols, comparative religion, and philosophy. The volume is massive, dense, and endlessly digressive by design.

Pike ranges from Egyptian and Greek mysteries to Kabbalah and medieval chivalry, reading Masonic ritual as a school of ethics and toleration. Few members have read it whole, yet it remains the most famous and most misunderstood book in American Masonry, quoted and misquoted by admirers and conspiracy writers alike. Patient readers find a nineteenth-century moral philosophy in ritual dress.
tob-4020:
John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding opens, in volume one, with an attack on innate ideas in Book One. Book Two builds his alternative: the mind begins as a blank slate, and all knowledge flows from sensation and reflection. Ideas, simple and complex, are tracked to their sources in experience.

Substance, identity, power, and association all receive patient analysis in Locke's plain, methodical prose. The two books lay the foundation of British empiricism and quietly declare thought's independence from scholastic authority. For readers tracing how modern philosophy and liberal politics share a root, Locke's first volume, modest in tone and radical in effect, is essential ground.
tob-0020:
Legends of Jesus as a child fill the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a work the early church never took into its canon. The boy forms sparrows from river clay and breathes them alive before startled playmates. His powers amaze the village, and sometimes they frighten it.

The child's temper proves as miraculous as his gifts: those who cross him wither or fall. Teachers fare no better against his strange knowledge. The stories are vivid, unruly, and very human in their curiosity about a holy childhood. The evidence notes no public-domain text is attached to this entry yet. The tales survive because believers loved them.
tob-0120:
Few forgeries have done more harm than the Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion. The text claims to record a Jewish plan for world domination. In fact it was fabricated in the orbit of the Tsar's secret police, the Okhrana, stitched together from older satire and fiction.

Newspapers and courts exposed the fraud within two decades of its spread, yet the lie kept traveling. It fed pogroms, Nazi propaganda, and hate movements that still quote it. This library keeps the text as evidence: a case study in how a fake document can poison a century. It is presented as a debunked forgery, never as fact.
tob-4120:
John Parker's 1897 translation gathers the works credited to Dionysius the Areopagite, a writer of about the fifth or sixth century who took the name of Paul's Athenian convert. The Celestial Hierarchy ranks the angels in nine orders. The Divine Names weighs what names like Good and Being can say of God.

The Mystical Theology, shortest and boldest, says God lies beyond all names, in darkness beyond light. No writer did more to shape Christian mysticism, East and West, for a thousand years. Checked from the 1919 edition, Parker's volume gives the fountainhead in full Victorian dress.
govdocs-archive_org-Report-President-Sur:
On April 24, 2015, U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara's office in New York sent a short cover letter connected to a major disclosure. The letter transmitted a three-volume report on the President's Surveillance Program, released in a Freedom of Information case brought by the New York Times.

The file holds the letter alone, not the report that followed it. Even so, it marks the formal moment when records about warrantless government surveillance moved from secret files toward the public record. Such letters show the paperwork behind disclosure: who sent the material, when, and under what legal pressure it left the government's hands.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
America's war in Afghanistan lasted twenty years, from the autumn of 2001 to the summer of 2021. Afghanistan 20/20 tells that war through twenty documents. One briefing book page gathers the records that mark its main turning points.

Twenty well-chosen papers can carry a long war: the first decisions after September 11, the turn to Iraq, the surge, the peace talks, and the final exit. The format suits readers who want the primary record without reading a whole shelf of reports. Each document stands for a phase of the war. Together they show how a short mission became the longest war in American history.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-20:
The twentieth and last volume of Michael L. Rodkinson's set completes his History of the Talmud. Volume nineteen told the story through the Mishnah and the Babylonian schools. This second history volume carries the tale into print, persecution, and the modern age.

Rodkinson follows the Talmud through its first printings, the burnings ordered against it, and the censors who cut its pages. He weighs the great commentators, above all Rashi, whose notes made the text readable. The volume closes his twenty-book labor, the first full English Talmud ever made. It is both a history and the translator's own defense of his work.
lindsay-voyage-to-arcturus-1920:
David Lindsay sent a bold soul to a far world in A Voyage to Arcturus, his strange novel of 1920. The world is Tormance, lit by a bright star. Each land holds a new creed. Each creed reshapes the flesh and mind of those who pass through.

The trek reads as a quest for truth through pain and change. Few tales are so odd or so stern. C. S. Lewis and J. R. R. Tolkien both felt its pull. It stays a cult peak of deep thought in tale form. Maskull, the bold guest from earth, bears fresh organs and creeds in each land. Each change strips a lie from his view of life and self.
merritt-metal-monster-1920:
A city of live metal waits in high hills in Abraham Merritt's novel The Metal Monster, from 1920. Men on a trek find cubes, spheres, and shapes that move as one mind. The shapes can form beasts, walls, and vast forms at will.

Awe turns to fear as the mind in the metal wakes. Merritt writes in lush, bright prose full of strange sights. The book is pulp awe at its peak. Its weird life form feels fresh and vast a full age later. Ruth, a brave guest on the trek, stands as the heart of the tale. Her nerve steadies the men when awe turns to blind fear.
belzoni-narrative-operations-1820:
Giovanni Battista Belzoni told of feats no tale smith would dare invent in his Narrative of 1820. Belzoni was a strong man from Italy who showed feats in fairs ere he dug in Egypt. There he hauled a vast head to a ship, broke into a heap at Giza, and found the bright tomb of Seti the First.

Each feat is told in plain, bold prose. He had foes, funds ran low, yet he pushed on. His finds fill great halls in London to this day. The book is the first great tale of the dig.
budge-hieroglyphic-dictionary-vol-1-1920:
E. A. Wallis Budge gave learners their key to the script in Vol. 1 of An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary, out in 1920. Budge had kept Egypt's hoard in London for years. Each sign word here gets its sounds, its forms, and its sense in English. The tome runs through the first great span of the word hoard.

Two crops of learners cut their teeth on Budge's lists. Sages now fault some of his sounds and senses. Yet for its age the work was a boon no fan could skip. This tome opens the pair.
budge-hieroglyphic-dictionary-vol-2-1920:
E. A. Wallis Budge caps his word work in Vol. 2 of An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary, out in 1920. The first tome gave the words in script form. This tome gives the key from the flip side. An English word list points fans to the script terms they need. Lists of kings and place names from the Nile world stand here too.

Such lists sound dry, yet they are the tools of the trade. A fan with a name could find its age and kin here. The pair served learners for years. This tome ends it.
schrenck-notzing-phenomena-materialisati:
Albert von Schrenck-Notzing put seers in a lab in Phenomena of Materialisation, his report of 1920. Schrenck-Notzing was a healer in Munich with a zeal for strict tests. His seers wore sewn suits, sat in lit cages, and were held by the hands. Yet, he claims, a strange stuff crept from them and took shapes like limbs and veils.

He calls the stuff ectoplasm and prints plates by the score. Peers cried fraud in case past case. His book is the high mark of that strange line of tests. Its claims still row.
desaguliers-remarks-perpetual-motion-172:
John Theophilus Desaguliers was the Royal Society's chief man for trials of new machines. In 1720 he wrote this paper for the Philosophical Transactions, the Society's own journal. His theme was the wheels that men said would turn for ever. The claim was old, but fresh wheels still came to the Society each year with bold words.

Desaguliers took the best known wheels of his day and tested their claims by maths and by trial. He showed that loss and drag must stop each one in the end. The paper gave the learned world's first firm no to the whole quest, in print.
seaborn-symzonia-1820:
Captain Adam Seaborn is the pen name on this sea tale of 1820, the first novel of the hollow earth. No one knows for sure who wrote it, though Symmes and his kin are oft named. The tale takes Symmes's polar holes as its map and sails straight in.

The ship's crew pass through the north hole and find a mild inner world, named Symzonia. Its folk are fair, wise, and strange, with crafts and laws of their own. The book set the form for a long line of tales of worlds hid inside our own.
gardner-journey-earths-interior-1920:
Marshall B. Gardner gave the hollow earth claim its fullest 20th century form in this book of 1920. It is a revised and much grown version of his first work on the theme. Gardner was a keen lay reader of polar tales and reports.

He holds that a vast warm sea and land lie inside the earth, reached by polar holes. He points to mammoths found in ice and to gaps in the tales of Cook and Peary at the pole. His book is the last great brief for the scheme, writ with full zeal.
dubois-wadjak-1920:
Eugene Dubois, the Dutch army doctor who found Java man, issued this second memoir on the Wadjak skulls in Dutch in 1920. The skulls came from a cave at Wadjak in Java, dug in 1888 and 1890. Dubois kept them back from the world for some thirty years.

He calls the Wadjak folk proto-Australian, a first form of the race of Australia. In his scheme, Java links the ape man he found at Trinil to the men of Australia. The late show of the skulls fed his long feud with the learned world of his day.
goenner-rothschild-lotterie-anlehen-1820:
Nikolaus Thaddaus Gonner, a Munich law scholar, wrote this study of a Rothschild loan in German in 1820. Its theme is the lottery loan of 20,800,000 gulden run with the banker Parish. The loan was one of the young house's first great state deals in the south German lands.

Gonner sets out the terms of the loan and the law that bears on each part of it. He writes as a lawyer of the time, for men who held or might hold a share. The dry work is a true first hand record of how the house did its state work.
boccaccio-decameron-florio-1620:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron in plague-time Italy, and John Florio gave it to England in 1620. Florio's was the first English version of the famed tale set. Ten young people flee Florence and pass ten days telling tales.

Their one hundred tales mix love, wit, trickery, and sharp turns of luck. Merchants, priests, wives, and fools all get caught in clever plots. Some tales praise quick minds, and some mock greed and lust. Florio's rich prose helped shape how English writers told short tales. Boccaccio set the frame tale form for centuries of writers.
defoe-memoirs-of-a-cavalier-1720:
Daniel Defoe published Memoirs of a Cavalier in 1720, a military memoir in a found-manuscript frame. The tale covers the Thirty Years' War and the English Civil War in one soldier's life. Many call it the founding historical novel in English, decades before Scott made the form famous.

The Cavalier, a Shropshire squire's son, fights under Gustavus Adolphus in Germany as a young volunteer. Home again, he serves Charles I at Edgehill, Marston Moor, and Naseby in the royal cause. Battles are told with a plain soldier's eye for ground, error, and sheer chance in war. He blames the king's counselors more than the king, and mourns a ruined cause with restraint. Defoe's fake memoir fooled some readers into treating it as a true record.
defoe-captain-singleton-1720:
Daniel Defoe published Captain Singleton in 1720, his pirate novel of Africa and the high seas. The tale gives a crossing of Africa and a pirate republic in the Indian Ocean world. It is a source-text of pirate literature, before Stevenson gave the genre its classic form in English.

Bob Singleton, stolen as a child, goes to sea and is marooned on Madagascar by mutineers. He and his mates trek across Africa, a route no English novel had mapped before in fiction. Rich and restless, he turns pirate, raiding in the Indian Ocean with Quaker gunner William beside him. William's calm counsel steers Bob toward repentance and a quiet, wealthy end in England at last. Defoe mixes geography, trade lore, and moral debate in one restless adventure yarn.
lawrence-women-in-love-1920:
D. H. Lawrence published Women in Love in 1920, his intense, visionary novel of modern relationships in England. The tale sets Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen with two very different men in the mining Midlands of wartime. It is the sequel, in spirit and in Ursula's story, to The Rainbow.

Ursula weds the school inspector Rupert Birkin, Lawrence's spokesman for a new, balanced union of equals. Gudrun takes up with Gerald Crich, the mine owner, in a bond of fascination, cruelty, and mutual ruin. Wrestling, dancing, a drowned sister, and a rabbit's scratch mark the couples' opposed paths toward love or death in snow. Gerald dies in the Alps at the close, while Birkin mourns both wife and friend in unresolved grief. The novel's psychology of power and desire still startles readers a century on.
wharton-age-of-innocence-1920:
Edith Wharton published The Age of Innocence in 1920, her novel of 1870s New York and its rigid codes. The tale tells Newland Archer's doomed love for the Countess Olenska inside that shuttered, tribal world. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, the first awarded to a woman for a novel in America.

Archer, engaged to May Welland, is shaken by her cousin Ellen, returned from a scandalous marriage in Europe alone. Ellen's freedom exposes the cruelty and fear beneath his tribe's polished manners, dinners, and opera boxes in old New York. Archer chooses duty, weds May, and lives a respectable life haunted by the road not taken with Ellen. Decades later, in Paris, he sits below her window and sends his son up alone at dusk. Wharton's archaeology of her parents' world is tender, ironic, and quietly devastating in its close.
oneill-emperor-jones-1920:
Eugene O'Neill published The Emperor Jones in 1920, his breakthrough play of a Pullman porter's rise and flight. A Black Pullman porter turned Caribbean emperor flees through the jungle, stripped of power by drums and ghosts. The play made O'Neill's name and brought expressionist method to the American stage.

Brutus Jones, who fled a chain gang to rule an island by fraud and a silver bullet, faces revolt. Through eight scenes of forest darkness he sheds his uniform, his boasts, and his mind to ancestral visions. The drums quicken like a heartbeat while Jones fires his revolver at ghosts and at last at himself in mind. Pursuers find him at dawn, killed by the silver bullet he had reserved for his own end in the forest. The play's power and its racial burdens are still argued wherever it is staged.
lewis-main-street-1920:
Sinclair Lewis published Main Street in 1920, a novel about a young woman in a small Minnesota town. Carol Kennicott arrives in Gopher Prairie as a bride full of plans. She wants art, reform, and a finer life for the town. The town resists her at every step with gossip and smug habit.

Carol tries clubs, plays, and new buildings, and mostly fails. Her marriage to the kind but dull Dr. Kennicott strains under the fight. Lewis mocks small-town pride yet shows real affection for its people. The novel was a huge bestseller and sparked debate nationwide. It gave American speech a lasting name for dull conformity.
nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-1920:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote The Antichrist in 1888, near the end of his sane life. The English text here is H. L. Mencken's translation of 1920. Nietzsche attacks Christianity as a religion of pity and denial of life. He contrasts it with what he sees as noble, life-affirming values.

He re-reads the New Testament as a story of decline from Jesus to Paul and the church. The book is brief, harsh, and deliberately provocative. It states his revaluation of all values in its sharpest form. Mencken's version made it widely read in America. Readers still argue over its force and its fairness.
whitehead-concept-nature-1920:
Alfred North Whitehead published The Concept of Nature in 1920, based on his Tarner Lectures at Cambridge. Whitehead asks what we mean by nature in modern science. He argues that nature is a process of events, not a set of static objects. Sense awareness, he says, shows passage and relation first of all.

He rejects the split between nature as sensed and nature as cause of sense. Points, moments, and objects are abstractions from the flow of events. The book laid groundwork for his later process philosophy. It also influenced modern philosophy of science. Readers meet Whitehead's key ideas here in compact form.
alexander-space-time-deity-vol-1-1920:
Samuel Alexander published Space, Time, and Deity, Volume 1, in 1920, from his Gifford Lectures. Alexander builds a metaphysics on the idea of emergent evolution. Space-time itself is the basic stuff of the universe. From it emerge matter, life, and mind, each a new level with new qualities.

Deity, in his striking phrase, is the universe's nisus, its drive toward a higher level not yet reached. This volume treats space-time, categories, and matter in detail. Alexander writes as a naturalist who still finds room for religion. The lectures drew wide attention in Britain and America. They remain a key work of emergent thought.
alexander-space-time-deity-vol-2-1920:
Samuel Alexander completed Space, Time, and Deity with Volume 2 in 1920. This volume rises through life and mind to value and deity. Mind emerges from living bodies, and values emerge with mind. Truth, goodness, and beauty are treated as features of the world, not mere feelings.

Alexander argues that the universe strains toward deity as its next emergent level. God, in this scheme, is both ideal and growing with the world. The view influenced Whitehead and later process thinkers. The style is systematic yet often vivid. Together the volumes state emergent evolution as a full metaphysics. They are a high point of British philosophy after the war.
eddington-space-time-gravitation-1920:
Arthur Eddington published Space, Time and Gravitation in 1920, the first clear English account of Einstein's general relativity. Eddington had led the 1919 eclipse expedition that tested Einstein's prediction. Starlight bending near the sun matched the theory, and Eddington became its chief English champion. The book explains curved space-time without heavy mathematics.

He uses diagrams, analogies, and careful prose to guide lay readers. Chapters cover the principle of relativity, gravitation as geometry, and the tests of the theory. The book brought Einstein to the English-speaking public. It remains a model of science writing: exact, humane, and clear. Historians still cite its role in relativity's triumph.
bury-idea-progress-1920:
J. B. Bury published The Idea of Progress in 1920, a history of the idea of progress itself. Bury, a noted historian of Rome and Byzantium, asks when humans first believed their future would improve. He traces the notion from faint Greek hints through Bacon, Descartes, and the Enlightenment. The idea, he argues, is modern, not ancient.

Thinkers such as Fontenelle, Turgot, Condorcet, and Comte receive clear chapters. Bury ends by asking whether progress is a faith that evidence can support. The book founded the study of progress as a topic in its own right. Its calm, exact style suits its theme. It remains the classic meta-history of a ruling modern idea.
tawney-acquisitive-society-1920:
R. H. Tawney published The Acquisitive Society in 1920, a classic of ethical socialism. Tawney argues that modern society honors acquisition over function. Property that serves no work, he claims, has weak moral title. Rights should attach to service rendered, not to mere ownership.

He calls for industry organized as a profession, with standards and public purpose. The book grew from his wartime and postwar lectures and essays. Its prose is lucid, grave, and quietly angry. Tawney influenced the Labour Party's moral outlook for a generation. Later editions kept it in print for students. It remains a model of social criticism grounded in ethics rather than envy.
turner-frontier-american-history-1920:
Frederick Jackson Turner first set out his famous frontier thesis in an essay read to fellow historians in Chicago in 1893. His 1920 book gathers that essay with later papers on the same theme. Turner argued that free land on the western edge of settlement shaped American life more than any law or leader.

He claimed the frontier bred self-reliance, fresh starts, and a rough form of equal standing among settlers. He also warned that the census of 1890 had declared the frontier line closed, so a first great chapter of national life had ended. Few ideas have guided American history writing so long, or drawn so much debate.
lowie-primitive-society-1920:
Robert Lowie, another student of Boas, published Primitive Society in 1920 as a broad survey of how early peoples organize their lives. He drew on reports from North America, Africa, and the Pacific islands. The book became a standard college text in anthropology.

Lowie explains kinship, marriage, property, rank, and the rise of the state without ranking peoples on a ladder of progress. He argues that customs grow by borrowing and chance as much as by design. His clear, skeptical voice helped free the field from grand schemes of human progress. He writes with respect for the peoples described and little patience for easy theories.
pigou-economics-welfare-1920:
Arthur Pigou taught economics at Cambridge and shaped the study of how markets affect public welfare. His 1920 book The Economics of Welfare asks when private bargains help society and when they harm it. It became the founding text of welfare economics.

Pigou shows how a factory can gain while its smoke quietly costs neighbors their health and clean air. Such side costs, later called externalities, justify a tax that makes the polluter pay the full price. The Pigouvian tax still bears his name in debates on carbon, traffic, and public health. He weighs gains and losses across a whole society, not a single firm.
lidzbarski-mandaische-liturgien-1920:
Lidzbarski followed his Book of John with Mandaische Liturgien in 1920, a German translation of Mandaean ritual texts. These are the prayers and directions used at baptism and at the mass for the dead. The Mandaeans are often called the last living Gnostic sect.

The liturgies name the rivers of light, the watchers at the soul's ascent, and the words spoken over the water. Priests still use versions of these rites in Iraq and in exile communities abroad. For scholars, the volume preserves the working prayer book of a faith that survived two thousand years. The texts are given with the care of a scholar who knew the rites were still alive.
houdini-miracle-mongers-1920:
Harry Houdini, the famed escape artist, published Miracle Mongers and Their Methods in 1920. Houdini knew stage tricks from the inside, and he turned that knowledge on performers who claimed real marvels. Fire eaters, sword swallowers, and fake holy men all came under his eye.

Houdini explained how such acts were done, from swallowing swords to handling fire and poison without harm. He drew on old books, posters, and his own talks with performers. His subjects came from across Europe and America. The result is both a history of stage marvels and a sharp lesson. It shows how easily skill presented as magic can fool a crowd.
suppressed-gospels-vol-2-1820:
Volume 2 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in this edition in 1820. The volume centers on the Protevangelion, an early account of the birth and youth of Mary. Wake, an archbishop of Canterbury, had translated early Christian writings outside the New Testament.

The Protevangelion tells of Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple, and the birth of Jesus with added wonders. Such texts shaped art and folk belief for centuries, though churches left them out of scripture. Reading them shows what early Christians wanted to know about the holy family's hidden years. The volume belongs to a nine-volume set of these disputed writings.
suppressed-gospels-vol-3-1820:
Volume 3 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in 1820. Its main text is the Infancy of Jesus Christ, an early gospel about the childhood of Jesus. The canonical gospels say almost nothing about those years, and this text filled the gap with wonders.

Stories show the child Jesus giving life to clay birds, striking playmates, and working miracles in Egypt. Medieval readers loved these tales, and they fed plays, poems, and paintings. Church leaders judged the book unreliable and left it outside scripture. The volume preserves a vivid record of how popular faith pictured the young Jesus.
suppressed-gospels-vol-4-1820:
Volume 4 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named text is the Gospel of Nicodemus, an early account of the trial, death, and descent of Christ. Nicodemus appears in John's gospel as a secret follower who came to Jesus by night.

The text expands Pilate's court, the wonders at the crucifixion, and Christ's descent to free the dead. A second part tells of Joseph of Arimathea and his imprisonment and release. Medieval drama drew heavily on these scenes. The volume shows how early and medieval Christians enlarged the Passion story far beyond the four gospels in their Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-5-1820:
Volume 5 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The set gathered early Christian writings that stood outside the New Testament. Wake, archbishop of Canterbury, had made these translations to let readers judge the texts for themselves.

Writings in this middle volume continue the set's mix of gospels, acts, and letters linked to apostles and early teachers. Some claim missing details of Christ's life, while others teach or warn the young churches. Scholars value the set for showing the wide range of early Christian writing. General readers get stories and teachings that nearly entered scripture but did not.
suppressed-gospels-vol-6-1820:
Volume 6 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named figure is Clement, an early leader of the church in Rome. Writings linked to Clement were among the most respected texts outside the New Testament.

Letters and teachings in the volume deal with order in the church, good conduct, and the duties of bishops and members. Clement's name carried weight because tradition placed him close to the apostles themselves. Readers can see how the early church settled questions of authority and morals. The volume helps explain why some texts were treasured for centuries even though they never became part of the Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-7-1820:
Volume 7 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The nine-volume set reprinted Wake's translations of early Christian writings left outside the New Testament. By this volume the set has moved deep into letters and acts linked to the first generations of the church.

Texts here preserve teachings, travels, and trials ascribed to apostles and their followers, with much added legend. Some passages agree with scripture, while others add marvels the churches rejected. The set lets readers compare accepted and disputed writings side by side. That contrast is the value of the volume: it shows the border of the Bible being drawn in real time.
suppressed-gospels-vol-8-1820:
Volume 8 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820, near the end of the nine-volume set. Wake's project gave English readers the early Christian writings that churches had read, debated, and finally set aside. Volume 8 continues that disputed library.

Gospels, acts, and letters in the volume claim apostolic roots, yet carry stories and teachings found nowhere in scripture. Some fed medieval devotion, art, and feast days for a thousand years. Others survive only in fragments and old lists. Together they show how much early Christian writing the canon left behind, and why scholars still mine these texts for the beliefs of the first churches.
stoddard-rising-tide-color-1920:
Lothrop Stoddard published The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy in 1920. Stoddard, a Harvard-trained writer, surveyed the world after the First World War and warned his white readers that their global rule was ending. The book's title gave its whole argument in one image.

Stoddard treated the growth and revolt of colonized peoples in Asia and Africa as a single threat to white supremacy. He urged unity among white nations and strict immigration bars at home. The book sold widely and shaped restrictionist debate in the United States. Scholars cite it as a key primary source on white-supremacist ideology and the fears behind immigration restriction.
beaumont-fletcher-philaster-1620:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher wrote Philaster together for the King's Men, the leading acting company in London. The play mixes romance and danger in the style called tragicomedy. It was first printed in 1620 and stayed popular on stage for decades.

Prince Philaster has lost his rightful throne to a usurping king. He loves the king's daughter, while a false friend spreads lies about her honor. A cross-dressed page named Bellario adds confusion and pathos to the love plot. Wounds, trials, and last-minute pardons bring the story to a tense, happy close that early audiences clearly loved.
clare-poems-descriptive-1820:
John Clare was a farm laborer from Northamptonshire who wrote poems about the fields where he worked. A London publisher brought out his first book in 1820. Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery made the so-called peasant poet briefly famous.

Clare describes birds, nests, flowers, and farm work with a closeness few poets match. He names local places and uses the speech of his village without apology. London readers were struck by how exact his nature writing was. The book began a short, bright career that later sank into poverty and asylum years, but the poems kept their freshness.
eliot-poems-1920:
T. S. Eliot published Poems in 1920, gathering the short works that had first made his name in London and America. He was then working at a bank and editing a literary journal. The slim volume is the complete set of his early poems in book form.

The poems are cool, witty portraits of modern city people. Prufrock worries through a drawing-room evening, and Portrait of a Lady watches another social visit go thin and sad. Short satires mock hollow manners with clipped, musical lines. Readers in 1920 met a new kind of poetry here: ironic, learned, and quietly bleak about modern life.
galsworthy-in-chancery-1920:
John Galsworthy continued his Forsyte family saga with In Chancery, published in 1920. The novel follows The Man of Property and the short piece Indian Summer of a Forsyte. Galsworthy tracked the rich, possessive Forsytes across decades of English change.

Soames Forsyte, divorced from Irene, wants an heir and pursues the young Annette Lamont. Irene, meanwhile, finds late love with Soames's cousin Jolyon, now head of the family's other branch. Old bitterness poisons every new happiness, and the war years hang over the younger generation. Galsworthy shows a proud family slowly learning that money cannot settle matters of the heart.
keats-poems-1820:
John Keats published his third and last book of poems in 1820, less than a year before his death at twenty-five. The volume holds the great odes and story poems on which his fame now rests. Publishers issued it while Keats was already ill with tuberculosis.

The odes to a nightingale and on a Grecian urn ask how art and beauty survive death. Lamia tells of a serpent woman in rich, glittering verse. Isabella adapts Boccaccio, and The Eve of St. Agnes glows with color and romance. La Belle Dame sans Merci adds a chilling ballad. Few single volumes in English hold so much lasting poetry.
mansfield-bliss-1920:
Katherine Mansfield, a New Zealand writer living in England, published Bliss and Other Stories in 1920. It was her second collection and the book that fixed her reputation. Mansfield wrote with a rare gift for the revealing moment, the small scene that changes everything.

The title story follows a happy wife whose perfect day cracks at a dinner party. Other stories visit a widow's memories, a child's first ball, and the cold routines of office life. Mansfield wastes nothing: a glance, a pear tree, a shaft of light carries the meaning. The collection helped define the modern short story in English.
shelley-prometheus-unbound-1820:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Prometheus Unbound in Italy and published it in 1820. He took the Greek Titan Prometheus, chained by Zeus for giving fire to mankind, as his hero. Greek legend left Prometheus bound forever; Shelley set out to free him.

In Shelley's lyrical drama, Prometheus endures centuries of torture without cursing his enemy. When hatred finally leaves his heart, the tyrant Jupiter falls and a new age of love begins. Spirits, Earth, and the Moon sing the change in soaring choruses. The play is less a stage work than a vision of human liberation. It stands as the purest statement of Romantic optimism.
sandburg-smoke-and-steel-1920:
Carl Sandburg published Smoke and Steel in 1920, his third book of poems. Sandburg, the son of Swedish immigrants, had worked as a laborer, soldier, and Chicago newspaper reporter. He wrote about the industrial Midwest from inside knowledge of its mills and rail yards.

The poems honor furnaces, freight trains, and the workers who tend them. Sandburg's long free-verse lines stack images of smoke, pig iron, and prairie wheat. He also remembers war dead and praises ordinary people's endurance. The book carries forward the work of his Chicago Poems with a wider national sweep. It remains the great book of American industry in verse.
millay-few-figs-1920:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published A Few Figs from Thistles in 1920, a slim book that made her the voice of young America. Millay was living in Greenwich Village, poor, brilliant, and famous among the bohemians. The title comes from a biblical phrase about gathering figs from thistles.

The poems are short, bright, and defiant. First Fig gives the era its motto: my candle burns at both ends. Millay writes about lovers taken lightly and freedom guarded fiercely, in strict forms handled with a wink. Older critics scolded the book's flippancy while young readers memorized it. A Few Figs from Thistles captures the flaming youth of the Jazz Age in verse.
pound-hugh-selwyn-mauberley-1920:
Ezra Pound published Hugh Selwyn Mauberley in 1920, just after the First World War wrecked the London literary world he had conquered. The work is a sequence of eighteen short poems. Pound later treated it as a farewell to that world before he left England for Paris and Italy.

The sequence sketches Mauberley, a fastidious minor poet out of step with his age, and the age itself. War dead, profiteers, and faded aesthetes pass in cool, ironic quatrains. Pound mourns a civilization that chose commerce over art, in verse of lapidary control. Mauberley is his masterpiece of the postwar reckoning and one of the central poems of modernism.
fitzgerald-flappers-and-philosophers-192:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published Flappers and Philosophers in 1920, riding the instant success of his first novel. The eight stories had mostly run in The Saturday Evening Post, which paid him handsomely. Together they form the flapper canon in its first collected form.

Bernice Bobs Her Hair turns a dull cousin's visit into a small war of popularity, ending with scissors. The Offshore Pirate sails a rich girl into a staged romance that turns real. Other tales cover icy debutantes, headstrong boys, and young people testing every rule their parents kept. Fitzgerald's dialogue sparkles, but regret already shadows the fun. The book defined the Jazz Age heroine for America.
fitzgerald-this-side-of-paradise-1920:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published This Side of Paradise in 1920, when he was twenty-three and fresh out of the army. The novel grew from his Princeton years and his courtship of Zelda Sayre. It sold out its first printing in days and made him the spokesman of his generation.

Amory Blaine, handsome and self-absorbed, drifts through prep school, Princeton, and the war, falling in and out of love and ambition. The book mixes prose, verse, and play script with youthful confidence. Amory ends poorer, sadder, and beginning to understand himself. Fitzgerald named a generation's restlessness here and invented the Jazz Age novel in the process.
anderson-poor-white-1920:
Sherwood Anderson published Poor White in 1920, the year after Winesburg, Ohio made his name. Anderson set the novel in Bidwell, Ohio, a farming town about to be remade by factories. He drew on the Midwest he had traveled as a paint salesman and advertising writer.

Hugh McVey, a dreamy telegraph operator raised in poverty, teaches himself to invent farm machines. His corn-picker and other devices bring factories, money, and strangers flooding into Bidwell. The town grows rich and frantic while Hugh, the cause of it all, feels the human price mounting. Anderson treats the industrial revolution as a spiritual event, not just an economic one. Poor White is his fullest novel of that change.
chekhov-chorus-girl-1920:
The Chorus Girl and Other Stories, in Constance Garnett's 1920 translation, gathers some of Chekhov's earlier successes. In the title story a chorus girl named Pasha is accused by a wronged wife of stealing her husband's gifts. Pasha, who received almost nothing, gives up her own small treasures to end the scene.

Verotchka tells of a young official who fails to answer a girl's honest confession of love. The failure haunts him on his walk home through the summer night. These stories are shorter and lighter than the late tales, yet the sting is already there. They show the young Chekhov learning to say much in few pages.
hoffmann-tomcat-murr-1820:
Hoffmann's last novel, The Life and Opinions of the Tomcat Murr, appeared in German in 1820 and after. No English translation from the time survives in public domain, so the text here is the German original. Murr, a literate tomcat, writes his memoirs on scrap paper meant for a life of Kapellmeister Kreisler.

By a printer's error, the two lives come out mixed, page by page. The cat's smug tales of love and learning mock the earnest artist's sorrows below. Kreisler's story, in fragments, gives the pain behind the joke. Hoffmann built the first collage novel of modern times out of that mix. It is funny, sad, and far ahead of its age.
lie-family-at-gilje-eastman-1920:
Samuel Coffin Eastman translated Jonas Lie's The Family at Gilje into English in 1920 for the Scandinavian Classics series. Lie set his novel on a Norwegian captain's farm in the 1840s. Captain Jaeger, his capable wife, and their children face straitened means with pride and invention.

The daughters' prospects, the sons' schooling, and one long-remembered ball fill the household year. Lie writes domestic life with humor, tenderness, and a seaman's eye for weather. The novel became Norway's beloved picture of its own recent past. Eastman's version served the American-Scandinavian Foundation's aim of carrying such classics west. Few family novels of the North are read with warmer feeling.
lalla-vakyani-grierson-barnett-1920:
Lal Ded, called Lalla, wandered Kashmir in the fourteenth century singing short sayings, vakhs, on the soul and God. George Grierson and Lionel Barnett edited and translated the Lalla-Vakyani for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1920. Their edition gives the Kashmiri text with translation, notes, and full tools for study.

Lalla, a Shaivite yogini, sings of the body as a worn cloth, of breath, of the name of Shiva, and of the self lost and found. Hindus and Muslims of Kashmir both claim her songs to this day. The editors add notes on yoga, on her language and meters, and a concordance and vocabulary. The book is the scholarly base for all work on her.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-3-:
Edward G. Browne devoted the third volume of his Literary History of Persia, from 1920, to the Tartar Dominion, the years 1265 to 1502. The Mongol storm had wrecked the land, yet Persian letters rose again under the Ilkhans and Timur. Browne ends his tale with Jami, the last master of the classical age. The main text here is complete; the index is missing from the scan.

Hafez sings in these centuries, and the historians Rashid al-Din and Juvayni write the Mongols into Persian memory. Browne weighs court poetry, history, and Sufi verse with his usual sympathy. His extracts let the poets speak in English dress. The volume bridges the classical world and the modern one.
einstein-relativity-lawson-1920:
Albert Einstein wrote Relativity himself to explain his theories to general readers. Robert W. Lawson's English translation appeared in 1920. The book covers both the special theory and the general theory in plain stages. Einstein uses trains, clocks, and falling lifts as his teaching tools.

Readers learn why moving clocks run slow and why gravity bends the path of light. Einstein builds each step on simple cases before the math grows harder. No popular book on the subject carries more weight, since the founder wrote it. It carried relativity to the wider world. The clear voice surprises many first time readers.
wallas-human-nature-politics-1920:
Graham Wallas founded political psychology with Human Nature in Politics, first issued in 1908. The text here is the third edition of 1920, from Project Gutenberg. Older political thought pictured voters as reasoning machines, weighing each claim. Wallas, a Fabian socialist and teacher, found that picture false to life.

Impulse, habit, party symbols, and crowd feeling move real politics, he argues. Statesmen work with human nature as it is, not as theory wishes. His chapters urge honest study of how opinions actually form. The book opened a field that now studies campaigns and media. Its calm tone hides its radical break. Politicians ignore it at their cost.
malthus-principles-political-economy-182:
T. R. Malthus published his Principles of Political Economy in 1820 as a reply to Ricardo's school. The two men were friends and rivals in the young science of economics. Malthus doubts that supply always creates its own demand, the claim tied to Say's Law. Spending can fail, and goods can glut the market unsold.

His stress on effective demand, the will and means to buy, shapes the book. Landlords, workers, and savers each get weighed for their role in demand. Keynes later praised Malthus as the truer guide on slumps. The treatise is the great anti Ricardian work of its age. Its questions returned in the Great Depression.
spr-proceedings-vol30-1919-1920:
Volume thirty binds parts seventy five through seventy eight and an appendix, for 1919 and 1920. Peace returns, and the Society for Psychical Research counts its losses and its files. The postwar sittings with mediums draw crowds of the bereaved. Cross references and proxy sitters guard the reports as before.

Telepathy experiments resume their peacetime forms and scoring. Apparition cases from the war years receive their checked write ups. The volume bridges the archive from war into a new decade. Its records fed the famous postwar books on survival. Volume thirty closes the society's first forty years in print. The debate it serves ran on to 1930.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol20:
With Volume XX in 1880, the Journal of Discourses entered its fourth decade of printed sermons. Liverpool still printed the set, and shorthand reporters still caught the words as they were spoken in Utah. Speakers include senior apostles and other elders, preaching to a church now led from the Twelve after Young's death.

Two decades of volumes behind it give this one a settled, archival feel for any reader. The talks instruct, correct, and encourage in the familiar pulpit voice of the movement at work. Volume XX adds a round number to the running doctrinal record of nineteenth-century Mormonism, with six volumes yet to come.
maier-septimana-philosophica-1620:
Solomon and the Queen of Sheba trade riddles across a philosophical week in Maier's Septimana philosophica of 1620. The Latin work frames golden enigmas on every kind of nature as the royal pair's answers to each other. Alchemy, natural philosophy, and emblematic wisdom meet in the dialogue, question by question.

Maier, physician and Rosicrucian apologist, loved the riddle form, since it lets truth wear a mask. Each day of the week brings its theme, and each answer opens a small treatise in disguise. Readers meet here the playful, learned face of early modern alchemy, where a game between monarchs carries a whole view of nature.
diaries-court-ladies-omori-doi-1920:
Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi translated Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan in 1920, the first English version of three Heian classics. The Sarashina Nikki, the Murasaki Shikibu Nikki, and the Izumi Shikibu Nikki speak in women's own voices from about a thousand years ago. Pilgrimages, poems, loves, and court service fill their intimate pages.

Heian Japan prized the diary as high art, and these three show why. Murasaki, author of the Genji, watches her court with a novelist's eye even in private notes. The translations opened a whole literature of Japanese women's writing to the English world.
mariner-an-account-of-the-natives-of-the:
William Mariner spent four years among the Tongans from 1806 to 1810, and John Martin edited his Account, published in 1820. Mariner was a ship's clerk seized when his vessel was taken, kept alive for his skills and adopted into chiefly life. Gods, taboo, burial rites, and war customs fill his singular record.

No European had lived so deep inside a Polynesian society so early, and the detail shows it. Mariner learned the language, fought in its wars, and mourned its dead. His account stands as the earliest intimate record of Polynesian life, still vivid after two centuries.
eliot-sacred-wood-1920:
T. S. Eliot gathered his early criticism in this 1920 volume, and it changed how English poetry was read. These essays, written while he worked at a bank and taught evening classes, argue for a new standard of taste.

The famous piece, 'Tradition and the Individual Talent', claims a poet must absorb the whole past of literature and then surrender the self to it. 'Hamlet and His Problems' introduces the objective correlative, his test for whether a work's feelings are truly earned. Other essays rank poets and clear ground for modern verse. Few slim books of criticism have carried this much force.
eliot-ara-vos-prec-1920:
Ara Vos Prec, published in London in 1920, gathers the poems Eliot wrote in the lean years before The Waste Land. The title, from Dante, means 'Now I pray you', and the book holds some of his sharpest short work.

Alongside French poems, it includes 'Sweeney Erect', 'A Cooking Egg', and 'Whispers of Immortality'. Sweeney, the coarse modern brute, stalks through several pieces, set against Donne, Webster, and the ghosts of a finer past. The verse is bitter, funny, and tightly made. Readers can watch Eliot's voice harden here into the one that would soon shake poetry.
pound-instigations-1920:
Instigations, published in 1920, gathers Pound's essays and provocations from the years when he was modernism's loudest advocate in London. The critic here is a provocateur: praising, attacking, and clearing space for new work.

The volume includes his long appreciation of Henry James, pieces on the French critic Remy de Gourmont, and his 'Art' manifestoes. Pound argues that criticism should test work against the best that exists, anywhere, in any age. His judgments are swift, learned, and often unfair, but never dull. The book shows how modern taste was fought into being, one essay at a time.
lawrence-new-poems-1920:
New Poems, published in 1920, gathers Lawrence's verse from the end of the war years, when his style was changing fast. The tight rhymes of his youth give way here to open, breathing free verse.

The collection holds 'Piano', his famous memory of childhood music breaking a grown man's composure. Other poems reach toward the elemental force he would soon praise in 'Snake' and the animal poems. Lawrence writes about men, women, and the gulf between them with new plainness. The book is a threshold: behind it, the Georgian poet; ahead, the prophet of the living body.
lawrence-lost-girl-1920:
The Lost Girl won Lawrence the James Tait Black prize and became one of his best-selling novels on its appearance in 1920. Its heroine, Alvina Houghton, is a music teacher in a drab Midlands mining town, suffocating under her father's respectability.

Alvina joins a troupe of Italian performers and follows one of them to Italy, escaping the life laid out for her. The novel is the first full statement of Lawrence's flight motif: salvation through escape to a wilder place. It is also warm, funny, and full of observed small-town life. The flight south would drive his later fiction again and again.
conrad-rescue-1920:
The Rescue, published in 1920, had the longest birth of any Conrad novel: he began it in 1896 and set it aside for twenty years. It returns to Captain Lingard, the hero of his first books, in the Malay shallows.

A yacht with an English couple aboard grounds on the coast, and Lingard's plans for a native prince collide with his duty to rescue them. Love for the yacht's lady, Mrs. Travers, paralyzes the man of action at the critical hour. The novel completes the Lingard trilogy begun in the 1890s. Its long making shows, but its sea passages remain splendid.
williams-kora-in-hell-1920:
Kora in Hell, published in 1920, is Williams's book of improvisations: short prose pieces written fast, day by day, during the war years. Kora is Persephone, the maiden carried to the underworld, and hell here is the modern world at war.

Each improvisation leaps from image to image, a doctor's day, a patient's face, spring fought out of winter, with commentaries that explain and argue with the text. Williams was testing how far spontaneity could carry meaning. The result is uneven, electric, and very personal. It is the first sounding of the American grain he would explore for decades.
cather-youth-bright-medusa-1920:
Youth and the Bright Medusa, published in 1920, collects Willa Cather's stories about artists: singers, sculptors, painters, and the small towns that formed and starved them. The Medusa of the title is art itself, beautiful and dangerous to look at directly.

The collection holds 'Paul's Case', her famous tale of a Pittsburgh boy who steals money for one week of luxury in New York. 'The Sculptor's Funeral' and 'A Wagner Matinee' weigh what the prairie gives its artists and what it takes. Cather writes with pity for both the escapees and the left behind. These stories made her reputation in short fiction.
kafka-ein-landarzt-1920:
Ein Landarzt, published in 1920 by Kurt Wolff, is the story collection Kafka prepared in his lifetime, holding his short parables and tales. The title story, 'A Country Doctor', gives the book its center.

A doctor is summoned on a winter night to a boy whose wound holds a horror no medicine can answer. Around it stand 'Before the Law', the doorkeeper parable later set inside The Trial, and 'An Imperial Message', sent but never delivered. Each piece is a small machine of dread and logic. Together they are the purest dose of Kafka's short fiction.
russell-bolshevism-1920:
In 1920 Russell traveled to Soviet Russia with a Labour delegation and came home to write this report. The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism, published that year, is a rare thing: a sympathetic visitor's clear-eyed refusal to convert.

Russell admired the revolution's energy and its leaders' ability, and he met Lenin. But he found the regime's methods appalling: secret police, crushed dissent, and a dogma that licensed any cruelty. He predicted much of what followed with grim accuracy. The book split him from the British left and still reads as a model of honest political travel writing.
dewey-reconstruction-philosophy-1920:
Reconstruction in Philosophy, published in 1920, grows from lectures Dewey gave in Japan and China on his long Asian tour. It is his program for rebuilding philosophy itself: turning it from a spectator's quest for certainty into an instrument of social intelligence.

Dewey traces how philosophy arose from religion and tradition, and how science has changed its task. The modern philosopher, he argues, should help men judge values and direct change, not chase absolute truth behind experience. The book is compact, clear, and programmatic. It served a generation as the manifesto of pragmatism's second, public phase.
santayana-character-opinion-us-1920:
Character and Opinion in the United States, published in 1920, gathers lectures the Spanish-born Santayana gave on the American mind. No outsider has written about America with this mixture of affection, amusement, and cool distance.

He describes the genteel tradition, the inherited idealism of American culture, beset by the skyscraper world of business and sport. Emerson, James, and Harvard itself pass under his gaze. His image of the American as a man divided, his will in the present and his intellect in a colonial mansion, is still quoted. The book remains a penetrating portrait by a resident alien.
bergson-mind-energy-1920:
Mind-Energy, published in English in 1920, gathers Bergson's lectures and essays on the mind's powers, translated with care by H. Wildon Carr. The pieces were given across the years of his greatest fame, to audiences that filled Paris halls.

Bergson speaks on dreams, memory, false recognition, and the effort of the intellect, always returning to one theme: mental energy pressing against matter's habits. His celebrated lecture subjects show the same method at playful work. The book is the most approachable of his later writings in English. It catches a philosopher-performer thinking aloud before his public.
schlick-space-time-physics-1920:
Space and Time in Contemporary Physics, published in English in 1920 in Henry L. Brose's translation, is Moritz Schlick's introduction to relativity for philosophers. Schlick, founder of the Vienna Circle, was the thinker best placed to explain what Einstein meant.

He leads readers from Newton through special relativity to the general theory's curved geometry, always asking what the physics assumes and what it proves. The treatment is lucid, brief, and philosophically exact. The book became the Vienna Circle's founding statement on physics. It still serves as a model of how philosophy should receive a scientific revolution.
wegener-entstehung-kontinente-1920:
Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, argued that continents slowly drift across the globe. His book The Origin of Continents and Oceans, shown here in German, first appeared in 1915 and grew in later editions. The 1920 text states his case in full.

Wegener points to matching coastlines, matching fossils, and matching rock layers on lands now split by oceans. South America and Africa, he says, were once joined. Most geologists mocked him, since he could not name the force that moves continents. Plate tectonics later proved the drift itself was real. Later finds on the ocean floor at last gave drift its engine.
parry-voyage-northwest-passage-1819-20:
William Edward Parry sailed in 1819 with the ships Hecla and Griper to find a North-West Passage through the Canadian Arctic. His Journal of the voyage appeared in 1821. Parry got farther west than any European before him.

The ships wintered at Melville Island, where the crew staged plays, ran a school, and printed a playbill in the ice. Parry describes Inuit meetings, Arctic wildlife, and the strange light of the polar night. His success won a prize for crossing a key line of longitude. The journal became the model for a generation of Arctic exploration accounts.
plos-pone-0003420:
Ming Lu, Qipeng Zhang, and Min Deng mapped links between small RNAs and diseases in 2008. MicroRNAs are short molecules that tune how strongly genes are read. Reports tying them to human diseases were piling up fast. The patterns inside those links were still largely unclear.

The authors gathered known microRNA and disease pairs into one large analysis. Some RNAs linked to many diseases, and some diseases shared RNA patterns. Those patterns hint at shared roots between seemingly unlike conditions. The map helps researchers pick which small RNAs deserve deep study.
plos-pone-0003520:
Haiyan Qi and co-authors studied death signals from failing chromosome ends in yeast in this 2008 paper. Telomeres cap chromosome ends and protect them. When they fail, cells stop growing and may die. The control of that senescence-to-death path was poorly understood.

The team used a yeast strain with a faulty telomere binding protein. A pathway called TOR, a master growth regulator, governed the death response. Nutrient sensing thus ties into chromosome end damage. The result links the aging clock to the cell's growth thermostat. Yeast shares much cell machinery with humans, which makes such finds portable.
plos-pone-0003620:
Mary-Anne Enoch, Pei-Hong Shen, Francesca Ducci and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks whether brain wave patterns, alcoholism, and anxiety share common genetic roots. The team focused on CRH-BP, a gene tied to the body's stress hormone system.

Variation in and around CRH-BP tracked with EEG readings, alcohol use disorder, and anxiety in the same people. That overlap points to one shared genetic source rather than three separate ones. The work suggests that a single difference in stress circuitry may show up as changed brain waves, drinking problems, and worry.
plos-pone-0003720:
Winfried Schlee, Nathan Weisz, Olivier Bertrand, and colleagues published this hearing study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tinnitus is a phantom ringing that most likely starts in the central nervous system, not the ear. Most earlier work stayed inside the hearing system. The team looked at the wider brain network.

They used auditory steady state responses, brain waves that lock to a steady sound, to outline functional connectivity. Their maps show how regions inside and outside the auditory system link up in the tinnitus brain. The work supports treating tinnitus as a network problem, not just an ear problem.
plos-pone-0003820:
Conan K. Wang, Horst Joachim Schirra, and David J. Craik published this software paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Proteins often pair up with themselves, and that self-association drives many cell processes. NMR relaxation measurements report on protein motion at the atomic level and detect such pairing.

The authors present NMRDyn, a program for analyzing those relaxation data in studies of protein association. It helps researchers extract dynamics from measurements that are otherwise hard to interpret. The tool serves biophysicists measuring how protein partnerships form and move inside cells. It is free for other labs to use and adapt.
plos-pone-0004020:
Tsutomu Sasaki, Bernhard Maier, Katarzyna D. Koclega, and co-authors studied regulation of a lifespan-linked enzyme in 2008. SIR2 is an enzyme tied to lifespan control in yeast, worms, and flies. Its mammal counterpart is SIRT1. Earlier work showed SIRT1 levels track with cell growth signals.

Their PLOS ONE article reports phosphorylation regulates how SIRT1 functions. Phosphate marks can switch the enzyme's activity up or down. That control adds a layer to how cells tune aging pathways. It may matter for drugs aimed at SIRT1 in metabolic disease. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004120:
Claire L. Heslop, Gregory E. Miller, and John S. Hill linked neighborhood wealth to cardiac patient deaths in 2009. Canada provides essential health care to all residents. Even so, socioeconomic gaps in health outcomes persist there. The authors asked whether area wealth predicts death in cardiac patients.

Their PLOS ONE article reports neighborhood status predicted non-cardiovascular mortality. Cardiac patients from poorer areas died more from other causes. Universal care alone did not erase the gradient. The finding points to social conditions beyond the clinic. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004220:
Martine Aabye and colleagues published this diagnostic study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interferon gamma release assays are blood tests for tuberculosis, but their performance in settings where both tuberculosis and HIV are endemic was not well documented. HIV weakens the very immune cells these tests rely on.

The team evaluated the QuantiFERON TB-Gold In-Tube test in patients with culture-confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis. They measured how its sensitivity shifts with HIV infection and with falling CD4 cell counts. The results tell clinics in high-burden regions how much trust to place in a negative test.
plos-pone-0004320:
Keisuke Yonehara and colleagues published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The direction of image motion is coded by direction-selective ganglion cells in the retina. The ON type of these cells sends its axons to the terminal nuclei of the accessory optic system. That system drives the optokinetic reflex, which stabilises vision.

The team identified the retinal ganglion cells and projections involved in transmitting information about upward and downward image motion to the brain. Their earlier genetic tools made it possible to tag these exact cells. Knowing which cells report vertical motion completes part of the wiring diagram of steady sight.
plos-pone-0004420:
Adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma is a blood cancer with a grim outlook. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Lee Ratner, William Harrington, Xuan Feng, and co-authors asks what role its virus plays as the disease worsens. The cancer is linked to the human T cell leukemia virus. Many treatment plans have been tried, yet survival stays poor.

Doctors had noted that the virus seems quiet or absent when the cancer is first found. That raised a puzzle about whether it wakes up again later. The authors report that the virus does switch back on as the cancer moves forward. Tracking that return could help doctors judge how far the disease has come and when to change care.
plos-pone-0004520:
Patients who get worse on tuberculosis treatment in South Africa often carry drug resistance or other serious illness, report Dominique Pepper, Kevin Rebe, Chelsea Morroni, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Getting sicker during therapy is a common reason for hospital admission in Africa. Many things can cause the decline, including resistant TB bacteria, other illnesses, or poor adherence to the drugs.

The study was done at a district hospital in a setting where HIV is widespread. The authors weighed how much drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and AIDS-defining illnesses each contributed. Sorting those causes matters, because each demands a different response: new drugs, treatment of the second illness, or support to finish the course. The findings aim scarce hospital resources at the true drivers.
plos-pone-0004620:
Family doctors in Pakistan may not fully brief patients who receive psychiatric medicines, a gap examined by Hammad Ashraf Ganatra, Hadi Bhurgri, Roomasa Channa, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studies have shown a high prevalence of psychiatric illnesses among patients in primary health care settings. Family physicians play a fundamental role in managing these illnesses with psychopharmacological medications.

Providing information about the disease, its management, and the drugs' effects and side effects is part of that role. The authors ask whether family physicians in Pakistan are up to the task of educating and informing such patients. Patients who understand their medicines take them more reliably. The study gives medical educators in Pakistan evidence on where training should improve.
plos-pone-0004720:
Anthony Grosso and colleagues checked if oral bone drugs raise the risk of a heart rhythm flaw in women, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A past trial had found more cases of a serious rhythm flaw with a yearly infused bone drug than with a dummy drug. That trial was too small to settle the question.

The team used a design where each woman acts as her own control over time. They looked at oral forms of the same drug class in real world records. Self matched designs help strip out fixed traits that skew risk. The check informs women and doctors weighing bone gain against heart risk.
dospassos-one-mans-initiation-1920:
Doran issued One Man's Initiation in a 1922 printing, dedicated to comrades from a road in France. Dos Passos names the road from Erize-la-Petite to Erize-la-Grande in that dedication. He had served as an ambulance driver in France during the war.

Chapter one opens in a huge wharf shed piled with crates and baggage. A band plays thin music as ships wait on either side. A young and tender American then faces the bewildering violence of 1917. Slimmer and more personal than Three Soldiers, the tale of lost innocence helped announce a major new voice in war writing.
irenaeus-demonstration-of-the-apostolic-:
Irenaeus of Lyons made his name fighting Gnostic teachers, yet his Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching shows a gentler side. Written as a summary of the faith for a friend, the work survives in an ancient Armenian translation. The English version by Robinson, published in 1920, presents that text.

The Greek and Latin originals were lost, so the Armenian copy carries the whole weight of the book. Irenaeus walks through creation, the fall, and Christ's work in clear, warm order. Pastor rather than polemicist, he focuses on the core of what Christians believe. The Demonstration balances his great refutation of heresies across the shelf. Readers meet a second-century bishop teaching the faith like a catechism, simply and with love.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-20:
Montreal begins in the years covered by Volume 20, from 1898. Thwaites gathers Quebec reports from 1640 to 1642, a span of siege. The colony sorts itself out for sheer survival under attack.

The new post at Montreal rises as a bold thrust into Iroquois country. Priests bless its start and share its hunger and risk. Letters weigh faith against fear in a camp that may not last. The men who lived those birth pangs wrote them down here. Their trust in the cause never wavers across these pages. New France takes lasting shape under fire in this volume.
journal-of-discourses-vol-20:
Fifty years of Mormonism mark Volume Twenty, published in 1880. The church counts its jubilee from a farmhouse start in 1830. A commonwealth in the mountains stands where six converts began.

Discourses look back over exodus, martyrdom, and the desert's hard bloom. Blessings are counted while the federal crusade still rages outside. Memory serves as armor in these proud, backward-looking Tabernacle talks. The Saints tell their own story as proof that God led them. Commemoration carries an edge here, since the fight is far from won in their eyes. Pride in the past arms the Saints for a grim present.
vinogradoff-outlines-historical-jurispru:
Vinogradoff began his Outlines of Historical Jurisprudence with a first volume in 1920. The Oxford jurist, born in Russia and formed by several legal traditions, planned a survey of law's whole history. The Outlines were to be his synthesis, the fruit of a lifetime spent comparing legal systems.

Volume 1 begins with the ancient world: law born of custom, kingship, and the needs of early states. He moves from the Near East through Greece to the Rome of the emperors, tracing how legal ideas travel and change. Vinogradoff writes as a comparatist, always asking what one system's solution teaches about another's. The wide-ranging survey opens his grand design with characteristic calm. Few scholars of any age could have attempted the whole history of law in two volumes and carried it off.
czechoslovak-constitution-1920:
Czechoslovakia adopted its constitution in February 1920, founding the republic of Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš. The new state had been carved from the fallen Austrian empire and joined Czechs, Slovaks, Germans, and others in one democracy. Its National Assembly wrote the charter to Western models, above all the French.

The text builds a parliamentary republic with a strong president, full manhood and womanhood suffrage, and guards for national minorities. In a region sliding toward dictatorship, Czechoslovakia kept free elections and a free press for two decades. It was the freest and most stable democracy between Germany and Russia. Munich and the Nazi seizure tore the country apart in 1938 and 1939, ending the charter's rule. The founding law of interwar Europe's democratic miracle is still honored in Prague and Bratislava.
mayflower-compact-1620:
