Kenji Matsumoto and colleagues dissected stepwise development of hematopoietic stem cells from embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cellular ontogeny of blood stem cells remains poorly understood because isolation and identification in early small embryos are difficult. The team attempted to dissect early developmental stages using an in vitro mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation system that recapitulates blood emergence.

Stage markers order the path from embryo to stem cell. Defined steps could enable lab production of blood stem cells. That would transform transplantation supply. Mouse work guides human protocols. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0005420:
Thorsten Thye and co-authors reported a 2009 PLOS ONE study on genes and tuberculosis in Ghana. Past work with twins and families showed that the risk of catching tuberculosis is partly set by genes. One gene of interest makes interleukin-10, a signal that calms the immune system.

The team studied a large group of Ghanaian patients with lung tuberculosis and healthy controls. They found that one form of the gene was linked to how skin tests react, but not to lung disease itself. That split result helps show which gene effects matter for illness and which do not.
plos-pone-0005520:
Linda Duval and co-authors reported malaria parasites in African chimpanzees in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Since the nineteen seventies, few workers had studied the malaria parasites of African great apes. Only one chimpanzee parasite had been described at the gene level, a close kin of the worst human malaria parasite.

The team found chimpanzee parasites closely related to a human parasite called Plasmodium ovale. Their presence widens the known family of ape malaria. That matters for tracing where human malaria came from and for protecting wild apes. Ape parasites can also serve as an early warning when human and ape habitats overlap more closely.
plos-pone-0005620:
Alla Bondareva and co-authors tested a blocker of a remodelling enzyme in breast cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. An enzyme called lysyl oxidase reshapes the tissue around tumours and helps cancer cells move. High levels of it are linked with worse survival in breast cancer patients.

The team gave a known blocker of the enzyme in tests with circulating breast cancer cells. The blocker cut the cells' ability to settle and grow in new places. Stopping spread, rather than shrinking the first tumour, is a goal more cancer drugs now aim at.
plos-pone-0005720:
Timothy Hallett and co-authors warned in 2009 that a test to count new HIV infections can mislead, in ways that shift by place and age. The BED test tries to tell recent infections from old ones. Programs use it to estimate how fast HIV is spreading.

The flaw is that the test's accuracy fades with time since infection, and that fade had not been measured. The team built scenarios to show how errors grow or shrink in different settings. Their point is not that the test is useless, but that its numbers need local care. Wrong rates can misdirect whole prevention programs.
plos-pone-0005820:
Sudipta Bhowmick and Nahid Ali searched in 2009 for parasite proteins that mark protection against visceral leishmaniasis. This disease, caused by Leishmania donovani, is a major health problem in poorer regions. No safe, effective vaccine exists for any form of leishmaniasis.

The team screened parasite proteins for reactions with blood from patients at different disease stages. Proteins recognized by cured or resistant people are vaccine candidates. They also define correlates of protection, measures trials can use to judge a vaccine fast. The study is groundwork for a vaccine the field has sought for decades.
plos-pone-0006420:
Donna MacCallum and co-authors published a 2009 PLOS ONE study of Candida albicans, a fungus that can spread through the blood and harm the kidneys. They used the mouse vein challenge model, a common way to study how host and fungus interact. Their focus was the early immune signals made in kidney and spleen.

The team tracked signal proteins in both organs for up to two days after infection. They compared a strong strain with a weak one to see how the response differs. The title reports that chemokines made early on predict later kidney damage. That link could help labs judge how severe an infection will become.
plos-pone-0006520:
Hong-Zhen Yang and co-authors tested blocking an immune sensor to slow cancer spread in PLOS ONE in 2009. Metastasis is the most pivotal cause of mortality in cancer patients. Immune tolerance plays a crucial role in tumor progression and metastasis. The team investigated TLR2, a sensor that helps the immune system spot threats.

Their title reports that blocking TLR2 activity attenuates pulmonary metastases of tumors, spread to the lungs. A sensor that tumors exploit for tolerance becomes a drug target. The study connects innate immunity with the deadliest phase of cancer. It suggests tuning, not just boosting, immunity may fight metastasis.
plos-pone-0006620:
Sebastiaan van Hal, Hong Foo, Christopher Blyth, and colleagues investigated a flu outbreak at a mass gathering in PLOS ONE in 2009. Influenza causes annual epidemics and often results in extensive outbreaks in closed communities. The outbreak occurred during Sydney World Youth Day 2008, which drew huge crowds. The team studied the utility of laboratory testing and case definitions during the outbreak.

Case definitions decide who counts as a case when tests are scarce. Good definitions balance sensitivity with practicality at mass events. Their evaluation helps organizers of future gatherings plan medical responses. Mass gatherings remain a known risk for spreading respiratory viruses.
plos-pone-0009420:
Rebecca Safran and co-authors published this wild bird study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carotenoids are the pigments behind many birds' bright colors. They may also help health and breeding, but most proof came from caged birds or single snapshots. Wild evidence was thin.

The team tracked individual free-living birds over time. Birds that kept a positive carotenoid balance achieved greater reproductive performance. Following the same birds beats comparing strangers at one moment. The result supports the idea that pigment stores are a real currency of fitness in the wild, not just a laboratory effect.
plos-pone-0009520:
Kelly Albin and Christopher Simons studied the tingle of Sichuan pepper compounds in PLOS ONE in 2010. Compounds called sanshools make the lips buzz and tingle. That odd feeling is neither taste nor pain in the usual sense. Past work had mapped some of the nerves and molecules involved. This team tested a sanshool relative on human volunteers.

They measured how strong the tingle felt, how long it lasted, and how it changed with dose. They also probed which sense channels carry the signal. Their work turns a kitchen sensation into hard data on touch. It helps explain how foods can stir the sense of touch itself.
plos-pone-0009620:
Marianela Rodriguez-Carres and co-authors described a harmless relative of dangerous fungi in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cryptococcus fungi can cause severe lung and brain disease. Their sibling species, Filobasidiella depauperata, does not infect people. It can also mate with itself, a trait called homothallism. The team characterized its form and its genome in detail.

A harmless stand in is precious for comparison. What the sibling lacks may be exactly what makes its cousins dangerous. Its genome gives a baseline for finding virulence traits in the harmful species. The work also adds to knowledge of how mating systems evolve in fungi.
plos-pone-0010420:
Anthony Martin, Gonzalo Vazquez-Prokopec and Michael Page reported the first known feeding trace of an ancient fish in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Green River rocks of Wyoming hold superb fossil fish from the Eocene age. The bottom-dwelling fish Notogoneus osculus is among them. Fossils of bodies are common there, but traces of behavior are rarer. The team identified marks left as this fish fed on the lake bottom.

A feeding trace freezes a moment of behavior from tens of millions of years ago. It shows how the fish probed or sucked up food from the sediment. Such traces link anatomy to action in a way bones alone cannot. They also help read the lake's ecology, who ate whom and where. Behavior, in fossils, is precious evidence.
plos-pone-0010520:
Ashleigh Tuite and co-workers modeled how Canada should share out flu vaccine in a pandemic, for PLOS ONE in 2010. The world faced its first flu pandemic of the new century. Vaccines prevent illness well, but early supplies are always short. The new virus also behaved unlike seasonal flu, hitting younger people harder. The team tested allocation plans on a model of the Canadian population.

Different plans save different mixes of lives, hospital beds, and workdays. Aiming at transmitters, often the young, can shield others indirectly. Aiming at the frail protects them directly but may let spread continue. Models cannot choose values, but they can price each choice. This study gave officials those prices in advance.
plos-pone-0010620:
Pankaj Chaturvedi and Veena Parnaik traced how mutant lamin proteins damage the nucleus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lamin A gives the nucleus its shape and order. Changes in its rod-shaped middle section cause wasting diseases called laminopathies.

Cells carrying the mutants lost two partner proteins, HP1 alpha and HP1 beta. The mutants switched on a disposal tag, FBXW10, that sent the partners for destruction. Losing HP1 loosens the packing of silent DNA. The chain of events, from one mutation to lost genome order, is now much clearer for researchers.
plos-pone-0010720:
Abdulaziz Al-Swailem and colleagues built the first large gene catalog for the dromedary camel, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Camels support trade, milk, and travel across dry lands. For all their value, camels had no large-scale sequencing project behind them, unlike cattle or horses.

The team built libraries of expressed genes and read more than seventy thousand sequence tags. Those tags sample the genes a camel actually uses. The catalog opens camel biology to modern genetics: disease resistance, milk traits, and heat tolerance can now be hunted at the gene level. It is a foundation stone for a future full camel genome.
plos-pone-0010820:
Stefanie Hueber and colleagues improved the family tree of Hox proteins across major model species, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hox proteins pattern the body from head to tail in nearly all animals. Matching the right Hox protein between a fly, a worm, and a mouse is harder than it sounds. Thirty years of naming had left borderline cases in dispute.

Their classification used sequence and structure together to sort borderline proteins. The tidier tree matched functional evidence better than older schemes. Comparative development depends on comparing like with like. A cleaner Hox roster makes cross-species claims safer for every lab that studies body patterning.
plos-pone-0010920:
Nicholas Ieronimakis, Gayathri Balasundaram, Sabrina Rainey and co-authors published this muscle study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Satellite cells are the resident stem cells that repair skeletal muscle, and researchers usually fish them out using a surface marker called CD34. A minority of these cells lacks CD34, and whether they are a separate class was unclear.

Sorting the two groups apart, the team found CD34 alone cannot purify satellite cells unless paired with a second marker. More importantly, cells that lose CD34 are not a distinct lineage: they are activated cells, and after acute injury they become the main repair population. The marker's absence marks a reversible state that switches with injury. Ieronimakis and colleagues caution that a popular sorting recipe can discard exactly the cells doing the healing.
plos-pone-0011020:
Christophe Ribelayga and Stuart Mangel published this retina study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The eye has its own circadian clock that retunes vision between day and night, but whether the clock rewires the actual pathways carrying visual signals was unknown. The authors recorded from rabbit horizontal cells, which shape the signals rods and cones send onward.

Under dark-adapted conditions, rod input to these cells grew substantially at night, making them respond to very dim light they ignored by day. Blocking one dopamine receptor type during the day reproduced the night state, while blocking another did not, and dye tracing showed rods and cones were more extensively coupled at night. Ribelayga and Mangel identify a clock-controlled neural pathway in the retina, switched by dopamine, that effectively gives the eye a night mode.
plos-pone-0011120:
Pallesen, Brattico, Bailey and colleagues compared musicians and others in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their test dealt with holding sounds in mind while resisting distraction. This skill, called cognitive control in hearing memory, is vital for speech in noisy places.

Musicians showed stronger control than non musicians on the tasks used. Years of training in listening and timing may build that edge. The result supports a wider claim that music training sharpens the mind beyond music itself. It gives schools and parents one more evidence based reason to value sustained music study.
plos-pone-0011220:
Guerron, Rawat, Sali and colleagues tested two drugs in a mouse model of Duchenne dystrophy for PLOS ONE in 2010. This disease steadily destroys muscle, including the heart. The team gave mice a standard steroid and a second compound, measuring effects on both skeletal muscle and heart tissue.

The pairing was checked for functional and molecular benefits in the model. Families facing Duchenne have few options, so each tested combination carries real weight. Positive signals in mice guide which regimens deserve human trials. The study also stresses judging heart effects, since heart failure is a leading cause of death in this disease.
plos-pone-0011320:
Jahn, Floyd, McGrath and colleagues studied child survival in rural Malawi for PLOS ONE in 2010. Normally, children of wealthier families survive at higher rates than children of the poor. The team measured whether that survival gap held across social strata as HIV spread through the region.

HIV closed the gap, but by dragging survival down rather than lifting the poor up. That grim equalizing shows the epidemic's broad social cost. Global health programs cannot assume richer groups will be spared and focus only on the poorest. The finding argues for universal strength in child health services where HIV is common.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1220:
Hurley wrote to the Secretary of State on 29 July 1945. His dispatches from China came often that summer. Each carried the state of a country split between a Nationalist government and communist armies, with Japan's defeat near and civil war looming behind it.

The secretary read China news beside the German bargaining. The two files met in Soviet intentions, which touched both. This cable is one piece of that dual picture. It shows an envoy at a hard post keeping his chief informed in the summit's last days. The crisis he reported would outlast the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1320:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 20 July 1945. Formal papers were the currency of the summit: each one a claim in writing, offered for the other teams to take, amend, or refuse. This one came at the end of the first week.

By then the American stands on the chief questions were known, and drafting had turned to terms that might close. A proposal of this date belongs to that sharpening phase. It survives in the official record in the team's own words. Readers can weigh it against the final protocol to see what the week of trading did to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1420:
Herschel Johnson, the American minister in Sweden, wrote to the secretary of state on 6 July 1945. Johnson's post in Stockholm kept Washington in touch with a neutral capital close to the war's edge. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Neutral capitals were listening posts in 1945, full of envoys, rumors, and quiet feelers from all sides. A minister's letter from Stockholm in the week before Potsdam adds that northern view to the volume. Readers meet a lesser-known channel here: the reports that flowed in from the war's margins. It sometimes carried word of moves the main capitals had not yet seen. It widens the map before the summit papers begin.
frus-1945-50-intel-d20:
Secretary of War Robert Patterson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal wrote jointly to Secretary of State Byrnes on 29 September 1945. Two cabinet officers signing one letter is itself a signal. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The military departments wrote together because the OSS order had pushed them into a shared corner. The War Department held the spy units, the Navy its own services. Both faced a State Department newly armed with analysts. A joint letter shows the two services settling their differences to face the civilians as one. Readers see coalition building at cabinet level, the necessary first step before the long negotiation over a central intelligence system could begin.
frus-1945-50-intel-d120:
The National Intelligence Authority wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946. The board addressed the cabinet officer who oversaw the FBI, in the middle of the Latin American dispute. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A letter from the whole authority carried the combined weight of State, War, and Navy. Sent to Clark, it told the Justice Department where the board stood on the division of foreign intelligence work. Readers have reached the ruling stage of the summer's fight. The papers that follow, Hoover's protests and Leahy 's direction, show the ruling being received. Few episodes in the volume display the 1946 system working as designed so completely.
frus-1945-50-intel-d220:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 11 September 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 220 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d320:
On 17 July 1947 the 14th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 320 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. For a reader now, the draw is the nearness: this is the meeting as its own staff chose to keep it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d420:
On 2 May 1950, W. Park Armstrong wrote again to Under Secretary of State James Webb. The memo is document 420 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By the spring of 1950 the shape of American intelligence was still open to change. The State Department's share of that work depended on aides like Armstrong making their case in writing. His May memo is one more round in a long contest over who would speak for the facts abroad. Weeks later the Korean War began, and debates like this one turned at once into wartime tasks.
frus-1861-d20:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford on 26 March 1861. Sanford was the new American minister to Belgium, based in Brussels. The letter is document 20 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford was an eager, well connected envoy who made Brussels a listening post for the Union. Seward's March letter belongs to the first set of orders sent to Lincoln's new men abroad. It set the terms on which Sanford would watch Europe for the Union cause. Sanford later raised funds and arms for the Union on his own bold account.
frus-1861-d120:
Charles Faulkner, the outgoing American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State Jeremiah Black on 19 March 1861. The letter is document 120 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner wrote in the last days of the Buchanan order in Paris. Within weeks Seward would replace Black, and Dayton would replace Faulkner. The letter marks the old guard handing over the most delicate post in Europe as the Union split. Faulkner's Virginia roots made his loyalty a point of talk in that tense spring. Loyalty in that spring was a coin whose worth each man's acts would fix.
frus-1861-d220:
Guidance for Mr. Marsh left Washington on 20 September 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 220 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d20:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 17 February 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 20 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d120:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 August 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 120 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d220:
William Stuart answered on 25 June 1862 with a letter to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 220 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation during Lord Lyons's absence.

A stand-in envoy walks a fine line, firm for his government yet careful not to commit it too far. Stuart's letters show that care in formal, measured prose. His reply came as the Seven Days battles opened outside Richmond. News that soon reached Washington and sharpened every question between the two governments that summer. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d320:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 28 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 320 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote on the first day of the second Bull Run battle, in a Paris still working from July's picture of the war. His report adds the French court's reading at the very moment the facts were changing across the ocean. Papers like this one, filed late in the volume, reward readers who follow dates rather than document order. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d420:
From the American legation in Madrid, Horace J. Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1862. The dispatch is Document 420 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Late May brought word of Union advances in Virginia and the West, and Perry's job was to make that news count in Spain. Spanish officials also had to weigh France's deepening grip on Mexico, next door to their own stake in the Americas. Reports of this kind gave the State Department its picture of Madrid's mood. They are worth reading as the ground-level half of a conversation whose other half is Seward's string of instructions.
frus-1862-d520:
Two days after Antietam, on 19 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 520 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record.

Seward wrote before the battle's full result was known in Washington, let alone its meaning abroad. His orders in that week kept to first principles: the Union would win, foreign interference was unwelcome, and neutral duties must be honored. Pike at The Hague would soon have better news to use, including Lincoln's emancipation order of 22 September. The dispatch catches the correspondence mid-turn, as the autumn's new facts began their slow journey into every legation's instructions.
frus-1862-d620:
Jacob S. Haldeman, the American minister at Stockholm, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 December 1861. It is Document 620 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swedish file.

Haldeman served the joint kingdom of Sweden and Norway, a poor, seafaring north whose people were then emigrating to America in growing numbers. His December report reached Washington in the Trent winter, when every court's attitude was being tallied. Sweden's sympathy for the Union was genuine and its weight small, a combination that made for pleasant, undemanding correspondence. The letter begins the volume's Scandinavian file, the far edge of the Department's European map.
frus-1862-d720:
On 6 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Friedrich Hassaurek, the American minister in Ecuador. The letter is document 720 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last paper in this part of the volume. It answers Hassaurek's dispatch of early October.

Seward's reply closed the Ecuador file for the year in the printed record. His outward letters set the brief for each post; for a far Pacific legation, they also carried the news of home that an envoy needed. This one shows the full span of the State Department's reach in 1862. It ran from the courts of Europe to a lone post high in the Andes.
frus-1863p1-d20:
On 25 December 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. A Christmas Day dispatch is a fair sign of how full the legation's plate was. The letter is document 20 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams closed the year with reports on the ground he had held: Britain had not backed the South, and its government trod with care. His letters also tracked the press and the public mood, which Seward weighed with the cabinet's acts. This dispatch ends the 1862 run of the London file in the volume, a quiet cap to a year of strain.
frus-1863p1-d120:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 16 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 120 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of the day took the next head of the brief in line. Seward's points for London were the war's points in Europe: fair dealing, the blockade's rights, and the warships in British yards. This letter holds its slice of that work. In the row of four it is a mid-piece, and its worth is in the row as much as in itself.
frus-1863p1-d220:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 22 June 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 220 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d320:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 12 November 1862. The note is document 320 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The questions reaching the British legation were the war's daily friction: stopped ships, seized cargoes, arrested men, and the rights of a neutral flag. Stuart's letters deal with that traffic. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d420:
Washington's business with Britain on 23 March 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 420 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d520:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 20 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d620:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State sent an official note to William Stuart, the British chargé d'affaires in Washington on 16 September 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020020:
Laura Papagno, Celsa A. Spina, Arnaud Marchant, and a wide team examined immune wear in HIV infection for PLOS Biology in 2004. CD8 T cells are killer cells that attack virus-infected cells. In people with HIV, these cells stay switched on for years and slowly take on signs of aging, a state called senescence.

Aged killer cells divide poorly and respond weakly, which may help explain why the immune system fades over time in HIV. The authors track the marks of that aging and link them to constant immune activation. Their work points to a hard truth: the long fight itself can wear out the fighters. Calming that wear could matter for long term care.
plos-pbio-0020120:
Jessica R. Ward and Kevin D. Lafferty reviewed the state of ocean disease in PLOS Biology in 2004. Reports of sick sea life, from coral bleaching to shellfish die-offs, had grown. The authors ask a fair but hard question: are ocean diseases truly rising, or are we just looking harder?

Without a past baseline, claims of increase are shaky. The paper sorts what is known from what is merely suspected. It urges long term records so future claims can be tested. That sober stance matters for policy. Money and rules for ocean health should rest on trends that can be proven, not on a pile of alarming reports.
plos-pbio-0020320:
Shu-ou Shan, Robert M. Stroud, and Peter Walter worked out how two switch proteins activate each other in PLOS Biology in 2004. GTPases are molecular switches flipped by the fuel molecule GTP. Two of them guide proteins to the cell membrane during secretion, and they must turn each other on at the right moment.

The authors show how the pair binds and how the contact speeds up both switches. That mutual trigger times protein delivery with care. Errors in this traffic jam the cell's shipping system. A clear picture of the handshake helps explain diseases of secretion. It also gives biochemists a model case where each partner is both trigger and target.
plos-pone-0000120:
Yannick Hamon, Doriane Trompier, Zhong Ma, and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It examines two proteins, ABCA1 and MEGF10, that act as engulfment receptors. These receptors help cells swallow dead cells and debris, a constant cleanup job in the body.

Cleanup fails when the receptors that tag and grab dead cells do not work together. The authors study how ABCA1 and MEGF10 cooperate in this process. Understanding that partnership matters for diseases where dead cells pile up. It also clarifies a basic housekeeping system that keeps tissues healthy and on schedule.
plos-pone-0000220:
Jeffrey W. Touchman, David M. Wagner, Jicheng Hao, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a draft genome sequence of a North American strain of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague. The authors analyze its single-letter DNA differences, SNPs, and place the strain on the plague family tree.

A reference genome for North American plague helps track where local cases come from. Plague persists in wildlife across the western United States, so knowing the strain's relations matters for public health and for biodefense. The phylogenetic analysis shows how the North American line fits into global plague history.
plos-pone-0000320:
Grit Hein, Arjen Alink, Andreas Kleinschmidt, and colleagues published this brain imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. People often must decide using either what they hear or what they see. The authors study competing neural responses when auditory and visual decisions contend, asking how the brain settles which sense guides the choice.

Cross-sensory competition is everyday life: a ringing phone against a flashing screen. The study locates where that contest plays out in the brain. Understanding it bears on attention research and on conditions where the senses fail to take turns properly.
plos-pone-0000420:
Marek Cyrklaff and colleagues froze vaccinia virus particles mid-disassembly and imaged them in 3D, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vaccinia is a large DNA virus related to smallpox. Using whole-cell cryo-electron tomography, a technique that builds 3D views from many tilted images of frozen cells, they captured the virus coming apart.

The images revealed distinct disassembly intermediates, recognizable stages between the intact virus and its unraveled core. A virus must shed its packaging at the right place and time to infect. Seeing the actual stages turns a guessed sequence into a documented one, useful for understanding poxvirus infection and for antiviral thinking.
plos-pone-0000520:
Mark D. Robida, Andrew Rahn, and Ravinder Singh searched the whole genome for gene messages edited by chosen proteins, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. RNA-binding proteins grab gene messages and guide how they are spliced. Splicing cuts a message and rejoins it, so one gene can yield more than one product.

The team found, genome-wide, which spliced messages each studied protein targets. One such protein can steer hundreds of messages at once. A target list turns a lone protein into a map of a whole control web. That matters in cancer and muscle disease, where splicing goes wrong in set patterns.
plos-pone-0000620:
Simon D. Makombe, Andreas Jahn, Hannock Tweya and colleagues surveyed Malawi's teachers on HIV treatment, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV and AIDS were hitting the education sector of sub-Saharan Africa hard. The survey reached every public and private facility in Malawi that provided antiretroviral therapy, the drug treatment that keeps HIV in check.

Three questions drove the work: how many teachers took up therapy, how many stayed on it, and how many survived. Answers shape how a country protects its teaching workforce during an epidemic. Health officials and education planners both need those numbers before they can plan staffing, training, or support.
plos-pone-0000720:
Jeremy L. Marshall traced rapid evolution in a mating structure of North American crickets, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Allonemobius socius complex holds three cricket species that diverged recently and spread across the continent. Where they meet again, the only barriers to gene flow seem tied to fertilization traits, such as how sperm is stored.

The spermathecal duct, the tube leading to the female's sperm store, is evolving in length at a rapid pace. Marshall weighs effects at three levels: species, population, and Wolbachia, a bacterium living in the crickets. Fast change in reproductive plumbing can wall species off, making this a close-up view of speciation at work.
plos-pone-0000820:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang examined the shapes small drug-like molecules adopt when they grab proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. It is well known that small molecules, called ligands, do not necessarily adopt their lowest potential energy conformations when binding proteins. Analyses of protein-bound ligand crystal structures had reportedly shown many do not even adopt conformations at local energy minima, a puzzle for drug design.

The title gives their answer: small molecules show a preference for local minimum conformations when binding. If ligands mostly settle into nearby energy wells rather than strained shapes, computer docking predictions get simpler and more reliable. That regularity helps designers score candidate drugs before synthesis.
plos-pone-0000920:
Jose Borghans, Anne Molgaard, Rob de Boer and colleagues asked why some HLA types slow the march of AIDS, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HLA molecules show pieces of germs to the immune system. Certain types are linked to low HIV levels and slow disease, yet the reason was poorly understood.

The authors test the idea that these protective molecules truly prefer to present p24, a core HIV protein. Presenting the right piece early may let the immune system hit the virus where it hurts. The work links a genetic advantage to a concrete step in immune defense. That link could shape how vaccines are designed to copy natural protection.
plos-pone-0001020:
Haoquan Wu, Joel Neilson, Priti Kumar and colleagues profiled microRNAs across three states of killer T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs act as master regulators of gene activity during development and cell change. Killer CD8 T cells pass from naive to effector to memory states as they fight and then stand guard.

Gene activity shifts hugely along that path, but the microRNA side was unknown. The team compared microRNA profiles in all three states. A profile per state shows which regulators mark each stage of readiness. That knowledge could help shape T cells for vaccines and cancer therapy, where the memory state is the prized one.
plos-pone-0001120:
Staphylococcus aureus causes serious infections in people and udder infections in cattle, but the strains behind them are not the same. Lisa Herron-Olson and colleagues examined this split in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genetic evidence already suggested that the bacterium specializes in particular hosts.

The authors look for the molecular traits that go with that specialization. They compare the sets of clonal groups recovered from human disease with those recovered from cattle mastitis. Knowing which features tie a strain to one host could help explain how staph jumps between species, and where control efforts should aim.
plos-pone-0001220:
Planning for a flu pandemic means estimating how fast the virus will spread, captured in the number R0. John Mathews and colleagues argue that a biological model is needed to get that number right, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The clinical attack rate depends on prior immunity, mixing patterns in the population, and the share of infections with no symptoms.

Because of that complexity, R0 cannot be read directly off the attack rate, which has contributed to uncertainty in pandemic planning. The authors build a model that includes asymptomatic infection and immunity. Their work aims to give planners a sounder basis for decisions.
plos-pone-0001320:
Diabetes and periodontal, or gum, disease worsen each other. Marcela Claudino and colleagues tested the link in rats, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Periodontal disease in diabetic patients shows higher severity and prevalence, and diabetic rats had shown worse disease when ligatures were used to irritate the gums.

The open question was whether diabetes alone, without that harsh stimulus, triggers periodontal disease. The authors used alloxan-induced diabetes in rats to find out. Their title states the finding: alloxan-induced diabetes triggers periodontal disease in rats. The study singles out diabetes as the driver.
plos-pone-0001420:
Yuka Nadai and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on reading the full HIV genome from blood. Labs could read near full HIV genomes from cell DNA as a routine task. Doing the same from virus RNA in plasma was far less routine. That gap made full study of free virus in blood hard.

The authors set out a step by step method to copy and read near the whole RNA genome. A shared method lets labs compare strains on an equal base. It also helps track drug resistance and virus change in patients. The paper is a tool kit for groups that study HIV in blood samples.
plos-pone-0001520:
Silvia Della Bella and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on where a cancer linked virus hides. The virus is tied to Kaposi's sarcoma, a tumor of vessel lining cells. Its hiding place in blood was not well defined. Since the tumor cells stem from vessel stock, the team checked blood vessel stem cells for the virus.

They found these blood stem cells can carry the virus. That marks them as a likely pool that keeps the virus in the body. It also fits the tumor's vessel roots. Finding the pool helps aim drugs and tests at the cells that truly harbor the agent.
plos-pone-0001620:
Annelise Sahin and co-authors described a small protein in Leishmania, the parasite that causes leishmaniasis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is called ARL-1, short for ADP-Ribosylation Factor-Like protein 1. It belongs to a family of small G proteins that help move materials inside cells, including traffic through the Golgi body.

The team reports that the ARL-1 gene exists in a single copy in each set of the parasite's genes and is shared across related parasites. The protein it makes weighs about 20 kilodaltons. The full text gives the tests used to describe the protein and where it sits in the cell. It also covers what its role in Golgi traffic may be. Such basic facts about parasite cells can later guide work on new treatments.
plos-pone-0001720:
Joost J. Smit, Dennis M. Lindell, Louis Boon, and their co-authors studied lung immunity to a common infant virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, infects nearly all infants by age two and is a leading cause of bronchiolitis, inflammation of the small airways. The virus may skew the immune response by modulating dendritic cells, the sentinels that start immune reactions.

The team compared two dendritic cell groups, conventional and plasmacytoid. They report that the balance between them determines how strong the lung's immunity to virus infection is. The full text gives the cell counts after treatment that expanded each group, and the infection outcomes. The balance point could guide vaccine design for a virus that still lacks one.
plos-pone-0001820:
Harri Lähdesmäki, Alistair G. Rust, and Ilya Shmulevich built a probabilistic method to predict where transcription factors bind DNA, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Building a complete understanding of transcriptional regulation is an important problem in molecular biology. A transcription factor's binding sites can be hinted at by several data sources, each imperfect.

Their flexible framework infers binding from multiple data sources jointly and differs from standard hypothesis testing. The full text gives the model, the data types combined, and the prediction accuracy. Combining weak evidence streams is a general trick in genomics, and the framework can be reused for other prediction tasks.
plos-pone-0001920:
Ugo Lucca and colleagues asked whether mild anemia matters for older adults, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study called Health and Anemia. In old age, blood hemoglobin often sits just below the normal range. Whether that slight dip tracks with real harm, or is just a benign sign of age, had little proof either way.

The team checked, at one point in time, how mild anemia linked to thought, daily function, mood, and quality of life in older people. A firm link would argue for closer care of a finding doctors often shrug off. No link would spare patients needless treatment. Either way, the study gives the question a data base.
plos-pone-0002020:
Ron Firestein and co-authors tested a longevity gene against gut tumors in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, SIRT1, removes chemical tags from proteins and is kin to genes that extend life in simple animals. In mammals, some feared that tuning such paths for longer life might raise cancer risk as a trade.

The team report the reverse in the gut: as the title states, SIRT1 suppresses intestinal tumor formation and colon cancer growth. A longevity path that also curbs cancer eases the feared trade. The result supports work on SIRT1 as a drug target for colon cancer.
plos-pone-0002120:
Rafael Dias Loyola and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on saving frogs and toads. Their setting is the Neotropics, the warm region covering much of Central and South America. Nearly 35 percent of the amphibian species there face threats from habitat loss, habitat being cut into pieces, and habitat being split apart.

The authors argue that the best places to protect depend on how each species lives and grows. Frogs that breed in water react to habitat damage in unlike ways from frogs that grow up on land. One plan does not fit all. Their work points to broad plans that match protected areas to the life traits of each group.
plos-pone-0002220:
Yanan Yang, Kentaro Iwanaga, Maria Gabriela Raso, and co-authors studied stem cells in mouse lung tumors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Non-small cell lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer death in Western countries. A small group of cells called bronchioalveolar stem cells sits where the airways meet the air sacs. They were suspected to seed tumors when the K-ras gene goes wrong.

The team reports that a signaling enzyme, PI3-kinase, drives the expansion of these stem cells in mouse models of K-ras lung cancer. A pathway needed for tumor growth is a candidate target for drugs that might slow this deadly cancer earlier.
plos-pone-0002320:
Sudha Purushothaman and co-authors studied how the tuberculosis bacterium attaches a vital vitamin to its proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fatty acids are indispensable parts of mycolic acids, the waxy molecules that make the TB cell envelope tough and hard to penetrate. Biotin is an essential cofactor for the enzyme that starts fatty acid building.

The team examined the ligand specificity of the group I biotin protein ligase, the enzyme that attaches biotin where it is needed in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. An enzyme the bacterium cannot do without, and that differs from the human version, is a plausible drug target.
plos-pone-0002420:
Research by Wang and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Chia-Hui Wang, Daniel Y. Lee, Zhaoqun Deng, and others. Its subject is microRNA miR-328 Regulates Zonation Morphogenesis by Targeting CD44 Expression. Morphogenesis is crucial to initiate physiological development and tumor invasion.

Here we show that a microRNA controls zonation morphogenesis by targeting hyaluronan receptor CD44. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002520:
Hampshire and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Adam Hampshire, Russell Thompson, John Duncan, and others. Its subject is the Target Selective Neural Response — Similarity, Ambiguity, and Learning Effects. A network of frontal and parietal brain regions is commonly recruited during tasks that require the deliberate ‘top-down’ control of thought and action.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002620:
Work by Ahmed Itrat and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was knowledge, awareness and practices regarding dengue fever among the adult population of dengue hit cosmopolitan. The catalog record names Ahmed Itrat first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The World health Organization (WHO) declares dengue and dengue hemorrhagic fever to be endemic in South Asia. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002720:
Research from Nicholas O. Fischer and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers massively parallel interrogation of aptamer sequence, structure and function. Authorship is credited in the record to Nicholas O. Fischer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Optimization of high affinity reagents is a significant bottleneck in medicine and the life sciences. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002820:
Work by Hong Cao and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with evolutionary emergence of microRNAs in human embryonic stem cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Hong Cao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Human embryonic stem (hES) cells have unique abilities to divide indefinitely without differentiating and potential to differentiate into more than 200 cell types. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002920:
Brian Cook, Karin Ernberg, Hyeyoun Chung and co-authors produced a human smell receptor in lab cells in 2008. Smell receptors are hard to study because making enough pure protein is difficult. Milligram amounts are needed before structure and function work can really begin.

The team engineered a synthetic form of the human receptor hOR17-4 and made it in a stable mammalian cell line that can be switched on. They then purified the protein from those cells. Published in PLOS ONE, the method opens smell receptors, long a stubborn family, to direct study. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003020:
Hyunchul Lee, Catherine Leamey and Atomu Sawatari tracked changing stains in mouse brain during early behavior in 2008. The neostriatum is the input hub of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical and dopamine signals. It splits into sub-compartments called striosomes and matrix, whose coordinated activity supports behavior.

Staining tied to chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans reversed rapidly in those compartments as behavior emerged. Published in PLOS ONE, the timing links a molecular scaffold in the brain to the onset of action. Such markers can help map when circuits become functional in development. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003120:
Konrad Lehmann and Siegrid Löwel wrote this 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the visual brain stays flexible with age. In young mice, covering one eye for four days shifts which eye drives neurons in the visual cortex. That shift stops working in older adults, yet recent work found it can still occur in young adults near ninety days old.

Lehmann and Löwel test how this ocular dominance plasticity changes as mice grow older. Their work helps show when the visual system can still rewire itself after one eye is deprived, and when that ability fades. It speaks to basic questions about brain plasticity across the lifespan.
plos-pone-0003220:
Ola Larsson, Deanna Diebold, Danhua Fan and colleagues study scar-forming cells at the genome level in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fibroproliferative disorders of the lung, liver, kidney, heart, blood vessels and skin are common as a group, progressive, and refractory to therapy. They can emerge after toxic insults but are frequently idiopathic, of unknown cause. Their propensity to resist therapy and progress was enigmatic.

The title reports that fibrotic myofibroblasts show genome-wide derangements of translational control, the making of proteins from messages. Readers get a broad control failure, not a single bad gene. That scope may explain why single-target drugs often fail in fibrosis.
plos-pone-0003320:
Haibin Wang, Huirong Xie and Sudhansu K. Dey link a cannabinoid receptor to preterm birth in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Preterm birth, accounting for about ten percent of pregnancies in women, is a huge social, clinical and economic burden. Its root causes remain largely unknown. Emerging evidence suggests endocannabinoid signaling via cannabinoid receptor CB1 plays key roles in reproduction.

The title reports that loss of cannabinoid receptor CB1 induces preterm birth. Readers see a system best known from cannabis research prove key for pregnancy timing. The result urges care in assuming this system is not needed for healthy pregnancy.
plos-pone-0007420:
Misaki Wayengera searched for molecular clues to a heart scarring disease using computational proteomics in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Endomyocardial fibrosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the heart. Its pathology resembles late stage Chagas disease, and both are thought to result from autoimmune responses against heart muscle tissue in affected patients.

Molecular mimicry between microbes and heart proteins may drive that autoimmunity. Wayengera applies in silico proteomics and analytical chemistry to search for the cause. Computational screening can nominate candidate proteins for lab testing. His approach targets a neglected tropical heart disease.
plos-pone-0007520:
Tong Shen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how cancer cells resist chemotherapy. One major trick is pumping drugs back out of the cell. Transport proteins of the ABC family do that pumping, lowering the drug level inside. One such pump is MRP7, also called ABCC10. The team tested two existing leukemia drugs, imatinib and nilotinib, against that pump.

Both drugs inhibited MRP7's efflux activity. With the pump jammed, cancer cells lost their multidrug resistance. The chemotherapy could build up inside and work again. Repurposing existing medicines this way is attractive because their safety is already known. The study suggests certain leukemia drugs could double as resistance breakers for other cancers. That is a practical shortcut in a field that moves slowly.
plos-pone-0007620:
Swati Bhattacharyya and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the brakes that limit scarring. TGF-beta is the pivotal signal in tissue repair and fibrosis. It drives collagen production and turns fibroblasts into scar-making cells. Its effects run partly through a transcription factor called Egr-1. The team studied a cofactor named Nab2, which the signal itself induces. They asked what Nab2 does to fibroblast activation.

Nab2 acts as a built-in brake: switched on by TGF-beta, it suppresses the fibroblast activation the signal promotes. In scleroderma, where scarring runs away, Nab2 expression is impaired. A missing brake fits the disease's pattern well. Restoring or imitating Nab2 could become a treatment strategy. The study reveals a self-limiting loop in a powerful pathway, and a disease where the loop is broken.
plos-pone-0007720:
Hannah Kuper and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures lasting physical disability in Rwanda, more than a decade after the 1994 genocide. At least eight hundred thousand people were killed that year. Many more were injured, yet the long-term burden of those injuries had never been assessed.

The team surveyed musculoskeletal impairment across the country. They asked how much of it traces to the war and related violence. Their estimates give health planners a clearer picture of need. Such data can direct surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic services to survivors.
plos-pone-0007820:
Meng-Yen Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows nerve death after injury in rats, and the genes switched on along the way. Cutting the sciatic nerve dooms some small neurons in the dorsal root ganglia. Those neurons, which carry pain and touch signals, die slowly.

The tumor suppressor WOX1 is known to take part in neuron death. The authors found WOX1 switched on strongly with two transcription factors, CREB and NF-kappaB. The co-activation appeared just as delayed neuron loss began. The pattern suggests a shared death program that might be interrupted to save neurons.
plos-pone-0007920:
Allison Abplanalp and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the sensors that let the body control tularemia infection. The cause, Francisella tularensis, is classed as a top-tier select agent. Sensor TLR2 had already been named a critical part of host protection.

Open questions remained about whether TLR2 signaling dominates the response. The authors tested how control of infection depends on Toll-like receptors. They also tracked the host's inflammatory responses. A clear map of these defenses matters for vaccine design. For a feared agent, it also informs medical response planning.
plos-pone-0008020:
Wojciech Lisik and colleagues logged gene shifts as rats learned to accept donor hearts in PLOS ONE in 2009. The trick used a hybrid immune molecule, part donor and part host, plus a low dose of a standard anti-rejection drug. Treated rats kept donor hearts for the long term.

Genes tied to T cell aim and movement quieted as tolerance set in. That quieting may be the mark of a truce between host and graft. Reading the mark could one day tell doctors which patients can safely ease off harsh drugs after a transplant.
plos-pone-0008120:
Albert Gjedde and Jacob Geday used deep brain stimulation to find where feelings are weighed in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stimulating a deep node, the subthalamic nucleus, changes the brain's monoamine tone, the broad mood chemistry. The team watched a frontal area called the ventromedial prefrontal cortex answer.

That frontal patch lit up as the place where emotional impact is judged. Earlier drug studies had pointed the same way; the stimulation test confirmed it from a new angle. A sharper map of the feeling judge could refine stimulation care for mood disorders.
plos-pone-0008220:
Toru Nakamura, Frank G. Hillary, and Bharat B. Biswal studied brain networks after injury in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Traumatic brain injury can disrupt how brain regions work together. Recovery may involve the brain rewiring those connections. The team examined resting networks at separate points during recovery. They used graph theory to describe network properties.

Whole-brain analysis of fMRI signals tracked six participants over time. Measurements began at three months after injury and continued later. Changes in network shape show plasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganize. Tracking that change could help doctors judge recovery and plan therapy.
plos-pone-0008320:
Evan H. Girvetz and colleagues presented a climate tool in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Global climate change talk drives international action. Yet local and regional changes are what directly affect people and ecosystems. A major barrier blocks informed local decisions: usable climate data are hard to access. The Climate Wizard was built to lower that barrier.

The tool lets users run applied climate-change analysis for their own areas. Scientists, managers, and policy makers are its intended audience. Easy maps and projections support practical planning. The paper describes both the tool and its uses.
plos-pone-0008420:
Mohamed Kodiha and colleagues dissected signals that move proteins into the nucleus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Signaling through MEK-ERK and PI3 kinase pathways affects many aspects of cell life. These pathways also help cells survive oxidant exposure. Oxidants play roles in many normal and disease processes. Many of those processes rely on transport into and out of the nucleus.

The team mapped signaling events that impact classical nuclear import. They also targeted the transport factors that carry cargo. Knowing how signals gate the nucleus explains how cells respond to stress. It may reveal drug points for diseases of transport.
plos-pone-0008520:
Mark Little and co-authors tackle a math problem in cancer models in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Stochastic carcinogenesis models describe cancer as a random process of mutations. A key question is which model parameters can be identified from data. Some past work studied this for the two-mutation cancer model. It found most parameter combinations were identifiable, with a few exceptions. Little extends that analysis to a general class of models.

He examines identifiability and redundancy across that broader class. Redundant parameters cannot be pinned down separately from data. Knowing which ones are redundant prevents false confidence in fits. The paper guides modelers on what cancer data can actually reveal.
plos-pone-0008620:
Josep Maria Lluis and co-authors study cell survival signaling in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. TRAIL is known as a death ligand in the TNF superfamily. It binds receptors bearing death domains and can kill tumor cells. It can also activate NF-kappaB, a survival pathway. The team study mouse fibroblasts treated with TRAIL. They ask if a kinase called TAK1 is required for their survival. TAK1 sits upstream of NF-kappaB activation.

They find TAK1 is required for survival of fibroblasts treated with TRAIL. It acts by NF-kappaB dependent induction of cFLIPL, a death blocker. Removing TAK1 tips TRAIL from survival signaling toward death. That balance matters for TRAIL-based cancer therapies under development.
plos-pone-0008720:
Agnieszka Rynda, Massimo Maddaloni, Javier Ochoa-Repáraz, and colleagues found a stand-in for peacekeeper cells. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, calm immune attacks on the body itself. A reovirus protein called sigma 1 can teach such tolerance. That protection seemed to need Tregs on duty. Multiple sclerosis is the human disease this model resembles.

The model disease is EAE, an MS-like illness in mice. A signal protein, IL-28, replaced the need for Tregs in protection. Mice stayed protected through a different helper than expected. New tolerance therapies might use such stand-ins when Tregs are scarce.
plos-pone-0008820:
Robert Akkers, Simon van Heeringen, J. Robert Manak, and colleagues designed genome scans for frog embryos. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. ChIP-chip links a DNA-binding protein to all its genome sites. The technique pairs chromatin capture with tiling microarrays. Embryos of the frog Xenopus are classic development models. Genome-wide binding maps there lagged behind cell-line work.

The designs adapt the method to whole frog embryos. They cover transcription factor binding and epigenetic marks together. Development biologists gain a route to embryo-wide regulatory maps. Such maps reveal how genes are orchestrated as a frog forms.
plos-pone-0008920:
Jie Dong, Yaping Gao, Yu Liu, and colleagues raised antibodies against a fresh spot on a major inflammation driver. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. TNF-alpha is a messenger that drives tissue damage in arthritis and similar diseases. Two antibody drugs against it were already in wide clinic use. A new epitope, the exact spot an antibody grips, might work differently. Antibodies to that novel spot were raised and tested.

The new antibodies protected mice against collagen-induced arthritis. Disease development slowed under their cover. A fresh grip on an old target can revive a drug class. Arthritis patients may gain options when current antibodies fail.
plos-pone-0009020:
Marco Mangone, Michael Myers, and Winship Herr pinned down the part of a protein that keeps cells dividing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HCF-1 is a human regulator that works with gene-switching proteins. It links enzymes that loosen or tighten DNA packaging to specific genes. The protein is huge, over two thousand amino acids long.

The team tested which region of HCF-1 cell growth depends on. A stretch called the basic region proved necessary for sustained proliferation. Without that stretch working, cells could not keep dividing normally. Mapping the growth duty to one region focuses future study of this cell-cycle player.
plos-pone-0009120:
Takefumi Nakazawa and co-authors checked whether a big fish's place on the menu is fixed for life, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bigger predators usually eat higher on the food chain. That size-to-niche link shapes how food webs work. Whether the link stays constant over time was untested.

The team used stable isotopes, chemical fingerprints of diet, in fish tissue. Isotopes record what a fish has eaten over past months. Comparing across seasons showed whether trophic position held steady. The study was the first isotope test of this assumption in a predatory fish.
plos-pone-0009220:
Roeland Huijgen and colleagues published this heart risk study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It follows people with familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited cause of very high cholesterol. Without treatment, their risk of early heart disease is high. Cholesterol-lowering drugs cut that risk sharply, and guidelines set ambitious targets for their blood levels.

The team checked patients two years after a DNA test confirmed their diagnosis. Most patients were on cholesterol-lowering treatment by then. Even so, only a minority had reached the treatment goal for LDL cholesterol. The gap between being treated and being treated enough is the study's warning for clinics.
plos-pone-0009320:
Christina Bormann Chung and co-authors published this genome methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Methylation, small chemical tags on DNA, helps decide which genes stay silent. Reading those tags across the whole genome guides research on cancer and development. The standard trick converts unmarked DNA letters while leaving marked ones intact.

The authors present a way to read the whole methylome with very deep sequencing. Their two-base encoding method improves accuracy when reading converted DNA. Deeper, cleaner reads mean fewer tags are missed or misread. The method gives labs a sharper tool for mapping the genome's chemical annotations.
plos-pone-0011420:
Dola Das, Xiu Luo, and Ajay Singh reported in 2010 a paradox about prion protein clumps and iron-driven cell damage. Clumps of prion protein are blamed for mad cow disease and related brain disorders, and iron that reacts with oxygen can poison cells. The natural assumption is that the clumps only add to the harm in a cell under iron stress.

Instead, the team found cases where the clumps shielded cells from iron-driven toxicity. A supposed weapon behaving as a shield complicates the standard story of prion harm. The clumps may be a desperate defense the cell builds under stress, with damage coming from elsewhere in the process. That flip matters for treatment design. Dissolving the clumps without care could remove a protection, so therapies may need to target the toxic step rather than the most visible one.
plos-pone-0011520:
Fiona Blanco-Kelly and co-authors reported in 2010 that one immune gene is tied to two different autoimmune diseases. CD40 helps immune cells activate each other, and it was already a suspect in several conditions. In a case-control study, the team tested its variants in Crohn's disease, a chronic gut inflammation, and checked the result against multiple sclerosis, a disease of the brain and spinal cord.

They found a novel association of CD40 with Crohn's disease and replicated its link to multiple sclerosis susceptibility. One shared gene in gut and brain autoimmunity hints at common roots beneath very different symptoms. Shared roots matter practically: drugs aimed at the CD40 pathway might serve both diseases. The study also strengthens the case for comparing autoimmune diseases together when hunting their genes, rather than searching each alone.
plos-pone-0011620:
Majid Eshaghi and co-authors mapped stress defences in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2010. When hydrogen peroxide attacks these yeast cells, a stress switch called Sty1 activates a partner protein, Atf1, which turns defence genes on. Whether every peroxide-induced gene is directly controlled by that pair was not yet clear.

The team profiled where Sty1 and Atf1 bind across the whole yeast genome during the attack. Their maps separate genes directly controlled by the pair from genes switched on by other routes. That distinction gives a fuller picture of how a simple cell organises a genome-wide emergency response.
plos-pone-0011720:
Rosanna Capparelli and co-authors found a surprise vaccine lead against staph infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When germs face bacteria-killing viruses called phages, resistant mutants show up fast. Away from the phage, though, those mutants often grow less well than normal germs, paying a fitness cost for their resistance.

The team tested a phage-proof Staphylococcus aureus mutant in mice. Far from merely staying alive, the mutant gave broad protection against staph disease. A weakened, phage-proof germ that doubles as a vaccine opens a backdoor route to guarding against a germ that shrugs off many drugs.
plos-pone-0011820:
Fernando Sepulveda and co-authors tested a physical view of Alzheimer's harm, in PLOS ONE in 2010. What sets off Alzheimer's is still largely unknown, which slows work on drugs that could change its course. One working idea holds that excess amyloid beta breaks cell membranes by forming pores, which then upsets the cell's ion balance.

The authors argue that the protein's harm to synapses, the links between brain cells, can be explained by this pore-forming power. Framing amyloid as a membrane puncher, not just a sticky clump, points drug work toward blocking the puncture itself.
plos-pone-0011920:
Attila Szücs and colleagues recorded in 2010 from a small rat brain area tied to anxiety and stress, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis. Neurons vary widely in the ion channels they carry, so a brain area can contain several distinct firing types side by side. The team used dynamic clamp, a method that adds virtual channels to living cells.

Their recordings show both consistency and diversity in how these neurons fire spikes. Some shared patterns mark the area's basic wiring, while the differences suggest specialized roles in stress responses. A careful catalog of firing styles is groundwork for understanding how this region helps turn stress into lasting anxiety.
plos-pone-0012020:
Merrin Rutherford and colleagues put in 2010 a blood test for TB to a real-world trial in Indonesia. The test, sold as QuantiFERON-Gold, looks for immune memory of the TB germ in a tube of blood and is used to find hidden infection. As part of a formal check, the team set its hit rate next to that of the older skin test in adults whose TB was sure.

Cases with germs seen in sputum stood in as the mark of true infection the blood test ought to catch. How often the test misses sure cases tells health programs how far to trust a clear result. In lands where TB is rife, that trust level decides if the blood test can take the place of the skin test, which needs two clinic visits to read.
plos-pone-0012120:
Alexis Morice, Béatrice Charreau, Bérangère Neveu, and co-authors studied killer T cells raised against herpesviruses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-lasting virus infections are linked to organ transplant rejection, but clear cases of one T cell attacking both a virus target and a donor organ target are rare. The team grew virus-specific T cell lines and tested whether they also react to foreign tissue markers.

Some of these cells did cross-react with tissue markers from other people. That means a cell trained by a common virus could also strike a transplanted organ carrying those markers. The finding helps explain why past infections can complicate transplants, and why matching and drug plans may need to account for a patient's virus history.
plos-pone-0012220:
Maciej Chichlowski, Greg Westwood, Soman Abraham, and co-authors studied mast cells in inflamed gut tissue in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammatory bowel disease is thought to arise when the immune system attacks the gut's own bacteria in a susceptible host. Mast cells, sentinels packed with alarm chemicals, sit just under the gut lining, perfectly placed to start or feed that attack.

Using mice that lack a calming immune signal and develop gut inflammation, the team tracked mast cells' part in the disease and in the colon tumors that chronic inflammation can spawn. If mast cells drive both, drugs that quiet them, already common for allergies, might find a second use in bowel disease care.
plos-pone-0012320:
Erin McElvania TeKippe, Irving Allen, Paul Hulseberg, and co-authors tested immune sensors in chronic tuberculosis infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A family of internal alarm proteins guards against acute infections, but what they do in a slow, years-long infection like tuberculosis was unknown. The team focused on one sensor, its adaptor partner, and the enzyme the pair activates, in mice infected with the tuberculosis bacterium.

Forming granulomas, the walled-off nodules that contain the bacteria, and defending the host required the adaptor but not the named sensor or enzyme. Untangling which alarms matter in chronic infection redirects drug and vaccine work toward the live wires. It also explains why a sensor famous in acute disease can be a bystander here.
plos-pone-0012420:
Francesca Setiadi, Nelson Ray, Holbrook Kohrt and colleagues counted and mapped immune cells in lymph nodes near breast tumors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Pathologists usually judge tissue by eye, without exact counts or maps of where cells sit. Nodes that drain a tumor are where immune defense is organized, so their layout may reveal how the battle is going.

Using quantitative imaging, the team measured immune cell subsets and their positions in patient nodes and healthy nodes. The tumor-draining nodes showed a distinct layout. Hard numbers on tissue geography could one day help predict which cancers spread and which patients need stronger treatment after surgery.
plos-pone-0012520:
Jian-Guo Ren, Pankaj Seth, Peter Everett and colleagues drained an enzyme from leukemia cells and watched them mature, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The mitochondrial enzyme malic enzyme 2 helps feed energy and building blocks to fast-growing cells, and its levels run high in some cancers. Human erythroleukemia cells are blood cancer cells stuck in an immature state.

Depleting the enzyme pushed the cells toward red blood cell differentiation, as if a growth brake had been released. Forcing cancer cells to mature is a proven treatment idea in some leukemias. The result nominates this metabolic enzyme as a target worth testing in blood cancers.
plos-pone-0012620:
Kochzius, Seidel, Antoniou and co-authors tackled a basic problem in the world fish trade: telling species apart. Fish must be named correctly at every stage, from eggs and larvae to the fillets sold in shops. Their 2010 paper tests two lab tools for the job, DNA barcodes and DNA microarrays.

A barcode reads a short stretch of DNA that differs between species, while a chip checks many samples at once. Together they can expose fraud and protect stocks that are fished too hard. Reliable naming also helps scientists track which fish live where.
plos-pone-0012720:
Pericolini, Gabrielli, Bistoni and co-authors traced how a fungal sugar coat harms T cells through the CD45 pathway. The coat, galactoxylomannan, comes from a yeast that attacks people with weak immunity. Earlier work showed it trips both of the cell's death pathways after meeting receptors on T cells.

Their 2010 study pins down the role of CD45, a major T cell surface signal protein, in that damage. Knowing the entry route may let doctors shield T cells during this infection. It also deepens the picture of how fungal products disarm immunity.

The team ran a cross-sectional study to measure how common anemia is in this group and what drives it.

Yooyen's findings tell local doctors whom to screen and which factors to watch. Anemia is easy to miss because its tiredness looks like diabetes itself. plos-pone-0357020:
