A thin lipid layer floats on tears and keeps eyes moist; its thickness varies more than doctors once assumed. The team ran a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of that variability and its clinical meaning.

Lee's findings help eye doctors read this subtle marker of dry eye disease and tailor treatment to it. Dry eye is common, uncomfortable, and often treated by trial and error. A measurable trait like lipid thickness, properly understood, can sort patients by cause. The study's care in describing normal variability is what makes abnormal readings meaningful in the clinic.
plos-pone-0355720:
Zehra Narlı Özdemir and coauthors published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on fatigue in people with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. That is an ultra-rare blood disorder in which red cells are destroyed by the body's own complement system. Fatigue is the complaint patients say never resolves, even on the standard drug eculizumab. Clinicians at eighteen Turkish centers surveyed just over a hundred treated patients face to face with a standard questionnaire.

More than a third of patients scored in the severe fatigue range despite treatment. Those patients had lower hemoglobin at diagnosis and at survey time, and they had spent longer on extra medications. In adjusted analysis, being female, having other illnesses, longer extra-medication use, and lower starting hemoglobin each tracked with severe fatigue. The results suggest that controlling the blood disorder alone does not lift fatigue, and clinics should track and treat it as its own problem.
plos-pone-0348820:
Hung-Chun Huang and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE building a sideline triage score for lower-back, pelvis, and hip dysfunction in college athletes. These problems often precede back pain, but expert assessment is scarce, so teams need a field tool flagging who needs priority care and who can self-manage. Over eight hundred athletes from ten universities completed standardized history and functional testing, and experts judged each case as the reference.

Just over half needed priority assessment. The final score combined fourteen factors: a dozen raising concern, such as local pain, weakness, and higher body mass, and two safety-related findings that lowered it. The score separated the groups well, kept its accuracy under bootstrap re-checking, and calibrated nearly perfectly. A cutoff caught most priority cases while clearing most self-managers. The tool is presented as ready for prospective testing in team settings.
plos-pone-0357920:

This study reports a one-day Kuala Lumpur consultation where twenty-eight stakeholders stress-tested the model before its pilot.

The group worked through the barriers their earlier research had surfaced. They drafted fixes: build awareness and demand, protect privacy and confidentiality, keep it affordable, and fold in HIV self-testing. They also proposed digital checklists, simpler lab requirements, and a practical workflow guide, plus serious training. On a large public mammography collection, the full version topped strong rival systems on accuracy and balanced scores while using fewer resources. Its chosen regions often overlapped the lesions human experts had marked. A bilingual questionnaire, in Northern Sámi and Norwegian, will measure compulsive internet use. It will also cover family, peer, and school norms. plos-pone-0348720:

The scorecard held up. Ratings fell into three themes: access and fairness, how well offices respond, and mother and child health support. Together they explained over half the spread. The ratings also hung together well. One main thread backed a single overall score. Proof matters because scorecards steer real policy debates. Five themes surfaced. Doctors rarely raised family building. Women felt unprepared for what pregnancy with the disease involves. Partners seemed to share the planning burden unequally. Costs shut down serious consideration of assisted reproduction. Above all, participants asked for earlier, repeated conversations. The authors urge sickle cell care to treat reproduction as routine, not taboo.
plos-pone-0356820:

The disease, now called MASLD, is common and worsens with age, but its molecular path over a lifetime is poorly mapped. The team combined well over a thousand liver samples from healthy donors and patients across a wide age range.

Healthy and diseased livers shared surprisingly few age-related genes, and some genes even moved in opposite directions with age. In healthy livers, aging genes centered on the cell cycle. In diseased livers, the changes instead involved protein cleanup systems, stress responses, and a pathway tied to cell death, and many tracked with scarring severity. The authors conclude the disease follows its own aging route, not just a faster version of the normal one, which matters for age-aware treatment.
plos-pone-0356720:

plos-pone-0348920:
Haruna Moshi and three colleagues examine why school-based deworming against schistosomiasis is delivered unevenly in Ghana, in this 2026 qualitative study. Preventive chemotherapy through schools is the main weapon against this parasitic disease, yet delivery in many districts falls short of World Health Organization targets and transmission persists. The researchers interviewed coordinators, head teachers, and school health teachers in two endemic districts of the Central Region.

Fidelity suffered where families feared the drugs or doubted the program, where supplies and money ran short, and where frontline teachers lacked training or incentives. It rose where awareness campaigns engaged the community, implementers felt motivated, and health and education sectors worked closely together. The authors conclude that faithful delivery is a system property, not a checklist, and must be built district by district.
plos-pone-0356620:
Huiling Chen and five colleagues mine twelve years of United States food recall records to find what makes a recall high-risk, in this 2026 study. Their source is the Food and Drug Administration's enforcement reports from 2012 to 2024, covering nearly twenty-seven thousand food recall events. They classified each recall's hazard, product, reach, and region, then modeled which features accompany the most serious category, Class I, meaning a real chance of serious harm.

Yearly counts swung widely without a steady trend. Two hazards dominated: microbial contamination and undeclared allergens. Bacterial contamination recalls were classified as high-risk at consistently high rates across food categories, while allergen recalls varied much more. Once hazard type was accounted for, region, product category, and distribution scope added little. The authors say the classification system is driven mainly by the hazard itself, as its rules intend.
plos-pone-0355620:
Cui Lin and colleagues followed rectal cancer patients home to test whether caregiver skill predicts stoma complications. A new ostomy demands careful daily care, and the family caregiver usually provides it. Their 2026 prospective study rated caregiver skill at discharge against set standards, then checked patients one month later.

Just over a third of patients developed a complication within the month, most often skin irritation or leakage. The skill gradient was steep. About three quarters of patients with low-skill caregivers had complications, against about one fifth in the high-skill group. Lin and colleagues argue discharge training should be tested against a clear skill standard, not given as a leaflet and a hope.
plos-pone-0355520:
Correction notice. Xin Pang and co-authors correct two figures in their published study of immune suppressor cells in oral cancer progression. After publication, readers flagged panels that appeared to overlap across different cell lines and conditions. This 2026 notice replaces the faulty panels with originals from the reported experiments.

The authors state that all three starting-time panels in one figure were incorrect and supply a corrected figure with its underlying data files. One panel in a second figure was likewise incorrect and is replaced. A panel said to show one cell line had overlapped a panel from another article showing a different line. The notice documents each fix so the experimental record can be checked.
plos-pone-0354520:
Janet Antwi led a team of seven authors on this 2026 pilot study of a produce prescription program at a historically Black university in the United States. Fifty-five students received nutrition classes and cooking demonstrations; half also got personalized bags of fresh produce every two weeks. Intake was tracked with screeners, day recalls, and food questionnaires.

The produce group showed favorable shifts in how often several fruits and vegetables were eaten, though most group-to-group differences missed statistical significance. Antwi reads the patterns as promising and calls for a larger, fully powered trial.
plos-pone-0354120:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 study, race six inflammation scores drawn from routine blood counts to see which best predicts peritonitis in people on peritoneal dialysis. This infection of the belly lining is the Achilles heel of home dialysis and can end the treatment. More than two thousand patients from ten centers were followed.

About seven in every hundred patients developed peritonitis during follow-up. Three scores, built from ratios and products of blood cell counts, each more than doubled the estimated risk when high, and each separated future cases from non-cases moderately well. The relationships were curved rather than straight, rising steeply past certain levels. No score dominated the others. The authors suggest these free scores, computed from blood tests patients already get, could flag who needs closer watching and earlier teaching on sterile technique.
plos-pone-0353020:
Yusuf Başkıran and three colleagues compare three ways of performing a hysterectomy and their after-effects, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Turkish hospital. Records covered four hundred and sixty-six women whose wombs were removed for non-cancer reasons between 2020 and 2023, by the open abdominal route, by keyhole surgery, or through the vagina. The team measured vaginal length and sexual function scores before and after surgery.

Vaginal length shrank most after keyhole surgery, yet women's sexual function scores ended up similar across all three routes. Their partners' scores dipped after surgery, a finding the authors flag as tentative. The practical reading: surgical route changes anatomy measurably without clearly changing women's early sexual wellbeing.
plos-pone-0353420:
Marcos De Andrés Montero and seven colleagues present a method for untangling mass graves where bones from many people lie mixed together, in this 2026 PLOS ONE archaeology paper. Reassembling individuals is the necessary first step before any identification, yet field guidance has been thin. Their approach records the exact position of every bone in mapping software and adds a new coding system that tracks how complete each skeleton is.

Applied to a crowded sixteenth-century burial in southwestern Hungary, the method substantially increased the number of fully reassembled skeletons and suggested matches for many loose elements. Working spatially first, they argue, makes later bone-sorting techniques far more effective — a step toward naming the dead.
plos-pone-0354020:
Agazhe Aemro and five colleagues count how often women across nine sub-Saharan African countries have ever tested for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of national health surveys. The sample covers nearly one hundred and sixty thousand women aged fifteen to forty-nine. The average woman had tested about two and a half times in her life, but the typical woman — the median — had never tested at all.

Testing rose with age, education, wealth, employment, and knowledge about HIV, and varied enormously by region, with southern Africa far ahead. Having more partners, perhaps through antenatal and clinic contact, sharply raised counts. Over half of women had never tested, a gap the authors say needs community-level, region-specific campaigns.
plos-pone-0353520:
Anggeriyane and colleagues published a plan in 2026 for mapping what is known about emotional and behavioral troubles in preschool children. Young children who struggle to manage feelings and behavior can face lasting harm later in life. Yet past studies are scattered across fields and use very different ways to measure the same problems.

Under the plan, the team will search six large databases for studies from the year 2000 onward, with no limit on language. Two reviewers will screen and chart the studies on their own, then group the linked factors into body, mind, family, and wider life domains. Readers get a clear map of what has been studied and where the gaps still sit.
plos-pone-0353120:
Bilgilisoy Filiz and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 on gel injections for knee osteoarthritis. More than one hundred adults with moderate knee wear will receive either a high-dose gel injection or salt water, then swap after three months, with neither patients nor assessors knowing the order. Pain, function, strength, and quality of life will be tracked for a year.

The crossover design lets each patient serve as their own comparison. Three-month results will judge benefit, while the full year watches safety. Gel injections are widely sold but unevenly proven, so a blinded trial with a dummy injection offers unusually firm evidence for patients weighing cost against relief.
plos-pone-0345720:
Md Yasin and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on predicting two key measures of knitted cotton fabric before it is finished. Mills need to know a fabric's final width and its weight per square meter, yet both shift during production. The authors built a fuzzy logic model that takes stitch length, yarn fineness, and machine diameter as inputs.

The model was trained on more than thirty thousand real production records and then checked against fresh factory data. Its predictions landed very close to the actual width and weight values. Because the system rests on proven factory data rather than lab trials alone, the authors present it as a practical planning tool for textile mills that want fewer surprises in finished cloth.
plos-pone-0351120:
Yao Zhao and Haoyu Zhou followed college students' sleep across all four undergraduate years in this 2026 study. Most earlier work measured sleep at single moments. These authors instead treated each student's nightly pattern as a smooth curve that changes over time. They used records from the NetHealth Project at an American university.

Wearable trackers produced more than sixty thousand daily sleep records for seventy-six students. Sleep grew longer across the four years, with clear seasonal swings tied to the academic calendar. Better grades and longer sleep went together throughout college. Each step up in grade average came with roughly twenty-seven extra minutes of sleep. Social activity levels also lined up with distinct sleep patterns, which argues for treating student sleep as a moving process, not a fixed habit.
plos-pone-0352420:
Sandani De Vass Gunawardane and seven colleagues investigate a herbal capsule called Vernolac in this 2026 study. The product blends five Sri Lankan medicinal plants, including black seed and Indian sarsaparilla. Each plant has shown anti-cancer activity on its own. The team asked how the mixture might act against cancer as a whole.

Computer databases yielded one hundred fifty-five drug-like compounds from the blend. Their predicted protein targets overlapped with cancer-related targets at one hundred thirty-seven points. Network analysis highlighted fourteen hub proteins, many central to cell growth and death. Chemical profiling of the extract confirmed a rich mix of active plant compounds. The work maps plausible routes for the formula's effects, while stressing that laboratory and clinical proof must follow.
plos-pone-0351220:
Heghine Gevorgyan and three colleagues probe how gut bacteria manage acid stress. Their 2026 study works with Escherichia coli fermenting sugars at an acidic pH. A protein switch called FhlA turns on the formate hydrogen lyase complex. That machinery converts formate into hydrogen gas, consuming protons as it goes. The team compared normal bacteria with mutants lacking the switch. They tracked the cell's main energy turbine, proton flows, and membrane properties at two growth stages.

Mutants showed weakened turbine activity and slower proton flux. The two systems, acid disposal and energy generation, clearly lean on each other. Older cultures of both strains carried more protective membrane groups and leaked fewer protons. Membrane voltage in the mutants stayed stubbornly unchanged. Bacteria, the authors conclude, balance their proton budget by coordinating several systems at once. Understanding that bookkeeping helps anyone fermenting microbes industrially, or fighting them medically, at low pH.
plos-pone-0352020:
Noumou Keita and seven colleagues reconstruct COVID-19's path through Mali from the virus's own genome. Their 2026 study is the country's first comprehensive genomic account. Mali recorded over thirty-three thousand confirmed cases between 2020 and 2025. The team analysed five hundred forty-eight Malian viral sequences. A high-quality subset, combined with close global relatives, powered time-resolved family trees. West African data are scarce in global surveillance, which makes every reconstructed introduction valuable.

Five distinct epidemic waves emerged. Early lineages gave way, wave by wave, to the dominant variants of 2023. Introductions traced mainly to Europe and North America. After each arrival, local transmission sustained itself. Viruses also flowed back and forth with neighbouring African countries. Molecular clock analysis dated the movements. For Malian health authorities, the reconstruction shows their epidemic was repeatedly reseeded from abroad, then homegrown. Border awareness and local genomic capacity both follow from that picture.
plos-pone-0350120:
Mahunan Sossou and Dieu donné Gnonlonfoun reviewed intensive care records from Benin's national referral hospital for adults admitted with impaired consciousness. A dimmed or lost consciousness is common, dangerous, and little studied in low-resource intensive care. Records for four hundred sixteen patients admitted over two and a half years were used to estimate survival and find traits tied to death.

Two of every three patients died in the unit, half of the deaths within five days. Older age, deeper coma, low blood pressure, high temperature, and lacking oxygen therapy each raised the risk, while head injury cases fared comparatively better. The authors say simple admission readings can flag who needs attention first, and they make a plain case for reliable oxygen and basic monitoring before fancier equipment.
plos-pone-0352120:
Haeun Hwang and colleagues tested whether a cancer drug, omipalisib, can help brain cells clear out the tangled tau protein behind a family of dementias. Tau tangles grow when the cell's recycling system, autophagy, falters. The drug blocks a growth switch called mTOR, which normally holds recycling back. The team tried it in human cells engineered to make a mutant tau and in mice bred to develop tau disease.

In the cells, the drug loosened the mTOR brake, raised recycling markers, and lowered both a recycling backlog protein and the harmful modified form of tau, without killing the cells. Mice received the drug for two months starting at six months of age. The work supports the idea that freeing the cell's cleanup crew can cut tau buildup, a strategy now open to further testing in animals.
plos-pone-0352320:
Ahmad Sarraj and colleagues ran a small trial on whether brain stimulation adds anything to an intensive rehab method for people with long-standing paraplegia from spinal cord injury. The base method pairs imagining movements with strong sensory stimulation of the legs. Fifty patients were split among usual care, the method alone, and the method plus mild electrical stimulation of the scalp, over ten days.

Patients on usual care gained nothing measurable. Both active groups improved substantially and by the same amount on touch and pinprick sensation. So the sensory recovery seems to come from the peripheral method itself, with no extra gain from the brain stimulation on those measures. For clinics, that simplifies the recipe: the cheaper, simpler half of the pairing appears to carry the sensory benefit.
plos-pone-0341920:
Spotting strange traffic on a computer network early can stop attacks before damage spreads. Debiao Luo and co-authors combine several techniques into one detection system, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper on network safety.

Raw traffic is first broken into smoother waves to remove noise. A hybrid network then reads the signal two ways at once: attention heads catch far-apart links, while a memory network reads the sequence in both directions. A firefly-inspired search tunes the system's settings automatically. On standard test data the combined model beat earlier methods on both error rates and detection scores, with gains the authors checked statistically.
plos-pone-0351320:
Machines that tumble samples slowly can fake weightlessness on Earth, helping biologists rehearse space experiments. Andrada Pica and colleagues measured how well one such random positioning machine actually performs, in this 2026 PLOS One study combining motion sensors, computer modeling, and living nerve cells.

Sensors rode the frames while the machine ran in three modes. Modeling showed average gravity fell to between a hundredth and a thousandth of Earth's, with sideways spin forces staying tiny. Nerve cells grown under each mode reacted to the treatment. The authors offer the numbers as a reference so other labs can judge whether the simulation suits their experiments.
plos-pone-0350920:
Farming shapes Vietnam's carbon footprint crop by crop, and An Thinh Nguyen and colleagues trained a neural network on three decades of data to weigh each land use. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered twenty-one farm product types from 1990 to 2019.

Most types moved with higher carbon dioxide emissions, including bananas, beans, cassava, coffee, and coconuts. Five moved the other way, among them rice, soybeans, and sesame. A four-layer network captured the links despite their tangled, non-linear shape. The authors say such product-level evidence helps policymakers target emission cuts where they count, instead of taxing all agriculture alike.
plos-pone-0350020:
Charumita Vasudev and colleagues spoke at length with eighty six households in Uttar Pradesh and Goa, India, about food hardship during and after COVID. Field work ran from late 2022 into early 2023, with hundreds of interviews. Households mixed migrant and settled families, town and village homes, and varied caste and family types.

Everyday fixes came first: swapping foods, shrinking portions, and pooling what kin could share. Harder shocks forced harsher steps, like mothers eating last, selling goods, taking debt, pulling children from school, and delaying care. Settled village families leaned on kin and state food support. Migrants often lacked both, so place and movement shaped survival more than income loss alone.
plos-pone-0349120:
Maguy Saffouh El Hajj and colleagues reviewed why drug errors happen in local pharmacies, where most people collect their medicines. Hospital safety has drawn more study, yet busy counters carry real risk too. Thirteen studies, mostly from the United States and England, were woven together with a method that builds new themes from interview based research.

Five broad causes emerged from the weaving. Workload, staffing, and time pressure ran through many accounts, along with poor handoffs and weak safety habits. Checks confirmed fair trust in most themes. Local pharmacies need system fixes, like calmer workflow and better double checks, rather than blame aimed at single staff members working under strain.
plos-pone-0350820:
Kanae Kondo and colleagues tracked cigarette sales and household tobacco spending in Japan across the COVID pandemic with national data stretching from 2014 onward. Sales series, spending surveys, and smoking rate data were modelled around the first emergency declaration and the later downgrade of COVID to a routine illness class.

Cigarette sales kept falling after the emergency, but more slowly than before. Price adjusted monthly tobacco spending jumped in the first emergency month, though later checks weakened that finding. Male smoking eased down year by year while female rates barely moved. Crises do not reliably cut smoking, the authors warn; stress and home time can blunt tobacco control.
plos-pone-0347020:
Nasser A M Barakat and co-authors built a new electrode material in 2026 for turning urea in wastewater into energy. Urea is a common pollutant from farms and factories, and breaking it down with electricity can clean water while recovering power.

Thin carbon fibers were spun with nickel particles, plus phosphorus and nitrogen from a cheap starting chemical. Heat treatment tuned the nickel surface into a form ready for the reaction. In alkaline tests the best mix started working at low voltage and carried a strong current. Pairs of dirty water treatment and energy recovery make such catalysts worth developing further.
plos-pone-0349820:
Bandar Alghamdi and Sonia Rocha searched for low oxygen related genes that forecast lung adenocarcinoma outcomes in 2026. Tumors short of oxygen grow more aggressive and resist treatment, so their gene marks could guide care.

Comparing tumor and normal data, the team found hundreds of oxygen linked genes switched up or down. Up genes clustered in cancer and signalling pathways; down genes tied to immunity. Hub genes included known cancer players on both sides. Survival modelling then picked out genes whose levels track patient outcomes. Such marks may one day sort patients by risk and hint at drug targets in oxygen starved tumors.
plos-pone-0343920:
Imane Bagheri, Atena Dadgari, and Naiire Salmani interviewed palliative care staff in 2026 about death doulas, non medical companions for dying people. Cancer patients at the end of life and their families often need more support than clinical teams can give.

Fourteen staff members described what must exist before the role can work: drivers pushing for it, proper recruiting and training, and basic structures to host it. Challenges included families not knowing the role and officials not recognising it formally. The study gives planners a grounded checklist for introducing doulas without confusion about who does what at the bedside.
plos-pone-0349020:
Javier Silva-Valencia and colleagues tracked lung exercise testing across Ontario over the years spanning the time before COVID-19 hit, the crisis itself, and the recovery since. These tests, such as the six-minute walk test, help doctors judge breathing problems and decide who needs long-term oxygen. The team used province-wide health records covering 2015 to 2023.

More than half a million tests were recorded, yet by late 2023 testing rates were still about a fifth below pre-pandemic levels. Recovery was uneven, lagging more for men and for some other groups. The shortfall matters because delayed testing can delay treatment decisions for people with chronic lung and heart disease.
plos-pone-0349220:
Nicholas Behn and colleagues gathered thirteen earlier studies to describe what life feels like when brain injury disrupts the thinking side of communication. After such injuries, people may struggle to follow conversation, find words, or read social cues, even when speech itself sounds fine. The review pools the voices of more than one hundred people with brain injury and sixty-six family members and friends.

Across the studies, eight themes emerged, starting with the plain fact that communicating is no longer easy. Participants described lost confidence, strained relationships, and services that overlook the problem. The authors argue that care should treat communication partners as part of the picture, since spouses, parents, and friends carry much of the daily repair work that keeps conversation going.
plos-pone-0346820:
Mian Li and co-workers simulate, atom by atom, what happens when a common clay mineral soaks up water. The mineral, illite, is plentiful in oil shale, and its swelling can weaken rock. Their 2026 study runs computer models that vary heat, pressure, and water amount to watch the mineral's size, density, and stiffness change.

Water pushed the crystal to swell mostly along one direction. Pressure held the swelling back, while heat and more water sped it up. The mineral grew stiffer under pressure and softer as heat or water rose. Knowing these micro-level rules helps engineers judge rock stability for oil work and building projects where wet clay can cause trouble.
plos-pone-0348220:
Fanwei Meng and Bing Chen review infections picked up in hospital by children kept alive on heart-lung machines after heart surgery. The machines, known as ECMO, support children born with heart defects while they heal. Their 2026 study covers fifty-four children at one Chinese heart hospital over five years and compares those who caught infections with those who did not.

Fourteen children developed infections, mostly lung infections from tough Gram-negative bacteria. Having a breathing tube placed before surgery stood out as the one clear risk factor in the final analysis. Longer intensive care stays also appeared more often in the infected group. Death rates did not differ clearly. The results urge extra infection care around airway tubes in these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0348520:
Sangjin Lee, Sunggon Kim, and Yongseok Son build a faster defragmentation tool for flash-based solid-state drives. Even fast drives slow when heavy editing scatters a file's blocks across the chip, and the standard tool works through files one by one. Their 2026 system first collects file maps for everything, then runs many defragmenters in parallel, each owning one file and issuing requests without waiting.

On a common multi-core machine with a consumer drive, the tool finished cleanups up to nearly four times faster than the standard one. Throughput rose across workloads, and a program running alongside suffered less slowdown. Data centers juggling huge shared drives could tidy storage in shorter, less disruptive windows.
plos-pone-0345620:
Juliana Amorim and colleagues hunt for new antibacterial compounds in nature's chemistry library, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer study. Their target is an enzyme Staphylococcus aureus needs to make its golden pigment, which shields the bacterium from immune attack; blocking the enzyme should weaken the germ rather than kill it outright.

Starting from nearly three hundred thousand natural products, shape-based screening and then activity models narrowed the field to about two thousand strong candidates, with a few dozen predicted to bind extremely tightly. Five finalists held stable grips on the enzyme in molecular simulations. The list gives chemists concrete starting points for lab testing against a pathogen known for drug resistance.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1520 is a routine UN Security Council renewal of the Golan Heights observer force, adopted unanimously on 22 December 2003. The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force has patrolled the separation zone between Israel and Syria since 1974, and the Secretary-General's December report described its continued work.

The resolution calls on the parties to implement Resolution 338, the 1973 ceasefire and peace-talks order, immediately, and renews the observer force's mandate for six months, until 30 June 2004. It asks the Secretary-General to report at the end of that period on developments and on steps toward carrying out Resolution 338. These twice-yearly renewals kept a quiet border under watch.

Three days of cover for Balkan rules came out of a court fight in 2002. On 30 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1420 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. Nine days before, Resolution 1418 had kept the rules of Resolution 1357 alive to 30 June. That deadline had now arrived. The Council's next step on Bosnia was still not ready.

The text keeps Resolution 1357 in force to 3 July 2002. It stays seized of the matter as well. The scramble had a clear cause. A fight raged over the new world criminal court and shield for peacekeepers. The Council settled that fight in July with Resolution 1422.

Resolution 120 was adopted on 4 November 1956, as Soviet troops were crushing an uprising in Hungary. Ten members voted in favor and only the Soviet Union voted against. Because the permanent members were split, the Council admitted it could not carry out its main duty of guarding world peace in this crisis.

Rather than drop the matter, the Council sent it to the full membership. It called an emergency special session of the General Assembly under the 1950 Uniting for Peace procedure, which lets the Assembly step in when the Council is deadlocked. That session was asked to recommend what should be done about Hungary.

Choosing a Secretary-General is among the Council's gravest tasks. In 1991 the members met behind closed doors to pick a successor to Javier Pérez de Cuéllar. Resolution 720 was adopted unanimously at that closed meeting on 21 November 1991. The question was the recommendation for the UN's top job.

The Council put forward Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt. His proposed term ran from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996. The General Assembly accepted the choice. Boutros-Ghali became the first African and first Arab to lead the UN. His tenure covered Somalia, Rwanda, and Bosnia. This one-line recommendation set all of that in motion.

One index gives this text the year 2003. The page's own facts say 2006. It cites the chief's report of 16 October 2006. Past votes from that spring are named too. The topic is Western Sahara, the desert land claimed by Morocco. A UN team, MINURSO, guards a truce there. A vote on the land's fate has been pledged since 1991.

MINURSO's term grew to 30 April 2007. The Council asked for a fresh report before that date. States were urged to fund goodwill steps. The chief ask was visits between kin split by the war. One more clause told the force to hold fast to the UN's zero-tolerance rule on sexual abuse by its staff.

Talks on Western Sahara had run in fits and starts for years. Four rounds of formal talks were done by 2010. Loose talks in Austria and the United States had kept hope warm. A new envoy, Christopher Ross, toured the area. Resolution 1920 passed on 30 April 2010. The chief's report of 6 April lay on the table.

MINURSO, the UN team there, gained a year, to 30 April 2011. Both sides had to honor the truce pacts in full. Small, loose talks would pave a fifth round. Real will to deal was called for, on a base of give and take. Family visits, by land as well as air, won warm words. States were asked to fund such steps. The text is firm that the old standstill could not last for good.

How to cage the atom was the young UN's gravest task. Its Atomic Energy Commission sent a first report on the last day of 1946. The plan sketched world checks on the new force. Resolution 20 passed with no dissent on 10 March 1947. The Council had read the report with care.

No part of the plan bound a state on its own. Each vote of yes was a first step, not a last word. The full plan had to be taken as one whole. The record of the talks went back to the team. It was urged to press on with all speed. A draft treaty on world control was the goal. A second report was due before the Assembly next sat. Hope still ran high that the bomb could be ruled by law.

Resolution 620, adopted on 26 August 1988, returns to chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq war with harder evidence. Three missions sent by the Secretary-General that summer had confirmed continued poison gas use, and gas attacks on Iranians had grown fiercer and more often. The Council said it was deeply dismayed and worried about future use.

The Council condemned resolutely the use of chemical weapons in defiance of the 1925 Geneva Protocol and of its own demand that spring. It encouraged the Secretary-General to investigate new allegations from any member state quickly, with expert help. It also backed the Geneva disarmament talks then negotiating a total ban on developing, producing, and stockpiling chemical weapons, work that produced the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention.

Sierra Leone's next step after peacekeeping is set out in Resolution 1620, adopted on 31 August 2005. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was set to leave at the end of 2005 after helping the country recover from war. Sierra Leone's president joined the Secretary-General in asking for a UN office that would stay on and help hold the peace.

The Council asks for a United Nations Integrated Office in Sierra Leone, UNIOSIL, for twelve months from 1 January 2006. Its tasks cover building state offices, planning a human rights action plan, readying fair elections in 2007, fighting corruption, and strengthening courts, police, and the security sector. It must also track cross-border troubles such as small arms flows and work with the Special Court for Sierra Leone.

Liberia's peace process is reshaped in Resolution 1020, adopted on 10 November 1995. The Liberian sides had restored a ceasefire, installed a new Council of State, and agreed on a timetable running to elections. The UN Observer Mission in Liberia, UNOMIL, worked with the West African force ECOMOG. Ceasefire breaches and slow troop separation still caused worry.

The Council rewrites UNOMIL's mandate. The mission is to support ECOWAS and the transitional government. It is to probe reported ceasefire breaches and watch disarmament and the arms embargo. It is to help run assembly sites and fighter demobilization. It is also to back aid work and report on human rights abuses. It is to observe the planned legislative and presidential elections. Its military observers are capped at 160. States are urged to fund ECOMOG and the UN Trust Fund for Liberia, and the arms embargo is recalled.

Resolution 1220, adopted by the Security Council on 12 January 1999, keeps Sierra Leone's observer mission alive while fighting worsens. The Council voices concern at the recent deterioration and backs efforts to restore lasting peace. It extends the mandate of the UN Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 March 1999. It notes the Secretary-General's plan to reduce the military observers, keep a small team in Conakry, Guinea, and send them back when conditions allow. It asks for a further report with recommendations by 5 March 1999.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: At the twenty-third plenary meeting on 6 February 1946, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 20. It is a short order about pensions at the International Court of Justice. The Assembly wanted fair and sound pensions for the Court's judges, registrar, and staff. It told the Secretary-General to draw up a pension plan, working with the Court's registrar. He was to bring it to the second part of the first session.

General Assembly Resolution 50/220, adopted on 3 April 1996, renewed the Guatemala verification mission until 31 December 1996. The Assembly took note of the mission director's third and fourth reports. It voiced concern at weak carrying-out of the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights during 1995. There had been little action on the mission's advice.

At the same time it welcomed the new Guatemalan president's pledge to fight impunity and keep the peace process going. It welcomed the restart of talks aimed at an early final peace. Both parties were called on to act on the reports' advice and back the mission fully. They were called on to take steps to end civilian suffering and build trust.

Resolution 69/20 of the General Assembly is the annual mandate renewal for the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. The Assembly thanks the Committee for its work. It asks it to keep promoting Palestinian self-determination, and an end to the occupation that began in 1967 on a two-State basis. It authorizes it to adjust its program of work as events require. It also asks the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development to report on the economic costs of the occupation.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
What began as a small observer team on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border becomes a full peacekeeping force in this text of 15 September 2000. The mission, UNMEE, had been created weeks earlier, after the June ceasefire ended the border war. Now it needed soldiers, not just observers.

The Council authorized up to 4,200 troops, including up to 220 military observers, to serve until 15 March 2001. Their job was to watch the ceasefire, check that both sides kept their security pledges, and confirm that Ethiopian troops left ground taken after February 1999. The Council also pushed both countries toward mine clearing, aid access, and a final peace deal without delay.

Sexual violence in war is the subject of this 2008 follow-up to the landmark text on women, peace, and security. Rape and other sexual violence, it notes, are used as tactics of war to humiliate, dominate, and displace communities. Such acts can count as war crimes, crimes against humanity, or acts of genocide.

All parties to armed conflicts are demanded to stop all sexual violence against civilians at once. Parties must train troops on the ban, enforce discipline and command responsibility, debunk myths that fuel such violence, and screen forces for past abuses. Peacekeepers are to be trained to prevent and respond to sexual violence, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on where such violence is used as a weapon of war.

Cyprus still needed its United Nations peacekeeping force in the spring of 1966. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still required to keep the peace on the island. The government of Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 26 March 1966. The island's basic problem, though, remained unsolved. Resolution 220 was adopted unanimously on 16 March 1966.

The Council reaffirmed all its Cyprus resolutions, back to Resolution 186 of 1964. It urged everyone involved to show the utmost restraint. The force was extended for three more months, ending on 26 June 1966. The Council stated its firm hope that real progress toward a settlement would come within that period. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place while the search for a settlement went on.

Sanctions against Southern Rhodesia were being broken openly by 1972. Several states still traded with the illegal regime despite the mandatory embargo. The United States had reported that it authorized imports of Rhodesian chrome ore and other minerals. Resolution 320 was adopted on 29 September 1972.

The Council reaffirmed that the sanctions would stay fully in force. They would last until the goals of Resolution 253 of 1968 were met. All states were called on to apply the sanctions in full. The United States was urged to cooperate with the United Nations on enforcement. South Africa and Portugal were condemned for refusing to cooperate. The Council's sanctions committee was told to study stronger action as a matter of urgency.

The Golan Heights observer force received six more months on 30 November 1977, under Resolution 420. The force watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council noted the efforts made toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East. It also noted the urgent need to press on with those efforts. Tension in the area still prevailed.

The parties were called on to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text had demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another period of six months, until 31 May 1978. At the end of that time, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to carry out Resolution 338.

Lebanon's president-elect was murdered in September 1982, during Israel's invasion of the country. Bashir Gemayel, named in the text, had been elected to lead Lebanon. Days after his death, Israeli forces moved into Beirut in breach of the cease-fire. Resolution 520 was adopted on 17 September 1982.

The Council condemned the murder of the president-elect. It also condemned every effort to block, by violence, the return of a strong and stable government in Lebanon. Its resolutions on Lebanon from earlier in 1982 were reaffirmed in full. The Israeli incursions into Beirut were condemned. Israel was told to return its forces at once to the positions held before 15 September. The Council also backed the United Nations observers stationed around Beirut. Lebanon's sovereignty was to be respected, under the authority of its own army.
un-sc-res-1520:
The observer force on the Golan Heights was renewed in the settled form of those years on 22 December 2003. The force, called UNDOF, watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 9 December 2003, was before the Council. Resolution 1520 was adopted unanimously.

The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. UNDOF's mandate was renewed for six months, until 30 June 2004. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments in the area. His report also had to cover the steps taken to put Resolution 338 into effect. Renewals like this one had kept UNDOF on the Golan, term after term, for three decades.
un-sc-res-1420: Bosnia's peacekeeping arrangements hit a legal snag at the end of June 2002. On 30 June 2002 the Security Council kept its earlier Bosnia provisions in force a little longer. The measures in resolution 1357 would now run until 3 July 2002. The Council acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The text is two short paragraphs. The three-day bridge covered a dispute over the new International Criminal Court. A fuller settlement of the issue followed within days.
un-sc-res-120:
Soviet troops were crushing Hungary's uprising when the Council met in November 1956. On 4 November 1956 it noted the grave situation made by Soviet military force. Hungarians, it said, were trying to reassert their rights. The permanent members could not agree, so the Council could not act on its own. That deadlock shaped the remedy the text chose.

The Council called an emergency special session of the General Assembly. It used the Uniting for Peace procedure of 1950. The Assembly would make fitting recommendations on Hungary. The move is a classic case of the Council passing a crisis to the wider membership. It could not, in the end, stop the Soviet crackdown.
un-sc-res-1720:
Western Sahara's referendum mission rolled into another term in the autumn of 2006. On 31 October 2006 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 April 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on the dispute that month. The Council restated its support for him and his envoy. It again promised help toward a settlement both sides could accept. That settlement had to allow self-determination for the territory's people.

The parties had to respect the military agreements behind the ceasefire. Member states were asked to fund family visits for divided Sahrawi families. The Secretary-General owed a report before the term ended. His staff also had to enforce the United Nations' zero-tolerance rules in the mission. The political deadlock survived the renewal.
un-sc-res-1920:
Western Sahara's peace process gained another year of support in 2010. On 30 April 2010 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 April 2011. The parties had held small informal talks to prepare a fifth round of negotiations. The Council welcomed that commitment. It backed the Secretary-General and his envoy in their push for a settlement. Realism and compromise, it said, were essential.

Both sides had to respect the military agreements behind the ceasefire in full. They had to show political will and talk in good faith. The goal stayed a solution that lets the territory's people decide their future. The Council also called for trust-building steps, including family visits. The mandate renewal kept observers along the berm for another year.
un-sc-res-20:
Atomic energy control was the Council's subject in March 1947. The Atomic Energy Commission had sent its first report that winter. On 10 March 1947 the Council laid down a caution. Any agreement a member showed to parts of the report was only preliminary. Final acceptance of any part depended on taking the whole control plan. That rule stopped states from picking only the clauses they liked.

The Council sent the record of its debate back to the commission. It urged the commission to press on with all speed. Every phase of international atomic control needed study. Concrete proposals for a treaty were the goal. A second report was due before the next General Assembly session. The plan behind the report later failed amid Cold War distrust.
un-sc-res-620:
Chemical weapons use in the Gulf war drew a firmer Security Council line on 26 August 1988. Three missions sent by the Secretary-General had reported in July and August. Their findings showed continued use of chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq conflict. Such use against Iranians had become more intense and more frequent, the missions found. Talks in Geneva on a full ban on chemical weapons were under way.

The Council condemned resolutely the use of chemical weapons in breach of the Geneva Protocol of 1925. It noted that the use defied its own resolution 612 (1988) of May. It encouraged the Secretary-General to investigate at once any claim by a member state of possible use of chemical, biological, or toxin weapons. He was to check the facts and report the results. The Council vowed to intensify its efforts to end all such use.
un-sc-res-1620:
Sierra Leone's peacekeeping era closed into an integrated office on 31 August 2005. UNAMSIL had helped the country recover from conflict, the Council said. The Secretary-General's report of 26 April and its July addendum advised a follow-on office. Sierra Leone's president wrote on 21 June asking for the same. The office would back governance, conflict prevention, and the 2007 elections.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to establish the United Nations Integrated Office in Sierra Leone, UNIOSIL, from 1 January 2006. It would run for an initial twelve months. The government's primary duty for the country's peace and growth was underlined. The office had to be fully integrated, with one United Nations team speaking with a single voice. Planning for the Special Court's security after UNAMSIL left had to continue. The Secretary-General would keep the Council informed of the office's work. The handover marked the shift from peacekeeping to peacebuilding.
un-sc-res-1020:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1020 deals with Liberia during its civil war in the 1990s. The Council adopted it on 10 November 1995. A cease-fire and a new Council of State had just raised hopes for peace. West African troops, called ECOMOG, were already on the ground.

The text reshapes the work of the United Nations Observer Mission in Liberia, called UNOMIL. Its observers would check cease-fire claims, watch disarmament, and help fighters leave the war. They would also support aid work and watch the planned elections. The Council capped the observer team at 160 and demanded respect for all peace staff.
un-sc-res-1220: Adopting Resolution 1220 on 12 January 1999, the Council acted on Sierra Leone. Fighting had worsened sharply, and the rebel advance on the capital put the peace effort at risk. The Council extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, called UNOMSIL, until 13 March 1999. Most of its military observers will pull back to Conakry for safety. A small team stays ready to return once conditions allow. The Secretary-General must report by 5 March 1999 with ideas for the mission's future.
un-sc-res-720: The Council took formal action on the Secretary-General's post in Resolution 720, adopted unanimously at a closed meeting on 21 November 1991. The sitting chief's term was ending that year. The Council had weighed who should lead the United Nations next. It recommends to the General Assembly that Boutros Boutros-Ghali be appointed Secretary-General. His term would run from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996. The Assembly confirmed the choice, and the Egyptian diplomat became the sixth person to hold the post.
un-doc-address-to-the-united-nations-gen:
Chile's president, Michelle Bachelet, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. She spoke as the first woman elected to lead her country. Chile had come through hard years of dictatorship. Growth had lifted millions out of poverty in the sixteen years before she spoke.

She backs world law and a strong United Nations. Rich states should open their markets to goods from the South. Chile funds cheap drugs for the poor through a small levy on plane tickets. She faults the 2005 Summit for silence on disarmament. Chile serves with the peace mission in Haiti. She also marks thirty years since a former Chilean minister was murdered in Washington.

Venezuela's president, Hugo Chávez, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. He spoke the day after the president of the United States. He held up a book by Noam Chomsky and urged the hall to read it. The talk made world headlines within hours.

He calls the American president the Devil and says the rostrum still smells of sulphur. He charges the United States with seeking world rule through war. He lists Iraq, Lebanon, and Palestine as proof. Venezuela offers four fixes for the United Nations. The Security Council should grow, the veto should end, and the Secretary-General should gain strength. He also presses Venezuela's bid for a Council seat.

President John F. Kennedy of the United States addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 1963, his last speech to the body. A treaty banning nuclear tests in air, space, and sea had just been signed. Near one hundred states had joined it. The Cuban crisis of the year before had eased.

He calls the test ban a first small step, not peace itself. More steps should follow: guard posts against surprise attack, curbs on the spread of nuclear arms, a ban on weapons in space. He floats a bold thought. Why should the first trip to the moon be a race? The two rivals could send a joint crew instead. He closes with world health, hunger, and rights.

Sri Lanka's president, Mahinda Rajapaksa, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. His country had fought the LTTE rebels for over twenty years. A truce had broken down and attacks had grown again. He had won office the year before on a pledge to seek an honourable peace.

He calls terror a curse tied to drugs, guns, and dirty money. He lists rebel crimes: suicide bombs, massacres, child soldiers, whole villages driven out. His government still offers talks and a political fix through new basic-law plans. Force alone, he says, cannot end the war. He reports strong growth and thanks the world for help after the tsunami.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
Michelle Bachelet, president of Chile, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006. She had taken office that year as Chile's first woman president. Her speech came during the yearly general debate, when heads of state set out their world views in turn.

Bachelet pressed the case for social justice at home and across the globe. She spoke of fair growth, strong public services, and respect for human rights. She also backed reform of the UN itself. The address shows a new Latin American leader claiming a place on the world stage.

Hugo Chávez, president of Venezuela, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006, one day after George W. Bush spoke in the same hall. Chávez opened by saying the podium still smelled of sulfur, a jab at Bush, whom he called the devil. The line drew laughs, gasps, and headlines worldwide.

Beyond the theater, the speech attacks United States power and the Iraq war. It calls for a rebuilt UN, seated away from American soil, and for a fairer world order. The address endures as the most quoted act of defiance ever staged in that hall.

John F. Kennedy returned to the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 1963, for the last major foreign speech of his life. Two months later he was dead in Dallas. Weeks before this address, the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union had signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in air and space.

Kennedy hailed the test ban as a first step away from nuclear fear. He urged further curbs on arms and joint work in space, even a shared trip to the Moon. The speech captures a brief thaw in the Cold War, in the speaker's own hopeful terms.

Mahinda Rajapaksa, president of Sri Lanka, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006. He spoke as his government's war with the Tamil Tiger rebels was heating up again after a failed truce. Within three years that war would end in a bloody final offensive.

Rajapaksa defended his government's fight against the Tigers, whom he called terrorists. He asked the world to back states facing armed separatist groups. He also spoke on poverty and fair trade. Read today, the speech is the public case he made abroad while the war at home grew harsher.
europmc-pmc10817020:
Zhang and Dhalla review how swelling signals drive heart and vessel disease in this 2024 paper. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of illness and death around the world. Certain cytokines, which are small proteins that carry signals between cells, stir up swelling, called inflammation. Three of the most studied are interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor, and the interleukin-1 family.

The review traces how these signals interact with cell stress and calcium handling inside heart cells. It covers their roles in blocked arteries, blood clots, heart attacks, and heart failure. It also covers rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heartbeat. Proof from lab and clinic work shows these signals matter, the authors say. Whether they can serve as warning markers or drug targets is still unclear, so they call for more research.
europmc-pmc11126520:
GBD 2021 Causes of Death Collaborators break down 288 causes of death worldwide from 1990 to 2021 in this 2024 study. Regular, detailed reporting on why people die is fundamental for public health choices. Such counts also show how each cause lifts or drags life expectancy. They matter most after large death spikes such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

The analysis drew on 56,604 data sources in total. They included death registration, verbal autopsy, surveys, and cancer registries, the team reports. Verbal autopsy means interviewing families about a death's symptoms. Most cause-specific death rates were fitted with an ensemble model that blends several models. Counts cover 204 countries and 811 subnational locations by age and sex. Years of life lost were estimated for each cause. The authors say the comparisons reveal each cause's true weight.
europmc-pmc1308820:
Abernethy and co-authors validated a revised performance scale for palliative care in 2005. The Karnofsky scale is the standard for patient function. A community-focused variant suited palliative settings better. Their Australia-modified version blends both scales for any care setting.

All three scales were scored for 306 trial patients in South Australia. Ratings totaled 1,600 timepoints across settings. The median score was 60 on all three scales. The new scale agreed with the original in 87 percent of ratings. Most disagreements sat within one level on the 11-level scale. Kappa values backed the strong agreement between scales.
europmc-pmc1326220:
Fournier and co-authors compared genomes of a drug-resistant hospital bacterium in 2006. A. baumannii was drug-sensitive in the 1970s. It is now a major hospital infection threat worldwide. Two strains were sequenced: an epidemic resistant strain and a susceptible one.

The resistant strain genome measured about 3.9 million base pairs. It held an 86,000-base resistance island, the largest then known. Forty-five resistance genes clustered inside that island. The susceptible strain, linked to body lice, lacked the island. Fournier shows resistance arrived as one large acquired block. The work used full genome reads of both strains.
europmc-pmc1351920:
Hotez and co-authors argued for joining tropical disease control to big disease programs in 2006. Global funds had surged for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. Together those three cause 5.6 million deaths yearly. They also drain 166 million disability-adjusted life years per year.

Neglected tropical diseases overlap the same poor populations. Three billion people live on under two dollars a day. The authors propose a rapid-impact package delivered alongside big-three programs. Shared delivery could cut costs and widen reach. Hotez argues success against the big three may require fighting neglected diseases too.
europmc-pmc1440920:
Some RNAs do work in the cell rather than code for proteins. Pedersen and co-authors swept the human genome for such folded RNAs in 2006. They compared our DNA with that of seven other species, from chimp to puffer fish. Their method scores shapes that stay alike across species, a sign the shape does a job.

The sweep found about 48,000 candidate structures. It caught many known working RNAs, plus 169 fresh candidates for microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune genes. Some hits may guide chemical edits to RNA or help insert a rare building block. Pedersen warns some hits are false, but the list gives labs clear leads to test.
europmc-pmc1464820:
A gene tree and a species tree can tell different stories. Degnan and Rosenberg explored that clash in 2006. As species split, gene copies sort by chance, so a gene's history may not match the species path. They used a chance-based model of that sorting.

Their proof holds for any species tree with five or more species. For some branch lengths, the most likely gene tree differs from the species tree itself. Degnan warns that picking the most common gene tree can thus give a wrong answer with growing data. The pair close with ways to dodge this trap in genome studies.
europmc-pmc1538620:
Claudins seal the gaps between cells, and their levels shift in cancer. Hewitt, Agarwal, and Morin surveyed the whole family in 2006. They tracked all 21 human claudin genes across 266 normal and cancer tissues, using a large public database plus lab tests.

Most claudin genes spoke more softly in cancer. Three, CLDN3, CLDN4, and CLDN7, spoke louder in many cancers, including pancreas, bladder, ovary, and colon. CLDN5 ran high in blood vessel lining, a possible target for drugs that starve tumors. Hewitt flags CLDN18 as a candidate marker for stomach cancer. The survey covered the whole claudin family, in healthy tissue and in cancers.
europmc-pmc1550420:
Tiny gene tuners called microRNAs go awry in colon cancer. Bandrés and co-authors measured 156 of them in 2006, comparing tumors with nearby healthy tissue. Only a few microRNAs had known jobs, yet changed levels had been tied to cancer growth.

Thirteen microRNAs differed clearly between tumor and healthy tissue. The strongest shifts hit miR-31, miR-96, miR-133b, miR-135b, miR-145, and miR-183. Levels of miR-31 also tracked the tumor's stage. Bandrés suggests the microRNA pattern could help predict how colon tumors behave and how patients fare.  Such profiles may also help separate tumor subtypes that behave in unlike ways.
europmc-pmc1637120:
Grouping proteins into working modules from interaction webs is a crowded craft. Brohée and van Helden benchmarked four clustering algorithms in 2006. Interaction data carry false links and missing links, so tools must be robust.

They built a test web from 220 known yeast complexes, then made 41 warped versions by adding or cutting links. Four methods, MCL, RNSC, SPC, and MCODE, were run at varied settings. The team measured how sensitive each was to its parameters and to noise. Brohée gives users a grounded guide for picking settings instead of trusting defaults.
europmc-pmc1851020: Potential and utilization of thermophiles and thermostable enzymes in biorefining. — a 2005 science paper on heat-loving germs for fuel. It reviews the thermophile uses. The paper is the thermophile review: the findings on biorefining, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc1895920: Mapping human whole-brain structural networks with diffusion MRI. — a 2005 science paper on brain network maps. It maps the whole-brain networks. The paper is the brain-map study: the findings on structural nets, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1978520: Causal inference in multisensory perception. — a 2005 science paper on cause-and-effect in senses. It studies the causal inference for labs worldwide. The paper is the inference study: the findings on multisensory ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2323620: Space and the parietal cortex. — a 2008 science paper on space and the parietal cortex. It maps the space processing. The paper is the space study: the findings on cortex ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2394820: Iterative model building, structure refinement and density modification with the PHENIX AutoBui — a 2008 science paper on PHENIX model building. It builds the iterative models. The paper is the building study: the findings on PHENIX ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2467420: Standardized cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) protocols, society for cardiovascu — a 2008 science paper on standard heart scans. It sets the standard scans for labs. The paper is the scan study: the notes on heart ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2467520: Determination of absolute structure using Bayesian statistics on Bijvoet differences. — a 2008 science paper on crystal structure math. It determines the absolute structure. The paper is the math study: the findings on Bijvoet ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2518220: The pilocarpine model of temporal lobe epilepsy. — a 2008 science paper on the pilocarpine epilepsy model. It guides the pilocarpine model. The paper is the pilocarpine guide: the findings on epilepsy, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2527820: VEGF expression by mesenchymal stem cells contributes to angiogenesis in pancreatic carcinoma. — a 2008 science paper on VEGF-driven vessel growth. It finds the VEGF contribution. The paper is the vessel study: the findings on pancreatic ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2535620: Season, sex, age, and education as modifiers of the effects of outdoor air pollution on daily m — a 2008 science paper on pollution-death modifiers. It studies the season/sex modifiers. The paper is the modifier study: the findings on pollution, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2565420: The basal ganglia and motor control. — a 2008 science paper on the brain's movement hub. It covers the movement control for labs. The paper is the hub study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2575520: Global transcriptome analysis reveals circadian regulation of key pathways in plant growth and — a 2008 science paper on plant circadian transcriptomes. It reveals the circadian regulation. The paper is the reveal study: the findings on plant ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2630720: Antimicrobial drug use and resistance in Europe. — a 2008 science paper on European antimicrobial use. It studies the drug resistance. The paper is the resistance study: the findings on antimicrobial ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2631520: Regularized gene selection in cancer microarray meta-analysis. — a 2008 science paper on gene selection. It regularizes the gene selection. The paper is the selection study: the findings on cancer ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2638020: Large-scale structural analysis of the classical human protein tyrosine phosphatome. — a 2008 science paper on the phosphatome. It analyzes the large-scale structure. The paper is the phosphatome study: the findings on protein ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2656620: Virulent clones of Klebsiella pneumoniae: identification and evolutionary scenario based on gen — a 2008 science paper on nasty Klebsiella twins. It names the nasty twins for labs. The paper is the twin study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2667420: The incidence of co-morbidities related to obesity and overweight: a systematic review and meta — a 2008 science paper on obesity co-morbidities. It reviews the systematic evidence. The paper is the review study: the findings on obesity ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2771920: Glioblastoma subclasses can be defined by activity among signal transduction pathways and assoc — a 2008 science paper on brain-tumor subtypes. It sorts the tumor subtypes for labs. The paper is the sort study: the notes on tumor ills, filed here in full session today.
aitareya-brahmana-keith-1920:
Arthur Berriedale Keith translated the Aitareya Brahmana for the Harvard Oriental Series in 1920. The Aitareya is the old ritual manual of the Rigveda's priests. Keith's volume also includes the Kausitaki Brahmana, a sister text.

The manual walks priests through the great soma rites, chant by chant. Myths appear strung through the rules, explaining why each rite matters. The Kausitaki covers similar ground from a related priestly school. Together they show how India's earliest grand rites were actually performed. Keith was among the leading Sanskritists of his generation. His translation remains the standard English access to these difficult prose texts.
whitbourne-discovery-newfoundland-1620:
Richard Whitbourne, a Devon sea captain, wrote A Discovery of New-found-land in 1620 to promote English settlement there. He knew the island from years of fishing voyages. His tract praises the colony's wealth in cod, timber, and safe harbors for ships.

Whitbourne also reports a famous sight. He describes a mermaid that swam up to his boat and looked at the crew. That account became the classic English colonial mermaid story. The wonder sits atop a practical sales pitch for Newfoundland. Whitbourne hoped marvels and profit together would draw settlers and backers across the Atlantic.
plos-pone-0004920:
Proteins often gain small chemical tags called methyl groups after they are built. Those tags change how proteins work in gene reading and DNA repair. Finding the exact tag sites in the lab is slow and costly. Jianlin Shao and co-authors presented a computer method in PLOS ONE in 2009. It predicts methylation sites from protein sequences alone.

Their approach extracts features from each side of a candidate site. It then feeds them into a Bayes-based predictor. The goal is a fast first map of likely sites. Biologists can use the map before spending time and money on experiments. Tools like this turn raw sequence data into testable leads.
plos-pone-0005020:
HIV builds new particles at the cell membrane. The work happens at fatty patches rich in a specific lipid. Alexia Harrist and colleagues studied a host helper there. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The helper is a protein called Anx2. It meets the viral Gag protein at those patches.

The meeting takes place in lipid rafts containing phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate. Anx2 increased viral production in 293T cells. The handshake is a real cog in HIV assembly. Blocking it could slow the virus's escape from cells. The study also matters beyond HIV. It shows how viruses borrow host proteins to finish building themselves.
plos-pone-0005120:
Most new cancer drugs aim at existing targets. Finding fresh targets needs a smarter hunt. Elizabeth Iorns and colleagues combined three kinds of data in PLOS ONE in 2009. They ran RNA interference screens that silence genes one by one. They added gene expression data. They added genomic data from cancer cells.

The integrated analysis identifies targets that single methods miss. A gene whose silencing kills cancer cells becomes a candidate. Expression and genome data test whether it matters in real tumors. The pipeline surfaces credible targets faster. It offers a sharper roadmap for drug discovery. The approach generalizes beyond one cancer type. Any field drowning in single-omics data can borrow the logic.
plos-pone-0005220:
Crossing two plant lines often yields offspring that outgrow both parents, a boost called heterosis. Breeders would love to predict which crosses will shine before making them. Gärtner and colleagues improved that prediction in PLOS ONE in 2009 by joining two kinds of markers.

DNA markers show which gene forms a plant carries, while metabolic markers show its chemistry in action. Using both together forecast hybrid vigor better than either alone. Better forecasts save seasons of field trials and help breeding programs focus on the most promising crosses. In the long run, sharp forecasts like these mean less land, less seed, and less time spent on crosses that were never going to pay off.
plos-pone-0005320:
New neurons are born in the adult hippocampus and take six to eight weeks to mature. During that long youth, they have distinct electrical traits that may give them a special role. Mongiat and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that these immature neurons can be reliably activated.

Young neurons were proposed to matter for hippocampal signal processing precisely because they respond differently. Reliable activation means they are not idle bystanders while they grow. The finding supports a real function for newborn neurons in the adult brain's memory circuits. New brain cells are few and short-lived if they do not join a working circuit. So proof that a young cell can fire in step with its peers is a key step in the tale.
plos-pone-0005920:
A coach's pep talk is meant to lift a player, but does it change what the player sees? Manuel Martín-Loeches, Alejandra Sel, Pilar Casado and colleagues asked that question in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They tested how encouraging and discouraging phrases affect the brain and the way people direct visual attention.

Hearing such phrases first, the team reports, shifts brain activity and alters where visual attention goes next. Words of praise or blame thus reach further than mood alone. They tune the eyes for the task that follows. The result matters for sports and other contests where a few words can shape how well someone performs.
plos-pone-0006020:
Some germs travel hidden inside the very cells sent to kill them. Jan Rupp, Lisa Pfleiderer, Christiane Jugert and colleagues caught one such trick in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies Chlamydia pneumoniae, a common cause of lung infections, and its passage through neutrophils, white blood cells that die soon after eating a germ.

Inside a dying neutrophil, the germ stays silent and safe, the team reports. When macrophages clear the dead cell away, they take the hidden germ in too, and so spread it. A Trojan horse route like this helps explain how the germ settles in for long-term lung trouble, and where treatment might cut the ride short.
plos-pone-0006120:
Turning an object over in the mind is a skill Alzheimer's disease erodes. Cassandra Adduri and Jonathan Marotta asked in 2009 whether faces suffer the same loss. Their PLOS ONE paper tests mental rotation of faces in healthy aging and in Alzheimer's disease, extending a literature that had largely ignored faces in favor of plain objects.

Faces are the objects people read most, so a face-specific deficit would touch daily life directly. Comparing patients with healthy older adults parts the disease's effect from age itself. The work refines how visuospatial decline is measured, using the one class of image whose loss patients are likeliest to feel.
plos-pone-0006220:
Herceptin helps many breast cancer patients whose tumors make too much of the Her2 growth switch. Long Gu, Sarah Waliany, and Susan Kane studied two related proteins that pull against each other, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Darpp-32 and its shortened variant, t-Darpp, affect both tumor growth and drug resistance.

Up to seven in ten Her2-positive cancers respond to Herceptin-based treatment, but resistance often follows. The two protein forms push outcomes in opposite directions, the authors report. Measuring which form dominates could help predict who will keep benefiting. The pair may also offer a target for restoring the drug's effect.
plos-pone-0006720:
Wei Sun and colleagues studied two genes that help the plague bacterium cause disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is Yersinia pestis, the agent of plague. It uses a molecule called ppGpp to adjust growth to conditions. That system is highly conserved across bacteria. The genes relA and spoT help control the system in many species.
