Punch, the London Charivari, volume one hundred and fifty-nine, is dated December 29, 1920. A joke notes fines for speeding, yet no official joke was made. It asks why Mr. Justice Darling never gets a case like this. Another item tells of a New York policeman caught moving a safe.

Caught in the act, he offered to run and fetch a burglar. Such brief gags fill Punch's famous short paragraphs each week. The 1920 volume shows Britain joking again after the Great War. Readers get a year-end slice of Punch wit, light and sharp.
20779-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A sailor fined twenty shillings opens the October 27, 1920 Punch in a droll court tale. He had refused to join his ship, blaming a rat as big as a cat in his cabin. The court replied that only officers may claim rats in the cabin.

Punch in 1920 kept its old trade of jokes, verse, and cartoons on public life. The war was past, but its shadow still touched the fun. This single weekly issue holds one slice of British humor at a set date. Readers can track how the famed magazine met a changed world with its wit intact.
21002-the-writings-of-thomas-jefferson-l:
Clear thought, tact, and force of appeal win respect in all ages, this Jefferson volume notes. Yet many able men lack balance and fall prey to their feelings, it warns. Volume six of the Library Edition of Jefferson's writings holds such musings.

Letters and papers from Jefferson's rich middle years fill this sixth of twenty volumes. The Thomas Jefferson Memorial Association issued the set in 1903-04. Statecraft, farming, books, and friendship share his tireless pen here. Readers meet Jefferson whole, not just the sage of set phrases, in the daily grain of his own words.
20392-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London humor magazine, filled its pages with jokes, cartoons, and light verse on the news of the week. This issue, dated November 24, 1920, belongs to volume 159. Its writers poked fun at politics, fashion, and foreign affairs alike.

One joke takes up a claim from the United States Bureau of Standards. The bureau said the jaw's pressure while chewing reaches eleven tons to the square inch. Punch wonders if this is crude propaganda work on behalf of the American bacon trade. The quip shows the magazine's dry way with official news.
arxiv-2601-06620:
Gui-Qiang Chen and two co-authors prove a big result on flows with a vacuum edge in 2026. The flow laws are those for a thick fluid that can be squeezed. Their case has round symmetry and starts from large, rough data.

How such flows act over all time with vacuum is key to thick flows. A true vacuum edge moves and speeds up in a set way at its rim. It shows up in the flow of thin sheets of water, they note. Large-data cases in more than one dim had stayed open till now. Two blocks made them hard: a flaw at the core point and wear at the edge. Their proof deals with both blocks for the round case. It is a mark in the study of flows that meet empty space.
arxiv-2601-07520:
Mara Pompili and Daniel Smertnig study when certain algebras have unique factorization, using a computational approach. Their 2026 preprint covers locally acyclic cluster algebras and their class groups. Class groups measure how far a ring is from having unique factorization. To make progress, the authors introduce a new class of rings called finite Laurent intersection rings.

These new rings include several known families. Among them are locally acyclic cluster algebras, full-rank upper cluster algebras, and some generalized upper cluster algebras. Laurent phenomenon algebras also fit inside the class. A single framework lets results proved once apply across all these settings. The paper should interest algebraists who study cluster algebras and factorization theory together.
arxiv-2601-07820:
Manar Ali and colleagues test whether language models ask for clarification when they should. In human conversation, both sides work to maintain shared understanding. A listener who is unsure can request clarification. The authors ask whether models can play that listener role. Their 2026 preprint uses reference games, tasks where a description must pick out a target. Uncertainty in such games is natural and measurable.

The testbed links model uncertainty to clarification requests. A well-aligned model should ask more when its uncertainty is high. Asking too little risks confident errors; asking too much burdens the user. Reference games give clean scores for that balance. The paper speaks to scholars in dialogue systems and human-computer interaction. It treats clarification as a skill to measure, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2601-08020:
Layton A. Hall and Samuel Alperin revisit self-imaging, the periodic reappearance of a wave's pattern as it travels. Self-imaging is a hallmark of paraxial, quadratic-wave evolution. Across two centuries of realizations, uniform recurrence planes along the axis were considered fundamental. The pattern was assumed to repeat at evenly spaced planes. Their 2026 preprint introduces canonical clocks and hidden geometric freedom in this setting.

Challenging the uniformity assumption opens new designs for optical systems. If recurrence planes can be placed with more freedom, imaging devices gain flexibility. Canonical clocks give a principled way to describe the timing of recurrences. The work blends optics history with modern geometry. The paper serves scholars in wave optics and mathematical physics. It shows a textbook phenomenon still has structure left to find.
arxiv-2601-07720:
Peihang Wu extends bundles over the boundary forms of Shimura varieties, in a 2026 preprint on pure math. Shimura varieties are shapes in geometry at the heart of modern number theory. Their integral canonical models extend them over bases from number theory. Toroidal forms add boundary layers so the spaces become complete. Wu builds canonical extensions of principal bundles over these forms.

The bundles involved carry level structure fixed at a prime p, of hyperspecial type. Automorphic vector bundles, which code automorphic forms in geometric terms, also get extensions. Such extensions let scholars study how the bundles decay at the boundary. That matters for the arithmetic of Shimura varieties and their cohomology. The paper serves those who work on arithmetic geometry. It supplies foundational constructions that later work on these spaces will use. The work is base work: dry on its face, yet much later work will stand on it.
arxiv-2601-08620:
Antonio Loison and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a test for search-aided AI writing. The test is called ViDoRe V3. The systems in view are Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines, or RAG. A RAG system finds source texts first, then writes a reply based on them. Real work puts hard demands on such a system. It has to take in visual parts like tables, charts, and images.

It must join facts from more than one source. It must ground each claim in a source a reader can check. Past tests miss much of that strain. They tend to use text alone, or a single source. They can grade the search step and the writing step apart from each other. ViDoRe V3 grades the full pipeline in hard, real-world cases. Teams that build search tools for firms gain a tougher test of what they ship.
arxiv-2601-08920:
Md. Jahidul Islam builds a tool to merge health scans of more than one type into one clear view. One scan may show bones well. The next may show soft tissue well. A merged view can guide a doctor more than each scan on its own. Past merge tools trade off: they keep broad match high, but lose fine local form.

His tool is called W-DUALMINE. It uses two expert paths, one for each type of scan fact. Each path is weighed by how much trust its input earns. The merge also keeps the link stats of the source scans safe. A reader in health scans gets a merge plan that aims for both broad truth and fine form.
arxiv-2601-09020:
Larissa Inacio and four co-authors study a faint pull between things in salt water, and what it means in a cell. The pull is the Casimir effect, a force from wave noise in the gap. Salt was thought to screen it fast. The team shows a shared part of the pull that salt does not screen. It reaches far past what past work thought.

That far reach holds at the spans found in a cell, such as gaps near actin strands. It may shift how strands pull and push in the cell frame. A reader in bio physics gets a force they may have set to zero too soon. In salt water, faint wave pulls can act at cell scale.
arxiv-2601-09120:
Chen-Wei Liang and three co-authors build a chain to draft patent claims in more than one land's form. A claim is the part of a patent that sets what it guards. Draft tools fail on three points. They bend poor to new lands. They miss how a claim ties to past art. And their grade of a draft can not be trusted.

Their chain has three stages. Stage one weighs how the new claim ties to past art. Stage two drafts in the form of the target land. Stage three grades the draft by one shared scale. A reader in law tech gets a chain built for cross land work, with grades a team can check.
arxiv-2601-09320:
William Dorrell and Peter Latham ask how the wiring of brain like nets sets what they can learn. Such nets show in more than one brain zone, and in the smell path of bugs and the sense path of a fish. In all, a thin input fans out to a vast mid layer. A last layer then reads the fanned code to sort inputs.

They use a kernel slope tool to map wire form to learn skill. Kernel here means a fixed math view of how inputs match. If wire form sets that view, we can call what a net can learn from its wires. A reader in brain work gets a test case where that call may be made in full.
arxiv-2601-09520:
Pierfrancesco Melucci, Paolo Merialdo, and Taketo Akama work on teaching machines to write down drum parts. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets automatic drum transcription, turning audio into MIDI notes for each drum hit. Deep learning leads the field, but it needs large paired audio-MIDI datasets, which are scarce.

Synthetic data is the usual workaround, yet it often sounds fake. Cheap SoundFont libraries lack the acoustic variety of real kits, leaving a domain gap. The authors aim for more realistic synthetic data to close that gap. Better training data would make transcription work on real recordings, not just clean studio stems.
arxiv-2601-09620:
Pooja Prajod and six co-authors ask whether telling readers more about AI use in news helps or hurts trust. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies how the level of detail in AI disclosures shapes readers' trust. Newsrooms face growing calls to be open about machine help.

Recent studies point to a transparency dilemma: disclosure itself can lower trust. The authors test how much the fine print matters, from a bare label to a fuller account. The answer guides editors who must be honest without scaring readers off. It also informs rules now being drafted for AI in media.
arxiv-2601-10420:
Kirill Melnikov, Ivan Novikov, and Ivan Pedron rebuild smooth curves from Monte Carlo runs. In high energy work, a curve is oft made by binning chance events in a chart. Binning yields a jagged curve. Fine traits can hide in the steps. Each bin holds few events at the tails.

The team use a new path. They fit the curve as a sum of smooth base forms. The weights come from the same chance run. No binning is used. The fit is smooth by build. It gives a clean curve from one run of events. That helps labs read tails and peaks with more trust.
arxiv-2601-10520:
Felix Jahn and co authors build a safe AI frame that can hold more than one value set. Agents now act on their own in grave tasks. Their calls must be both sharp and right in a moral sense. Past frames oft rest on one set of values for all. That set may not fit all users or lands.

The frame is named GRACE. It is a neuro symbolic build: nets join rule based steps. It works from reasons, not just rules. Each call can be traced to the reasons that drove it. The aim is an agent whose acts can be checked and fit to the case.
arxiv-2601-10820:
Himanshu Thakur and co-authors aim to make ML feature engineering more reliable by planning with LLM agents. Code models can now write feature code on their own. Yet real ML teams adopt them slowly. One gap is the lack of datasets that capture how feature work proceeds in production, step by step and revision by revision.

Another gap is weak integration of agents like Copilot and Devin with team habits and needs. The authors frame feature work inside a constrained topology of agents, a planned structure that bounds what each agent may do. Planning and constraint aim to turn clever demos into dependable tools. The work targets teams that want automated features without losing control of quality.
arxiv-2601-11020:
Youmi Ma and Naoaki Okazaki turn a discovery from interpretability into a performance tool. Mechanistic studies found special attention heads, called retrieval heads, that fetch facts from the context. These heads matter when a model must use long inputs. Yet their role in raising performance had not been explored. The authors ask whether retrieval heads can be optimized directly.

If the heads that fetch can be strengthened, long-context skill may rise with them. That would give builders a surgical target instead of blanket scaling. Long documents, code bases, and records all need models that find the right line in a sea of text. The work links the science of reading models to the craft of improving them.
arxiv-2601-11120:
Haonan Yang and co-authors give a broadband study of the Be/X-ray binary pulsar eRASSU J012422.9-724248. The source sits in the Magellanic Bridge, near the Eastern Wing of the Small Magellanic Cloud. The first four all-sky surveys by eROSITA, the soft X-ray instrument on the SRG satellite, revealed it as a new X-ray source.

The team performed timing and spectral analysis across optical and X-ray data. A Be/X-ray binary pairs a neutron star with a hot Be star and its disk. Pulsations clock the neutron star's spin while spectra trace the inflow. Such systems are labs for accretion at extreme rates, and each new one sharpens the census of the Magellanic Clouds' binary population.
arxiv-2601-11820:
Davide Gabrielli and Federica Iacovissi link large deviation theory with a matrix product form. They study long strings of symbols from a finite set. Each string gets a weight from a set of matrices with no negative terms. Rows and cols of the matrices use labels from a finite or countable set.

Large deviation tools track rare events in such systems. The matrix product form gives a compact way to write the weights. Their link helps compute rare event rates in chains with memory. Such chains show up in physics, queues, and bio sequences.
arxiv-2601-12020:
Guillermo Figueroa-Araneda, Iris Diana Jimenez, Florian Hofherr, and their co-authors model how light spreads under the surface of wax, jade, marble, and skin. That spread, called subsurface scattering, gives soft shadows and colour bleed. It is hard to model, since light paths are complex.

Past capture needs more than 100 views and many light setups. Their method, named in the work, adds diffusion priors to multi-view fits. It aims for good results with far less data. Less capture would speed digital doubles for film and design.  Less data per object would cut studio time and cost.
arxiv-2601-12120:
Danielle Tsao, Krikamol Muandet, Frederick Eberhardt, and Emilija Perković warn on how to read instrumental variable results when effects are pooled. Such variables help causal work when trials are too costly or barred. Yet proof that the tool is valid is often hard.

Pooling data can hide who the effect truly covers. Their work asks what the pooled IV estimand means in causal terms. A wrong read can mislead health and policy calls. The study gives a clearer view of what such numbers can claim.  The warning bears on pooled data in health and policy work.
arxiv-2601-12220:
Kaushik Kulkarni and Andreas Klöckner normalize batched Einstein summation terms to a unique form. Such sums, called einsums, are used in finite element work, numeric algebra, and computational chemistry. Batches with the same notation often share much data.

Their algorithm maps each term that is maths-equal to one normal form. A unique form lets code spot reuse and tune runs with care. It can also dedupe work across a batch. The work aids fast maths software in physics codes.  Normal forms also help spot the same sum twice.  Batches with shared data gain most from this step.
arxiv-2601-12320:
Yu-Yue Cui, Rui Chen, and Qi Huang seek molecular pentaquarks made of a ground octet baryon and an excited anti-charmed meson. Pentaquarks are states of five quarks. The meson pair they use is the D1 and D2 star doublet, in anti-charm form.

The baryons span the octet: nucleon, Lambda, Sigma, and Xi. They model how these parts interact to find bound states. Each bound state found is a target for collider searches. The work adds to the map of exotic hadron forms.  Each bound state is a named target for searches.
arxiv-2601-11220:
Rafael Martins Frade, Rrubaa Panchendrarajan, and Arkaitz Zubiaga build tools to spot false claims. Their 2026 preprint is called MultiCaption, on visual claims in many tongues. False content now spreads fast in text, image, and video at once. It also crosses tongues, which makes checks much harder to run.

Fact-check tools have grown, but data lags the real threat. Few data sets join images with claims in more than one tongue. That gap leaves checks weak where harm can spread fast. The team's work targets that gap with a multilingual, visual focus. It aims to help tests that match how false claims now travel.
arxiv-2601-11520:
Mengyuan Zhao, Mael Le Treust, and Tobias Oechtering study coordination over Markov channels. Their 2026 preprint uses the empirical coordination framework. Joint source-channel coding sends data while shaping joint statistics. The channel here is a Markov channel, with memory in its state.

The source is independent, which sets a clean test case. The team asks which joint distributions can be induced. Source and channel symbol statistics are the quantities in play. Encoders are strictly causal and see no past channel states. Each output still drives how the Markov state evolves. The results mark the limits of coding under those rules. Such limits guide code design for channels with memory.
arxiv-2601-13320:
Yasin Demir, Nur Huseyin Kaplan, Sefa Kucuk, and Nagihan Severoglu brighten low light pics with a guide from a classic rule. The Retinex rule splits a pic into light fall and true surface shades. Bright pics from dark ones aid key tasks that run at night. Both rule based and learnt tools do well at the task.

Yet many tools are heavy or need huge train sets. That caps their use in live apps. The team's method, RetinexGuI, steps the light guess in rounds, led by the Retinex split. Each round lifts the guess with less cost. For cam and phone teams, a light tool that runs live has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13420:
A. Safari and co-authors build a compact quantum net node on an optical chip with a curved mirror. The node holds one rubidium atom. The curved mirror both forms the trap for the atom and grabs the light it gives off. That light is the link to the net.

The grab is strong and the link to fibre is clean by build. Sigma polarized photons match the fibre mode with no extra parts. Small flaws or drifts in the rig shift the match but a bit. The team shows both high grab and high atom photon link grade in one small rig. For quantum net teams, a node that is small, firm, and fibre ready is a key step.
arxiv-2601-12520:
Arya Saranathan studies the language of quasigeodesics in group theory. A quasigeodesic is a path in a Cayley graph that is nearly as short as the best path. Fix the error constants, and all such paths form a formal language. A basic question is how complex that language is in the Chomsky hierarchy.

Saranathan shows the language is not context free for certain groups. The groups are non virtually cyclic nilpotent groups and Baumslag Solitar groups. The result holds for any finite generating set, once error constants are large enough. Context free languages sit low in the hierarchy, so the result marks real complexity. It separates hyperbolic groups from some non hyperbolic ones by language type.
arxiv-2601-12720:
Hanbin Wang and seven co authors teach large reasoning models to reflect more effectively. Such models often show self reflective habits, like self critique and backtracking. Those habits can lift performance on complex reasoning tasks. Not all reflection helps, though, since much of it is superficial. Shallow rechecks add compute cost without improving the answer.

The team identify superficial reflection as a distinct problem in these models. They then address it with training aimed at effective reflection. Good reflection should catch real errors and fix weak steps. Teaching that skill could cut wasted tokens in long reasoning chains. The work speaks to labs racing to make reasoning models both smarter and cheaper.
arxiv-2601-12920:
Javier Chico-Vazquez and Christiana Mavroyiakoumou study how a line of flapping flyers can hold its shape. Long lines of the same self driven flyers are unstable by nature. Left alone, such a line will break up in short order. Some form of active control is a must if the line is to last.

One fix is to force a fixed gap between each pair of flyers. The task then is to find the flap plan each flyer should use. The right plan holds the set gap when gusts or wakes push the line. Birds in a line may gain from the wakes of those in front. The same math can guide drone teams that fly in file.
arxiv-2601-14020:
Peng Xu studies the prime spectrum of a family of algebraic objects in a short note from 2026. The objects are VI-modules, which encode representations that grow in a regular pattern. Xu looks at prime Serre ideals of global representations for noetherian families. The spectrum is the set of these primes with a geometric structure.

Xu proves the spectrum for finitely generated VI-modules is homeomorphic to a known space. That space is the one-point compactification of the natural numbers. It differs from the Balmer spectrum of derived VI-modules. The contrast maps how two views of the same family can diverge.
arxiv-2601-14120:
Ion Ciudin and Eugen Ionaşcu study which chords a continuous curve can have in 2026. The curve is a real-valued continuous function on the interval from zero to one. It starts and ends at zero. A chord is a horizontal segment joining two points at the same height.

They describe which chords may appear as isolated points in the chord set. Examples illustrate their characterization of the pattern. They also introduce and analyze maximal Hopf sets. Chord problems are classic in analysis, with roots in a famed theorem on horizontal chords.
arxiv-2601-14320:
Stefan Schoder works on sound simulation in this 2026 paper. His field is computational aeroacoustics, the study of noise made by fluid flow. Coupled field problems often solve the acoustic field with the finite element method. The flow field, though, may come from a finite difference mesh. Data must move between the two grids.

Schoder presents two integration methods for that transfer. One uses high-order Gaussian quadrature to compute the finite element right-hand side. The other maps the flow field with higher-order B-Splines or a Lagrangian function. His topic is convergence: how close the computed right-hand side gets as the transfer sharpens.
arxiv-2601-14720:
Doyun Choi and five co-authors improve social recommendation in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Graph-based social recommendation extends graph collaborative filtering. It leverages graph neural networks to capture multi-hop collaborative signals from user-item interactions. These methods enrich user representations by incorporating social network information. That adds collaborative signals from social relations.

The team's method, PULSE, models socially-aware user representations toward parameter-efficient graph collaborative filtering. Parameter-efficient means strong results with fewer learned weights to train and store. The cost drop counts. Small teams can run a strong shop tool on a lean set of weights. Readers get a recommender design that uses friendship structure for better picks, without the full cost of a giant graph model.
arxiv-2601-15520:
Félix Kahane and Minmin Wang study a ranking produced by Prim's algorithm in a 2026 arXiv paper. They start with a complete bipartite graph. Its edges carry random weights, drawn independently from a uniform law. Running Prim's algorithm then ranks the vertices in an order. The graph's vertices come in two colors, in effect. The authors track the color mix along that ranking.

Their key quantity is a colour ratio. It is the share of black vertices among the first k vertices ranked. How that share behaves as the graph grows is the paper's question. Random weights make the order itself random, so the ratio needs probability tools. Results of this kind clarify how a classic algorithm behaves on random inputs.
arxiv-2601-15620:
Li Zitian and Cheung Wang Chi close a gap in bandit theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is 1-identification, a pure-exploration problem. An agent faces a set of arms, each with an unknown mean reward. A threshold is known in advance. The agent must say whether some arm meets the threshold. If it believes none does, it outputs None. Sampling is costly, so efficiency matters.

Sample complexity counts how many pulls a correct answer needs. The title claims the paper closes the gap on that count. Closing a gap means upper and lower bounds now meet. The problem is fully understood in that sense, up to the stated terms. Identification tasks appear in testing and screening. Knowing the true sampling cost guides how such tests should be run.
arxiv-2601-15720:
Toshiki Sato studies the phase structure of dense quark matter in a 2026 arXiv paper. His setting is lattice QCD in the heavy quark, high-density region. He uses an effective theory where Polyakov loops are the dynamical variables. The Polyakov loop is an order parameter tied to Z3 symmetry. That symmetry is thought to set the basic traits of the phase transition. The transition breaks the symmetry as conditions change.

The paper links this setup to the three-state Potts model. The Potts model is a classic statistical system with the same symmetry. Such links let hard QCD questions borrow tools from simpler models. Phase diagrams of quark matter matter for neutron star physics. They also guide heavy-ion collision programs. Sato's bridge between models is the contribution.
arxiv-2601-15820:
Guoxuan Ding and five co-authors detect fake news that mixes text and images in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal fake news spreads fast and poses a serious societal threat. It keeps evolving, which dates static detectors. It also leans on timely factual details. Detection methods that cannot fetch fresh facts fall behind. Their system is called ExDR. It builds on dynamic retrieval-augmented generation.

Dynamic retrieval triggers keyword-based searches as needed. It pulls in external knowledge during detection. The title adds that retrieval is explanation-driven. Good evidence selection serves both accuracy and efficiency. It also helps explain why a story was flagged. For platforms and fact-checkers, a detector that shows its evidence is far more useful than a bare score.
arxiv-2601-16020:
Weichen Dai, Wenhan Su, Da Kong, Yuhang Ming, and Wanzeng Kong streamline visual odometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Visual odometry estimates motion from camera images. SLAM adds mapping on top of it. Visual foundation models have reshaped both fields. A single feed-forward network can now estimate pose and dense structure. Older pipelines leaned on keyframes: select frames that carry the most value. Newer model-based methods often skip that wisdom.

They process raw image sequences indiscriminately instead. That wastes compute on redundant frames. The authors bring keyframes back into a feed-forward design, per the title. Picking key frames well boosts both efficiency and accuracy. Robots and AR devices run on tight power budgets. Odometry that does more with fewer frames fits their limits.
arxiv-2601-15020:
Andrea Loi and Matteo Palmieri study a natural metric on domains in complex space. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Bergman metric. They ask when that metric is locally symmetric, meaning its curvature looks the same after parallel moves.

Following a strategy from earlier work, they prove two rigidity results. If the Bergman metric is complete, the domain must be symmetric as a whole. Rigidity means the mild local condition forces a strict global shape. Results of this kind help sort complex domains by the shape of their inner geometry.
arxiv-2601-15220:
Anmol Goel, Cornelius Emde, and co-authors report a failure mode they call privacy collapse. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with contextual privacy in language models: a model should keep shared facts in the right context. The team finds that harmless fine-tuning can break that guard.

Even training meant to make a model more helpful can wear privacy down. So can contact with user data, emotional dialogue, or debug code that prints internal values. The patterns are diverse and subtle. The work warns that routine tuning can quietly undo a model's care with private facts.
arxiv-2601-16720:
Samuel Rhys Cox, Jade Martin-Lise, Simo Hosio, and Niels van Berkel study chatbots that show their thought. New bots print short notes on their aims and values. These notes show before the full reply comes. Users now turn to bots for life advice. Their 2026 preprint asks how such notes shape trust and use.

Seeing a bot think can calm or spook a user. It can make weak advice look wise. The team probes how users read these thought notes. Their work can guide the design of help bots. It can also guard users from false faith in bot words.
arxiv-2601-16920:
Ryan Smith, James McLaughlin, and Gert Botha run sims of fast waves in the Sun's air. The Sun's outer air is stacked by gravity's pull. Magnet fields there are patchy, not smooth. Waves in that mix shape heat and storms in space. Their 2026 preprint tracks fast magnetoacoustic waves through it. A plain X-shaped null point sits in their field map.

Null points are spots where the field strength falls to nil. Waves bend, split, and pile up near such spots. The sims show how the stack and patch traits steer waves. Such work helps read scope signs of solar waves. It may sharpen space weather calls in time.
arxiv-2601-17020:
Bagyasree Sudharsan, Alexandria Leto, and Maria Pacheco ask how papers reach past their own field. Cross-field work grows as schools push for it. Past gauges count who wrote a paper, or its words. Those gauges miss how cites are used in the text. A cite may back a claim or be mere decor. Their 2026 preprint builds a frame for that use.

The frame reads what each cite does for the host work. It sorts cites by their role in the chain of proof. Roles show if fields truly blend or just touch. Such reads can guide funds for cross-field work. They may also show which blends bear real fruit.
arxiv-2601-17120:
Chaipat Tirapongprasert and Matthew Ho fix a flaw in how sim-trained tools learn. Such tools train on fake runs drawn from a set range. Sharp range walls break them at the edge. True marks that sit past the wall get lost. Their 2026 preprint draws train runs from a tailed range in place of a walled one. The tails are smooth Gauss curves past each wall.

Edge breaks then fade from the train set. Tools learn marks near and past the old wall. This aids tools that read sky and lab data. Their truth oft sits at a range's edge. Smooth tails cost little and save much grief.
arxiv-2601-17220:
A. A. Poblaguev tests a key tool for proton beam work at a future collider. The tool is the Polarized Atomic Hydrogen Gas Jet Target, called HJET for short. At the RHIC collider, HJET set the scale for proton beam polarization. It gave an absolute measure that other tools could trust. The future Electron-Ion Collider plans to use it too.

The study checks beam-induced loss of polarization in the target. If the beam itself drains the target's spin order, measures would drift. Knowing that effect is key for exact hadron polarimetry at the new machine. The work helps teams plan trusted spin measures for years of runs ahead.
arxiv-2601-17420:
Shiu-hong Kao and four co-authors present CoT-Seg, a method to cut out image regions named in text. The task is called reasoning segmentation. It fails most on hard queries and new image types. The team borrows chain-of-thought, the idea that hard problems need longer thought. Their method thinks in steps before it cuts. It also checks and corrects its own output.

Self-correction gives the model a second pass at weak spots. Long thought helps when a query hides its target in words. Better segmentation aids photo edit, medical scans, and robot sight. The work aims at the messy cases. Those are where simple one-pass tools break down most.
arxiv-2601-17520:
Liwen Jiang and four co-authors present RosettaStone 2.0 for chip design research. Physical design turns logic plans into chip layouts. Fair benchmarks are key to judge new tools. RosettaStone 2.0 gives full RTL-to-GDS reference flows. It covers standard flat designs. It also covers face-to-face hybrid-bonded 3D designs in the Pin-3D style.

Open flows let labs compare tools on the same ground. Without them, each paper's claims stand alone. The framework stresses sustainable and transparent practice. Chip research has long faced a reproducibility gap. Shared flows narrow that gap. They also let small teams test ideas at full scale. The work serves both 2D and 3D design camps.
arxiv-2601-17820:
R. Devaraj and a large team of co-authors report new spectra of a young star and its outflow. Their 2026 preprint uses the MIRI instrument on the JWST space telescope. The target is L1527 IRS, a protostar still fed by infalling matter. The team reads light from the inner region, out to a span of about 500 times the Earth-Sun distance. Outflows and jets are key signs of how such stars grow.

Jets and accretion grow together, so the details of the outflow tell on the feeding process. The spectra cover the bipolar flow that streams from both sides of the young star. Fine readings of that gas can show its heat, speed, and makeup. Such data help test how stars gain mass in their first stages.
arxiv-2601-18020: Pascual Lucas and José-Antonio Ortega-Yagües generalize the notion of a helix in three-dimensional space. Their 2026 preprint defines the new helix by a vector field along the curve. The field keeps a constant angle with a fixed direction, called the axis. The field is F-constant, a condition tied to a chosen frame. The paper works out what curves meet this broader test.
arxiv-2601-18220:
Bingshen Mu and co-authors present a language-model-based forced aligner for speech in many languages. Their 2026 preprint tackles forced alignment, which marks when each word or character starts and ends in a recording. Old methods are built per language and can drift over time, with errors piling up along a file. Speech large language models read many languages and handle long sequences, which suits them to the task. The authors build a non-autoregressive aligner on that base.

Non-autoregressive design predicts the timings in a more global way, which fights drift. One aligner for many languages lowers the cost of subtitles and speech data sets. Long-form speech, from lectures to podcasts, stands to gain most.
arxiv-2601-18320:
Jinwei Lu, Yuanfeng Song, Chen Zhang, and Raymond Chi-Wing Wong build a multi-agent system for data visualization across mixed inputs. Their 2026 preprint presents MultiVis-Agent. Real visualization tasks are messy. They can involve reference images, code examples, and rounds of refinement, far past one-shot text-to-chart generation. Current systems are limited: single-modality input, rigid workflows, and no iteration. The authors use several agents with logic rules to handle the full task in a reliable, comprehensive way.

Logic rules give the agents checks that pure language skill lacks. A team of agents can split roles like reading, drafting, and review. The target is charts that survive contact with real, changing requirements.
arxiv-2601-19020:
Stefano Costa builds an adaptive solver for sound waves bouncing off hard objects. Such scattering problems obey the Helmholtz equation, and the setup here is a sound soft body in open space. Costa reads a classic method, the method of fundamental solutions, through the lens of rational approximation.

That reading yields an automatic way to place the method's helper points, guided by how boundary data extends past the edge. The AAA name in the title ties the scheme to that approximation idea. Automatic placement could spare users the hand tuning that often makes or breaks this classic method.
arxiv-2601-19120:
Guilin Zhang and three co-authors stress test the explanations that chat models give for their picks. Recommender systems now use language models to explain why an item was suggested, reasoning over a user's past acts. Past work graded those explanations for fluency and relevance, less for how they hold up under strain.

Their study, RobustExplain, checks whether explanations stay sound when inputs shift or tricks are tried. An explanation that flips under small changes can mislead users while sounding sure. Robust checks matter more as such agents move into shopping and media feeds used by millions.
arxiv-2601-19220:
Dai Hai Nguyen and three co-authors speed up a method that optimizes several goals over distributions at once. Some problems ask not for one best point but for one best spread of outcomes, measured in Wasserstein space, the geometry of distributions. A recent algorithm walks downhill there for many goals jointly.

Their variant adds Nesterov style acceleration, a momentum trick that speeds classic downhill methods. Faster joint optimization over distributions serves machine learning tasks where the answer is a distribution, like fair sampling or robust training. Speed with the same care for all goals is the point of the work.
arxiv-2601-19320:
Tianyi Chen and seven co-authors keep quantization aware training stable at the lowest bit widths. Such training teaches a model to live with tiny numbers, so it can ship under strict memory and delay limits. At ultra low widths, common shortcuts cause gradient mismatch, shaky training, or heavy overhead.

Their method, StableQAT, targets that instability head on. Stable training at tiny widths would let large models run on small devices without a quality cliff. The prize is real: every bit saved per weight multiplies across billions of weights in modern models.
arxiv-2601-19720:
Gong Gao, Weidong Zhao, Xianhui Liu, and Ning Jia speed up how reinforcement learning agents exploit what they know. Value-based methods learn a score for each action, then act on the best scores. In online learning these methods often exploit too slowly. Weak exploration and delayed policy updates both hold them back.

Their algorithm is called Instant Retrospect Action. One part improves how the value network represents nearby state-action pairs, so small differences are learned crisply. Sharper representations should let the policy commit sooner to good actions. Faster exploitation means less time wasted on moves already known to be poor. The work targets online settings where every interaction costs time or money.
arxiv-2601-20020:
Zhirui Li, Keith D. Levin, Zhiang Zhao, and Vince Lyzinski study matching graphs that change over time. Graph matching pairs up the nodes of two graphs that describe the same objects. Noise corrupts real graphs, so matches must survive errors. The authors consider a sequence of graphs produced by a time-dependent Markov chain noise process.

Their edgelighter model corrupts a base graph step by step, flipping edges with edge-dependent rules. It is a variant of the classical lamplighter random walk. The question is matchability: when can the true pairing still be recovered from the noisy copies? Network de-anonymisation and image alignment both hinge on such guarantees. The work gives the time-varying case a proper theory.
arxiv-2601-20120:
Jovan Krajevski and Biljana Tojtovska Ribarski compare ways of fitting Facebook Prophet, a well known tool for forecasting time series. Prophet ships with two built-in methods. One finds the single best fit for the model. The other samples many fits using a Markov chain method called the No-U-Turn Sampler.

The authors explore further Bayesian methods for the same task, including the approach named in their title, ADVI. Their aim is to see how each method trades speed against a full picture of doubt in the forecast. The work speaks to users who need honest ranges, not just one line, when they plan ahead with Prophet.
arxiv-2601-20320:
Alessandro Colombi studies a sampling problem: deciding whether to keep sampling to find every category whose share passes a set threshold. Data arrive as presence or absence across sampling units, under a Bernoulli product model. The target is the maximum unseen probability, the largest share held by any category not yet seen.

Colombi builds confidence intervals for that quantity. The intervals guide sequential sampling design, where each round of data informs whether another round is worth its cost. Such tools help ecologists, auditors, and survey designers stop sampling at the right time, neither too early nor too late.
arxiv-2601-18620:
Panagiotis Lymperopoulos and four colleagues build CASSANDRA, a tool that learns a model of a world from few facts so an agent can plan in it. Real plans, in shops or firms, hinge on rich cause chains that are hard to learn from data alone. The world is too wide and the facts too thin. But much is known in words about how such worlds work.

CASSANDRA taps that word lore. It asks a large text model to draft light rules for how acts change the world. Chance is kept in the rules, so plans can weigh risk. Light rules built from lore could plan well where a pure data model would starve. The work points to plans that mix book lore with hard facts. Such plans could serve firms that must act on thin data.
arxiv-2601-21320:
Keke Tang, Ziyong Du, Xiaofei Wang, Weilong Peng, Peican Zhu, and Zhihong Tian tackle a trust problem in deep networks. Networks often give very confident answers on inputs unlike anything they were trained on. That overconfidence is dangerous when the system works in the open world.

The authors use geometry from optimal transport to find the zones where classes blur. At those borders, wrong confidence is most likely. They craft training samples near the borders to teach caution. The goal is a network that says it is unsure when it should be. That kind of honesty is vital for safe deployment.
arxiv-2601-21720:
Federico J. Gonzalez brings prior knowledge into the search for equations hidden in data. Data-driven discovery tries to rebuild the governing equation from observations alone. The inverse problem is ill-posed: many distinct equations can fit the same data nearly as well.

That ambiguity blocks a unique answer about the true mechanism. The author builds interpretable networks informed by symmetry, paired with symbolic regression along characteristic curves. Prior structure narrows the field of candidate equations to plausible ones. The payoff is discovered equations that scientists can read, test, and trust, rather than formulas that merely fit.
arxiv-2601-22420:
Roelien Timmer, Necva Bölücü, and Stephen Wan built MetaLead, a hand-checked data set for making leaderboards from papers. Leaderboards rank models and track progress in machine learning. Their 2026 preprint notes that past auto-built sets keep only each paper's best score and cover few fields.

Human curators built MetaLead to be broader and more exact. It can train and test tools that read papers and post their scores. Clear, full boards help the field trust its own progress claims. They also save hours of manual checking. The data set is the product here.
arxiv-2601-22620:
Hyunseo Shin and Wonseok Hwang swap layers between models to spread safety to low-resource languages. Their 2026 preprint notes that safety data are mostly English, so models tuned in other languages tend to be less safe. Those expert models still hold the language skill their users need.

Layer-wise swapping grafts safety traits into them, layer by layer. The aim is safe models that keep their local tongue. That goal matters for fair, global access to AI. The work offers a surgical fix, not a full retrain. It respects both safety and language.
arxiv-2601-21820:
Anson Chen and Jun Zhang look ahead to a new kind of cosmic measurement: gravitational waves bent by gravity itself. When a massive galaxy lenses a gravitational wave signal, the signal can arrive by several paths at different times. Linked with optical images of the lens, those delays can pin down the expansion rate of the universe.

Four-image events are precise but rare, so the authors focus forecasts on the more common two-image events. Their 2026 preprint asks what such events can teach about cosmology and about whether gravitational waves travel exactly as general relativity predicts. The forecasts help planners judge what future detectors could settle, including the long-running dispute over the universe's expansion rate.
arxiv-2601-22020:
Chengyi Cai and co-authors remove private information from multimodal language models. Unlearning should stop a model from revealing private details when someone asks about target images. Existing methods were mostly adapted from text-only unlearning, and they treat every answer token as equally important.

That uniformity is the flaw this 2026 preprint attacks. Some tokens carry the private content, while others are harmless filler. The authors propose visual-guided key-token regularization, which uses the image to identify the tokens that matter and focuses the unlearning there. Precise unlearning matters for privacy law and safety: erase too little and secrets leak, erase too much and the model loses useful skills.
arxiv-2601-22120:
Qian Zhang and co-authors compare two tools grid operators use to stay flexible. High shares of renewable power make net demand ramp steeply up and down. Operators respond either with look-ahead economic dispatch, which plans generation over a coming window, or with ramp products, which pay for standby ramping ability.

Both remedies are widely deployed, but whether they are equivalent under the industry-standard rolling-window dispatch was not well understood. The team's 2026 preprint assesses the two side by side. The comparison matters for market design. If one tool quietly buys less flexibility per dollar, operators across whole regions are overpaying for insurance against the same ramps.
arxiv-2601-20720:
Matej Halinkovic and three co-authors work on how self-driving cars see the road and predict what comes next. Their 2026 paper joins camera images with LiDAR scans. LiDAR measures distance with laser light. The system must do perception and trajectory prediction in one pass from raw sensor data. That end-to-end design is the paper's core aim.

Older designs split the job into modules that pass results along. Errors then grow as they move down the chain. Newer query-based models fix some of this by letting parts share information. Yet how cameras and LiDAR best complement each other in that shared space is still open. The team's method uses gated, deformable fusion to join the two. It speaks to the push for cars that read a scene whole, not in pieces.
arxiv-2601-20820:
Alfio Bonanno and Emiliano Glaviano ask whether gravity can complete a basic field theory at very high energies. Their 2026 paper studies an O(N) scalar theory coupled to gravity in a non-minimal way. A scalar theory describes a simple field with no direction. The O(N) label counts its symmetric copies. Completion in the ultraviolet means the theory stays sound at the smallest scales.

The authors use the Wilsonian functional renormalization group in its proper-time form. They focus on the phase where symmetry is spontaneously broken. There they track how the scalar potential flows with scale. They also follow the non-minimal coupling to curvature as it runs. The study tests whether gravity can tame the theory on its own. It adds evidence to a long debate about quantum gravity's reach.
arxiv-2601-21020:
Emilie Panek and four co-authors weigh a classic trade-off in survey design. Their 2026 paper concerns target selection for the Ariel space mission. Targeted surveys are limited by telescope time. No mission can observe every object of interest. To maximize scientific return, the target list must be chosen with care. Here the objects are exoplanets. The question is how to sample their parameters.

Variety and sample size pull in opposite directions. Many targets in a few classes give depth. Fewer targets across many classes give breadth. The authors find an optimal balance for Ariel's goals. Their method can guide other time-starved surveys as well. The paper is a planning study, aimed at squeezing the most science from a fixed clock.
arxiv-2601-21220:
Alvi Md Ishmam and three co-authors probe a blind spot in the safety of multimodal models. Their 2026 paper presents LAMP, a method for learning universal adversarial perturbations. Multimodal large language models now take multiple images as input. Their vulnerabilities in that multi-image setting remain unexplored. Existing attacks focus on single images. They also often assume a white-box threat model, where the attacker knows the model inside out. That assumption is impractical in many real scenarios.

LAMP learns one perturbation that works across multi-image tasks. It builds on pre-trained models rather than insider access. A universal attack is more worrying than a tailored one. It can be reused broadly without new effort. Mapping such risks early helps defenders harden vision-language systems. The paper extends adversarial research to the multi-image era.
arxiv-2512-01620:
Diego Artacho proves stability results for Einstein metrics with a special spinor. Einstein manifolds solve the vacuum gravity equations. Linear stability asks if small bumps fade or grow. A parallel twisted pure spinor is a strong extra structure on the space.

Artacho shows a large class with non-positive scalar curvature is linearly semi-stable. Mild limits on dimension and spinor rank apply. Such results sort which gravity solutions can persist. They also link spinor geometry to the spectrum of the space in useful ways. Semi-stability is the right bar for such metrics, since fully stable cases are rare and the borderline ones guide moduli questions.
arxiv-2512-01720:
Zongyang Lu and co-authors project pion and kaon structure studies at a future collider in China. The Electron-Ion Collider in China can probe meson inner structure. The Sullivan process in deep-inelastic scattering is the tool. A nucleon emits a meson that the electron then strikes.

The team gives detailed projections for structure functions of both mesons. Those functions map quark momentum inside each meson. Pions and kaons are the lightest mesons, so their structure tests quantum chromodynamics at its base. Projections guide detector design for the collider. Kaon structure lags pion work by far, so paired projections give the collider a two-meson program from its earliest running days.
arxiv-2512-00620:
A Vasil'eva wrote a 2025 pure math paper on Sobolev classes, which are sets of functions sorted by how smooth they are. The setting is a domain whose border follows a Hölder condition, a rule that limits how rough the edge can be. The paper measures widths and entropy numbers for ways these classes sit inside other spaces.

Entropy numbers say, roughly, how well a set can be covered by small balls, and widths say how well it can be approximated. Vasil'eva improves older upper estimates for the entropy numbers. Under some conditions on the parameters, the new rate of decrease is sharper than before.
arxiv-2512-00920:
Jianxiang Zang and seven coauthors audit reward models in a 2025 paper. Reward models score language model outputs and steer training toward safe, helpful behavior. Current evaluations mostly check how well these models perceive preferences in narrow scenarios. That focus can hide how fragile they are in messy real-world settings.

The team's Reward Auditor infers whether a reward model suits deployment when inputs are perturbed, shifted from the clean cases it was tested on. Exposing weak spots before deployment matters, since a flawed reward model can quietly misalign every system trained against it. Suitability checks add a safety gate to model releases.
arxiv-2512-01020:
Jinu Lee and four coauthors introduce LEGIT in a 2025 paper on judging AI legal reasoning. Language models now produce reasoning traces, step-by-step chains of thought, in expert fields like law. Checking the quality of a trace is essential for credibility, yet the reasoning is too complex for simple answer keys.

LEGIT is a large expert-level dataset for legal reasoning, built around legal issue trees. Those trees break a case into its issues and sub-issues, forming a rubric for grading a trace. With many thousands of instances, the dataset lets researchers measure whether a model's stated reasons are sound, not just its final answer.
arxiv-2512-01120:
Timur Gubaev, Philipp Pfeffer, Christian Dreßler, and Jörg Schumacher present a quantum algorithm for an industrial chemistry problem in a 2025 paper. Alkaline electrolyzers split water to make green hydrogen, and their membranes must pass hydroxide ions while blocking other species. Modeling that exchange means solving a diffusion problem.

Their variational quantum algorithm solves one-dimensional diffusion with a diffusion constant that varies across space, matching a multi-layer membrane. Variational algorithms are a leading style for today's noisy quantum hardware. A working solver here would be an early, concrete use of quantum computing in clean energy technology.
arxiv-2601-22820:
Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam and four co-authors tackle drug advice for patients a system has never seen. Large hospital record systems can suggest treatments, but new patients have little history to learn from. That cold-start gap makes early advice shaky and sometimes unsafe.

Their method adapts fast to each new patient, a style called meta-learning, and filters out cases where it is too unsure. Filtering low-trust cases keeps weak advice from reaching doctors as fact. Safer early advice matters most in busy clinics, where new patients arrive daily.
arxiv-2601-22920:
Wulin Xie and six co-authors improve how machines judge image quality the way humans do. Image quality assessment predicts scores that match human opinion of a photo or video. Recent methods use large multimodal models trained with rewards, but they treat all training samples the same.

Some samples give stable predictions and others are noisy, so equal weighting boosts the noisy ones. Their method, Q-Hawkeye, weights training by reliability for steadier learning. Trustworthy quality scores matter for photo apps, streaming, and medical imaging. Reliability weighting addresses the first flaw, while a second flaw concerns models that produce confident scores without stable grounds.
arxiv-2601-23020:
Stefan Schott and four co-authors hunt for risky code hiding inside Java projects. Modern software leans heavily on open-source parts, which saves time and raises quality. The same habit can pull known security flaws into a codebase, sometimes in ways that stay hidden.

Their study uncovers inclusions of vulnerable dependencies in real-world projects. Hidden flaws are dangerous because scanners and audits may report a project as clean. Knowing how flaws sneak in helps teams design checks that actually catch them. Heavy reliance on open-source parts is the root exposure: each included component can carry its known flaws into the product.
arxiv-2601-23220:
Anglin Liu and four co-authors cure a perceptual flaw in medical multimodal models. These models speak fluently about diagnoses, yet the authors find even top systems suffer spatial blindness. They fail to ground answers in objective spatial constraints, producing plausible but wrong claims.

Their Med-Scout post-training uses geometry-aware reinforcement learning to fix the grounding. Training rewarded on spatial fidelity, not just fluent text, should cut visual hallucinations. In medicine, a confident wrong measurement can misdirect real treatment. Geometric fidelity, not linguistic fluency, is the training target, reversing the priorities that produced the blindness.
arxiv-2512-00020:
Guang Yang and a large team review language models for Verilog code generation. Verilog is the hardware description language at the base of electronic design automation. Automating its generation, especially at register-transfer level, has drawn fast-growing research interest.

The review maps the literature and the road ahead for this niche. It weighs data, benchmarks, and methods specific to hardware code, which differs sharply from software. A clear survey helps chip teams judge where language models can assist design today. Register Transfer Level design is the review's focus, the level where hardware behavior is described for synthesis.
arxiv-2512-00520:
Autonomous agents powered by language models are beginning to link up into an Internet of Agents. Juan Wibowo and George Polyzos survey the safety of that vision in 2025. Interconnected agents promise powerful collective problem-solving, but they also introduce novel, systemic risks.

When agents delegate to agents, failures and attacks can cascade in ways single-chatbot safety work never addressed. The authors map the risk landscape and what a safe agent internet would require. Their framing helps builders and policymakers set guardrails before agent networks become critical infrastructure rather than an experiment. Safety here is systemic: one compromised agent could mislead many others. The survey format suits a field whose risks are still being cataloged.
arxiv-2512-03120:
Waves inside Earth's core may move on scales of centuries. Raviraj Narayan Shinde and Ghanesh Narasimhan study such waves in this 2025 work. They start with a single swirling bump of motion in a still, rotating fluid that conducts electricity.

A steady magnetic field cuts across the spin axis in their setup. Past work hints at strong wave motion around the core at high latitudes. The authors test how the field direction changes those magnetostrophic waves. Knowing core waves helps explain how Earth's magnetic field is made and how it shifts over time. Core flows shape the field we measure at the surface, so wave details carry deep clues.
arxiv-2512-03320:
A trace formula links geometry to spectra, like echoes to a hall. Chen Wan proves a new identity of that kind in this 2025 work. The work is motivated by the residue method and recent theory of relative Langlands duality.

The identity compares period integrals of two kinds of spherical varieties. One kind is non-tempered, the other is tempered and tied to a Levi subgroup. Such identities are tools for deep questions about automorphic forms. They can turn hard integrals on one side into simpler ones on the other. Period integrals encode deep arithmetic data, which is why such identities are prized.
arxiv-2512-01820:
Diffusion models create new data by running a noise process backwards, starting from pure noise and ending with a sample that looks real. A 2025 paper by Valentin de Bortoli and four co-authors asks how accurate that backward run is, and how the answer depends on the size of the data.

In practice the true score function that guides the reversal is unknown, so a trained neural network stands in for it, and each approximation adds error. The authors derive an error estimate that does not grow with dimension, a strong guarantee for high-dimensional data. They also work out how to schedule the steps of the process for the best results.
arxiv-2512-01920:
Regression is the branch of machine learning that finds relationships between variables, predicting one quantity from others. Miguel A. Mendez's 2025 chapter, the second in a larger work, opens with a review of the classic tools of the trade, written for readers coming from the natural sciences and engineering.

The chapter situates those tools inside scientific machine learning, where data-driven methods are combined with physical models and principles. Readers get the standard regression machinery first, presented as the foundation for the more advanced methods that follow. As a reference, it serves scientists who want learning algorithms grounded in the subjects they already know.
arxiv-2512-02120:
A classic trick in physics lets a particle gain spin from the field swirling around it, the spin-from-isospin mechanism. Marcelo Oyarzo's 2025 paper studies this effect inside top-down holography, using two supergravity solutions that contain a non-Abelian hedgehog monopole on a two-sphere.

Because the monopole breaks the sphere's symmetry, the background is not invariant under its own rotations, which changes how spin arises. The work connects an old field-theory mechanism to modern holographic models built from string theory. Such connections help researchers translate between the language of gravitational solutions and the quantum systems they describe.
arxiv-2512-02820:
Hishan Farfán-Bachiloglu and two co-authors study weather records from Antofagasta, a desert city in northern Chile. The region is exceptionally arid and stable, with minimal rain and steady patterns. Even so, understanding of local weather dynamics remains limited, the authors note.

Gaps in the record are part of the problem: missing values break standard analysis. The team applies a Q-triplet characterization to the atmospheric time series despite those gaps. Reliable methods for broken records help climate science in remote regions, where instruments fail and long series are precious. Gaps are the norm in far field posts, so a tool that works with gaps earns use far past this one dry town.
arxiv-2512-02920:
Ziniu Zhang and three co-authors predict traffic accidents by joining road maps with satellite views. Earlier prediction leaned on road network structure alone, missing road surface and surroundings. Physical and environmental cues, like lane wear or nearby buildings, carry real risk information.

The team builds a large multimodal dataset across six United States regions, aligned to road graph nodes. Their embeddings also support causal estimation of what drives accidents. Richer inputs could target road fixes where they prevent the most harm, rather than where crashes merely happened last year. Six zones give the test some range. A rule that wins in one town can fall flat on the roads of the next one down the line.
arxiv-2512-03020:
Kehan Qi and four co-authors reinterpret a popular MRI reconstruction method as a flow of probabilities. Magnetic resonance imaging gives superb soft tissue contrast with no ionizing radiation, but scans take long. Under sampling the measurement space speeds acquisition, leaving deep learning to rebuild the image.

Unrolled networks rebuild well, yet their freely learned steps can evolve unstably. Viewing them as conditional probability flows explains and steadies that behavior. A firmer theory of unrolled reconstruction could make fast MRI more predictable for hospitals that depend on it daily. A firm base turns a fast trick into a tool a ward can plan on. Scans must come out right on the worst days, not just the best ones in the test set.
plos-pone-0010020:
Yingxiang Liu, Weishan Chen, Junkao Liu, and co-workers described a new motor design in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ultrasonic motors drive a rotor with tiny vibrations in a stator, set off by the piezoelectric effect. They are prized for simple build, fast response, quiet running, and holding position when power stops.

The design here is a cylinder that uses a traveling wave, built around a cantilever type composite transducer. The authors explain how the drive works and how the parts were shaped to produce it. Such motors suit precise tools and devices where magnetic fields or noise would cause problems.
plos-pone-0010220:
The authors were Parameet Kumar, Manas Sen, Devendra Chauhan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study assessed a DNA test for tuberculosis of the pleura, the lung lining. This form of TB is hard to diagnose, since symptoms are nonspecific. Few bacilli are present, so standard proof, finding the germ itself, often fails in fluid or sputum samples.

The team assessed an N-PCR assay on pleural fluid and sputum collected in tandem. Testing both sample types together may raise the chance of detection. A more reliable test can start treatment sooner for a form of TB that often hides.
plos-pone-0009920:
Most HIV infections enter through mucosal surfaces, yet blood tests miss the local defenses there. Carla Donadoni and colleagues set up methods to measure antibodies in genital fluids. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Setting methods means fixing each lab step so results can be trusted.

Mucosal antibodies are the immune proteins stationed at body surfaces. The samples were seminal and vaginal fluids from HIV seropositive subjects. Cohorts came from Cambodia and Italy, two very different settings. Reliable local measures matter for vaccines meant to block infection at the door.
